topics.title: Foothold
topics.summary: A foothold is the first durable, repeatable point of access an intruder establishes inside a target environment, giving command execution and a base from which further objectives are pursued. It is deliberately distinguished from full compromise: a foothold may be a single low-privileged shell on an internet-facing host, a valid credential pair, a session on a remote access appliance, or code running inside a user's active browser session, and its value lies in reliability rather than breadth. topics.title: GDPR
topics.summary: The General Data Protection Regulation is the European Union legal framework governing the processing of personal data, and it applies to organisations established in the EU as well as organisations outside the EU that offer goods or services to, or monitor the behaviour of, people in the EU. topics.title: Hardening Baseline
topics.summary: A hardening baseline is an agreed, version-controlled set of secure configuration settings applied to one class of system, such as an operating system build, a container base image, a database or a network device, and used as the reference for provisioning, auditing and drift detection. topics.title: Hardware Security Module
topics.summary: A hardware security module is a tamper-resistant physical device that generates, stores and uses cryptographic keys inside a boundary that never exposes the raw key material to the calling system. topics.summary: A hardware security module is a tamper-resistant device that generates, stores and uses cryptographic keys inside a boundary the host operating system cannot read across. topics.title: Hashing Algorithms
topics.summary: A hashing algorithm maps an input of any length to a fixed-length digest that behaves as a fingerprint: the same input always yields the same digest, a one-bit change produces a completely different digest, and recovering the input from the digest should be computationally infeasible. topics.title: HIPAA
topics.summary: HIPAA is the United States federal law that governs the privacy and security of protected health information, and its security obligations are expressed through the Security Rule together with the Privacy Rule, the Breach Notification Rule and the Transactions and Code Sets Rule. topics.title: HMAC
topics.summary: HMAC is a keyed message authentication construction defined in FIPS 198-1 and RFC 2104 that wraps an unkeyed hash function in a specific two-pass structure using inner and outer padding constants. topics.title: Honeypot
topics.summary: A honeypot is a decoy system, service, account or file with no legitimate production purpose, placed where it should not be touched, so that any interaction is suspicious by construction and produces high-signal, low-noise detection. topics.title: Host Firewall
topics.summary: A host firewall is a packet filtering engine that runs on the endpoint itself, so rules can be written against that machine's interfaces, programs, users and services rather than only against network addresses. topics.title: Human Risk Management
topics.summary: Human risk management is the practice of measuring and reducing the chance that ordinary working behaviour leads to a security incident, rather than treating staff as a blameworthy weakest link. topics.title: IAM Policy
topics.summary: An IAM policy is a structured document that grants or denies permissions to a principal in a cloud platform, evaluated by the provider's authorisation engine on every API call. topics.title: Identity Governance
topics.summary: Identity governance is the set of processes and controls that decide who should hold which access, prove that the access remains appropriate, and remove it when the reason for it disappears. topics.title: IDS and IPS
topics.summary: An intrusion detection system monitors network or host activity and raises alerts on behaviour that matches known attack signatures, deviates from a statistical baseline, or violates an explicit policy, while an intrusion prevention system sits inline and can drop the offending traffic in real time. topics.title: Immutable Backup
topics.summary: An immutable backup is a copy of data that cannot be modified or deleted for a defined retention period, even by an identity that holds administrative rights over the source system. topics.title: Incident Response Playbook
topics.summary: A playbook in security operations is a documented, versioned procedure that specifies how a defined class of alert or incident is handled, from the first acknowledgement through to closure and follow-up. topics.title: Indicators of Attack
topics.summary: An indicator of attack describes the behaviour and intent of an adversary during an intrusion rather than a fixed artefact left behind. topics.title: Indicators of Compromise
topics.summary: An indicator of compromise is a concrete, observable artefact that suggests a system, account or network has already been breached: a file hash, a malicious domain or address, a registry key, a user agent string, an unexpected scheduled task or service, an anomalous account, or a specific line in a log. topics.title: Industrial Control System
topics.summary: An industrial control system, or ICS, is the combination of hardware, software and communication networks that directly monitor and drive a physical process, such as a water pump, a turbine or an assembly line. topics.title: Infostealer
topics.summary: An infostealer is malware whose primary purpose is to harvest and exfiltrate credentials and other valuable data from an endpoint quickly and with minimal footprint. topics.title: Infrastructure as Code Scanning
topics.summary: Infrastructure as code scanning is the automated static analysis of declarative infrastructure and configuration definitions, such as cloud resource templates, Kubernetes manifests, container build files, serverless definitions and policy bundles, looking for misconfigurations that would create security exposure when the code is applied. topics.title: Infrastructure as Code Security
topics.summary: Infrastructure as code security is the practice of treating the definition files that create servers, networks, identities and storage as reviewable, testable artefacts and of enforcing security requirements on them before anything is deployed. topics.title: Insecure Deserialization

topics.title: Insecure Direct Object Reference
topics.summary: An insecure direct object reference is an access control defect in which an application exposes an internal object identifier, such as a database key, file name, invoice number or account identifier, and then serves the object named by the client without verifying that the requester is entitled to it. topics.title: Insider Threat
topics.summary: An insider threat is harm to an organisation caused by someone who already holds legitimate access, such as an employee, contractor, supplier or a partner account, rather than by an external attacker who must first break in. topics.title: ISO 27001
topics.summary: ISO/IEC 27001 is the international standard that specifies requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining and continually improving an information security management system. topics.summary: A jump host, also called a bastion host or jump server, is a hardened intermediary that administrators connect to before reaching systems on a protected network. topics.summary: Kerberos is a network authentication protocol built on symmetric cryptography and a trusted third party, in which a client proves its identity to a service without sending a password across the network. topics.summary: A Kubernetes admission controller is a plugin in the API server request path that inspects or rewrites an object after authentication and authorisation succeed but before the object is persisted to etcd. Mutating controllers may modify the incoming request, for example injecting a sidecar or defaulting a field, while validating controllers can only accept or reject it; mutating controllers run first so that validating ones see the final object. Admission is where policy genuinely becomes enforce

topics.title: Kubernetes Network Policy
topics.summary: A Kubernetes network policy is a namespaced object that declares which pods may send traffic to, or receive traffic from, which other endpoints in a cluster. Rules are written with label selectors rather than addresses, so a policy attaches to a group of pods by label and describes allowed peers, ports and protocols. topics.title: Kubernetes RBAC
topics.summary: Kubernetes role-based access control is the authorisation system that decides whether an authenticated request against the API server is permitted, by matching the requester's identity and group memberships against rules that name API groups, resources and verbs. Permissions are granted through Role objects scoped to a namespace or ClusterRole objects that apply cluster-wide, and they take effect only when bound to a subject by a RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding. topics.title: Lateral Movement
topics.summary: Lateral movement is the progression from one compromised system or identity to others inside the same environment, performed to reach valuable data, higher authority, or a position from which the final objective can be achieved without returning to the internet. It rarely relies on a novel exploit; most real intrusions reuse credentials, sessions and administrative tooling that already exist. Typical mechanisms include interactive remote access over desktop, terminal or remote management protoco

topics.title: LDAP
topics.summary: The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) is an application protocol for accessing and maintaining distributed directory information services, and it remains the directory backbone behind Active Directory, OpenLDAP and most enterprise identity stores. Data is organised as a hierarchical tree of entries, each identified by a distinguished name and described by attributes constrained by a schema, with object classes determining which attributes are permitted. topics.title: Least Privilege
topics.summary: Least privilege is the principle that every user, process, service account and device should hold only the access required to perform its current task, for only as long as that task lasts. It is one of the oldest ideas in computer security, usually traced to the early 1970s, and it underpins most modern control frameworks. Mechanically it is implemented by starting from deny by default and adding permission only in response to a documented need: role based access control groups rights by job fun

topics.title: Lessons Learned Review
topics.summary: A lessons learned review is the structured debrief a team holds after an incident has been contained, in which participants rebuild the timeline, agree on contributing causes and commit to specific changes. It is deliberately blameless: the goal is to find weaknesses in systems, tooling, documentation and decision making, because a culture that punishes individuals causes people to withhold detail and produces a report that no longer matches what happened. topics.title: Living Off the Land Binary
topics.summary: A living-off-the-land binary, commonly shortened to lolbin, is a legitimate, usually signed and pre-installed executable that an intruder abuses to perform an action such as downloading content, executing a payload, compressing data, or establishing persistence, without introducing a file that a signature-based control would flag. topics.title: Log Source Onboarding
topics.summary: Log source onboarding is the engineering process of bringing a new telemetry source into a central logging or security analytics platform so that its events are collected reliably, parsed into a common schema and made usable by detections. It is more than pointing an agent at a server. The work spans scoping which events and fields actually answer questions, sizing and routing the transport path, agreeing a documented transport such as an authenticated syslog or agent channel, writing or tuning

topics.title: Macro Malware
topics.summary: Macro malware is malicious logic delivered inside a document or spreadsheet that uses the host application's built-in scripting facility to execute when the file is opened or when the user enables content. The classic form targets office productivity suites, where a document containing an embedded macro reaches a user as an email attachment, a link to a shared file, or a file hosted on a legitimate service, and relies on social engineering to persuade the recipient to click through the security

topics.title: Malware Sandbox
topics.summary: A malware sandbox is an isolated, instrumented environment where a suspicious file or link is executed and observed, so that analysts can learn what it does without risking real systems. Detonation is the deliberate execution of the sample, and the value comes from the instrumentation rather than the isolation alone: monitored system calls, registry and file changes, process trees, network capture and memory inspection produce a behaviour report that is far more durable than static indicators. topics.title: Mean Time to Detect and Respond
topics.shortTitle: Mean Time to Detect and Respond
topics.summary: Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) is the average elapsed time between the moment a real intrusion begins or a malicious action occurs and the moment a monitoring system or analyst first recognises it as such; Mean Time to Respond (MTTR, sometimes split into time to acknowledge, contain, eradicate and recover) measures the elapsed time from that detection to the point where the incident is contained or resolved. Both are averages over a population of alerts or incidents, so the underlying case definitio

topics.title: Memory Dump
topics.summary: A memory dump is a capture of the contents of a system's physical or virtual memory, preserved as an image file for later analysis. It is the primary source for evidence that never touches disk: running and recently terminated processes, injected code regions, loaded drivers, kernel structures, network connections, command histories, encryption keys and, in many intrusions, the only surviving copy of fileless malware and its configuration. Dumps are taken either from a live host with a trusted a

topics.title: Memory Forensics
topics.summary: Memory forensics, also called volatile memory analysis, is the acquisition and interpretation of a system's random access memory, or RAM, to reconstruct what was happening at the moment of capture. It exists because a large amount of high value evidence never reaches disk: running processes, loaded drivers and kernel modules, open network connections, injected code regions, cached credentials, encryption keys and chat or document contents held by an application. Acquisition must occur while the

topics.title: MFA
topics.summary: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is an authentication control that requires a principal to present evidence from two or more distinct factor categories before a session is granted. The categories are knowledge (something you know, such as a password or PIN), possession (something you have, such as a hardware token, smart card or registered phone), and inherence (something you are, such as a fingerprint or face geometry), with location and behavioural signals sometimes treated as additional cont

topics.title: MISP
topics.summary: MISP is an open-source threat intelligence platform designed for storing, correlating, sharing and consuming structured indicators together with the context that makes them usable. Its central data structure is the event, a container that groups attributes describing an incident, campaign or sighting. Attributes are typed key-value pairs covering network indicators, file hashes and names, email artefacts, registry keys, financial data and free text, and they carry a category, a distribution sett

topics.title: Mobile Device Security
topics.summary: Mobile device security is the set of platform, policy and operational controls that protect smartphones and tablets, and the business data they hold, across a lifecycle of enrolment, daily use, loss, repair and retirement. The technology rests on hardware backed storage encryption tied to a passcode, verified boot and platform integrity checks, application sandboxing, permission mediation and signed application distribution. Because these platforms restrict third party agents, control is normall

topics.title: Modbus
topics.summary: Modbus is a simple, openly published industrial communication protocol, introduced in 1979, that lets a controlling device read and write data in industrial equipment. It uses a client and server model, historically called master and slave: one device polls and the others answer, and there is no peer to peer conversation. Requests carry a function code that names the operation and an address in a flat register space, covering coils for single bits and holding or input registers for 16 bit values

topics.title: Model Supply Chain Risk
topics.summary: Model supply chain risk is the exposure created by the origin, packaging, storage and delivery of machine learning models and their associated artefacts. A model is not merely a data file: it is a collection of weight tensors, serialised code, configuration, tokenisers and dependency metadata, and many common storage formats reconstruct objects when loaded, so unpacking an untrusted model can execute attacker supplied code on the loading host. topics.title: MTTD and MTTR
topics.summary: Mean Time to Detect and Mean Time to Respond are the two headline measures of security operations performance. Mean Time to Detect measures the elapsed interval between when malicious activity actually began and when it was first identified, while Mean Time to Respond measures the interval from identification to containment or resolution, depending on how the organisation defines the endpoint. Both are averages and both are therefore easily misread. A mean computed over a handful of incidents is

topics.title: Mutual TLS
topics.summary: Mutual TLS, often written mTLS, is the ordinary TLS handshake with client authentication enabled: during the handshake the client also presents an X.509 certificate, and the server verifies that certificate against a trusted issuing authority before any application data flows. topics.title: Netflow and IPFIX
topics.summary: NetFlow and its open equivalent IPFIX are flow-export technologies that summarise network conversations rather than capturing every packet. A router or switch observes packets, groups them into flows keyed by source and destination address, ports, protocol and other fields, and periodically exports records that describe each flow with counters, timestamps and interface information. topics.title: Network Access Control
topics.summary: Network access control is the set of technologies that decides whether a device may join a network and what it may reach once connected. A typical deployment authenticates the device or its user before granting access, commonly through 802.1X with a RADIUS server, MAC authentication bypass for devices that cannot run a supplicant, or a captive portal for guests and unmanaged endpoints. After authentication the platform evaluates posture, covering operating system version, patch level, endpoint p

topics.title: Network Access Control
topics.summary: Network Access Control is the set of mechanisms that decide whether a device is allowed to join a network segment and what it may reach once joined, enforced at the point of connection: a switch port, a wireless association, or a virtual private network concentrator. A typical deployment uses port-based access control described by the IEEE 802.1X standard, where the switch acts as an authenticator, the device runs a supplicant, and a central server such as a RADIUS server validates credentials u

topics.title: Network Address Translation
topics.summary: Network Address Translation is the process of rewriting the source or destination addresses, and often the ports, in IP packet headers as the packet crosses a router or firewall. The common form used at the internet edge, sometimes called port address translation or NAT overload, lets many internal hosts share one public IPv4 address by mapping each flow to a distinct source port and keeping a state table of active translations. Other forms rewrite destination addresses to reach internal servers

topics.title: Network Segmentation
topics.summary: A network segment is a bounded group of systems that share a communication policy, and segmentation is the practice of inserting enforced boundaries between those groups so that a single compromised host cannot reach every other asset. Boundaries may be physical, built from separate switches and cabling, logical, built from VLANs with router or firewall access control lists, or identity-based, built from microsegmentation agents and policy engines that decide per workload rather than per subnet.

topics.title: NIST Cybersecurity Framework
topics.summary: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework is a voluntary, outcome-based framework that organises cybersecurity activity into a common vocabulary so that technical teams, executives, auditors and regulators can discuss risk using the same terms. Its core is a set of Functions, historically Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, each broken into Categories and Subcategories that describe desired outcomes rather than prescribing specific products. topics.title: NIST SP 800-53
topics.summary: NIST Special Publication 800-53 is the United States federal control catalogue for information systems and organisations, and it has become the de facto reference control set for regulated industries well beyond government. topics.title: NIST SP 800-61 Incident Handling
topics.summary: NIST SP 800-61 is the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology Special Publication titled Computer Security Incident Handling Guide. It is guidance, not law: it describes how an organisation can build and run an incident response capability, and it is widely used as the reference structure that incident response plans, tabletop exercises and audit questions are mapped against. Its central contribution is a lifecycle view of incident handling, commonly summarised as preparatio

topics.title: Nonce Reuse
topics.summary: Nonce reuse is the failure to supply a unique per-operation value to a cryptographic algorithm that requires one, and it quietly converts otherwise sound constructions into broken ones. The consequences depend on the mode. In counter-mode authenticated encryption such as AES-GCM, reusing a nonce with the same key leaks the XOR of the two plaintexts and exposes the authentication subkey, which allows an attacker to forge messages and, in many deployment patterns, to recover plaintext outright. In

topics.title: OAuth 2.0
topics.summary: OAuth 2.0 is an authorisation framework that lets a client application obtain limited access to a resource on behalf of a user or another service without handling that user's credentials. It defines roles (resource owner, client, authorisation server, resource server), grant types (authorisation code, client credentials, device code, and the deprecated implicit and resource owner password grants), and token types, most importantly the access token and the optional refresh token. The framework de

topics.title: Object Storage Misconfiguration
topics.summary: Object storage misconfiguration means a bucket or container in a service such as Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage or Google Cloud Storage is left readable or writable by parties who should not have that access, or is placed behind controls that do not actually restrict reachability. The mechanism is rarely a software bug: the storage API behaves exactly as configured, but the effective policy is wrong. Common causes are public access granted deliberately for a one-off file transfer and never revoke

topics.title: Open-Source Intelligence
topics.summary: Open-source intelligence is the collection and analysis of information from publicly available sources to answer a specific intelligence question, together with the discipline of judging how reliable each piece is. The term refers to the sourcing, not to how secret the conclusion is: a report built entirely from public material can still be classified once it is combined and assessed. Sources include corporate registries, job advertisements, certificate transparency logs, domain registration rec

topics.title: OpenID Connect
topics.summary: OpenID Connect (OIDC) is an identity layer built on top of OAuth 2.0 that gives clients a standardised way to verify a user's identity and obtain basic profile information. It adds an identity token, a JSON Web Token whose claims describe the authentication event and the subject, and it standardises discovery through a well-known configuration document, key distribution through a JSON Web Key Set, and user information retrieval through a dedicated endpoint. Because the identity token is signed a

topics.title: OpenID Connect
topics.summary: OpenID Connect, usually shortened to OIDC, is an identity layer built on top of the OAuth 2.0 authorisation framework. OAuth 2.0 was designed to grant an application scoped access to a resource without handing over a password, and it deliberately left the question of who the user is to other specifications; OIDC answers that question by defining an identity token, a signed JSON Web Token that the identity provider issues to the client and that contains claims such as a subject identifier, the is

topics.title: Operational Security (OpSec)
topics.summary: Operational security, usually shortened to OpSec, is the practice of controlling the observable traces an activity produces so that they do not reveal capability, intent, identity or infrastructure to an observer. The classic process has five steps: identify the information that must not be disclosed, analyse who is collecting against it, analyse the weaknesses in how the activity is conducted, assess the risk each weakness creates, and apply countermeasures in proportion. topics.title: Operational Technology Security
topics.summary: Operational technology security covers the protection of systems that interact with the physical world, including industrial control systems, building management, medical devices and transport signalling, where the governing priority is safe and continuous operation rather than data confidentiality. topics.title: OT Network Monitoring
topics.summary: OT network monitoring is the practice of gaining visibility into operational technology networks, the systems that control physical processes in factories, utilities and transport, by observing traffic rather than by installing agents on the controllers themselves. topics.title: OWASP Top Ten
topics.summary: The OWASP Top Ten is an awareness document published by the Open Worldwide Application Security Project that lists the categories of risk most commonly found in web applications, ordered by a combination of how widespread the weakness is, how often it is exploited and how much impact it has. topics.title: Packet Capture
topics.summary: Packet capture is the recording of network traffic at the frame level for later analysis, produced either by copying traffic to a monitoring interface, by a hardware tap inserted in the link, or by a capture agent on a host that sees only its own traffic. Each captured frame is normally written with a timestamp, and the analysis software decodes protocol layers so an analyst can follow a conversation, measure timing and reconstruct what was transferred. topics.title: Passkeys
topics.summary: A passkey is a cryptographic credential that replaces a password for a specific account, standardised through the Web Authentication specification that is maintained by the World Wide Web Consortium with input from the FIDO Alliance. topics.title: Passwordless Authentication
topics.summary: Passwordless authentication means a user proves their identity without supplying a shared secret that they know and type, so the primary factor is something they hold or are, such as a hardware key, a platform authenticator, a certificate, or a short-lived code delivered to a registered device. topics.title: Passwordless Authentication
topics.summary: Passwordless authentication is a set of authentication methods in which the user proves possession of a registered authenticator bound to their identity and never supplies a shared secret that can be phished, reused or cracked offline. The two dominant families are asymmetric key credentials based on the Web Authentication standard, where the private key stays in a hardware security key or platform authenticator and the public key is registered with the relying party, and certificate-based authe

topics.title: PASTA Threat Modelling
topics.summary: PASTA, the Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis, is a seven stage, risk centric threat modelling method that starts from business objectives rather than from a list of technical flaws. It was published by Tony UcedaVelez and Marco Morana and is described in the book Risk Centric Threat Modeling. topics.title: Patch Management
topics.summary: Patch management is the governed process of finding out which software versions you run, learning which of them have known defects that affect security, and getting fixed versions onto those systems in a controlled way. It is a lifecycle, not an event: inventory, advisory intake, risk based prioritisation, test, staged deployment, verification, and documented exception handling. topics.title: Payload Staging
topics.summary: Payload staging is the practice of splitting the code or configuration that achieves an objective into a small delivery component and one or more larger components retrieved after execution begins. topics.title: PCI DSS
topics.summary: The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard is a contractual requirement imposed by the card brands and administered by the PCI Security Standards Council on any entity that stores, processes or transmits account data, or that can impact the security of the cardholder data environment. topics.title: Penetration Testing Methodology
topics.summary: A penetration testing methodology is the documented, repeatable process a tester follows so that an assessment is scoped, authorised, evidenced and reproducible. Public frameworks such as the Penetration Testing Execution Standard and NIST SP 800-115 describe the shape of that work, and most providers add their own internal standard. topics.title: Persistence
topics.summary: Persistence is the collection of mechanisms an intruder uses to retain access across reboots, password changes, session expiry and partial remediation, so that initial access does not have to be won again. Host-based persistence attaches to legitimate startup behaviour: autostart entries, scheduled tasks, system services, logon scripts, shell profiles, and browser or office extensions. topics.title: Phishing
topics.summary: Phishing is a social engineering technique in which an attacker sends a message that impersonates a party the recipient already trusts, so that the recipient takes an action the attacker wants: entering a password on a lookalike page, approving a multi-factor prompt, opening an attachment, or paying an invoice into a changed bank account. topics.title: Phishing Simulation
topics.summary: A phishing simulation is an authorised exercise in which an organisation sends realistic but harmless lure messages to its own staff in order to measure and improve behaviour. The simulation platform records who opened, clicked, entered data on a teaching page, or reported the message through the report button, and never captures real credentials. topics.title: PICERL
topics.summary: PICERL is a six-phase incident response lifecycle - Preparation, Identification, Containment, Eradication, Recovery and Lessons Learned - that gives a security team a shared vocabulary and a gated decision path from the moment an alert fires to the moment an incident is formally closed. topics.title: Post-Quantum Cryptography
topics.summary: Post-quantum cryptography is the family of public-key algorithms designed to remain secure against an adversary equipped with a large-scale quantum computer, alongside the migration work required to deploy them. The threat is asymmetric in time: Shor's algorithm would break RSA and elliptic curve cryptography outright, while Grover's algorithm only modestly reduces the effective strength of symmetric primitives, so AES-256 and SHA-384 remain comfortable. topics.title: Pretexting
topics.summary: Pretexting is a social engineering technique in which the attacker invents a believable situation, or pretext, to make a target release information, access or a favour. The pretext supplies three things: a role the caller claims, a reason the request is routine, and pressure that makes refusal feel rude or risky. topics.title: Privacy by Design
topics.summary: Privacy by design is the principle that protection of personal data is built into a system, a process or a product from the beginning rather than added after it is finished. topics.title: Privilege Escalation
topics.summary: Privilege escalation is the set of actions that convert ordinary user or service access into authority the account was never intended to hold, whether that means higher rights on the same host or rights that reach across a domain or cloud tenant. topics.title: Privileged Access Management
topics.summary: Privileged access management (PAM) is the discipline and tooling set that controls, brokers, records and audits the use of accounts with elevated rights, including domain administrators, root, database superusers, cloud root and organisation owner roles, and the service accounts that hold equivalent power. topics.title: Privileged Access Management
topics.summary: Privileged access management is the set of controls that govern accounts with elevated rights, such as domain administrators, root on Unix hosts, cloud owner roles, database administrators and the service accounts that automation uses. topics.title: Process Injection
topics.summary: Process injection is a family of techniques in which code is placed into the address space of another running process so that it executes under that process's identity, privileges and trust context. topics.title: Prompt Injection
topics.summary: Prompt injection is a class of attack against systems built on large language models, in which an attacker places instructions inside content the model will read, such as a document, a web page, an email, a code comment or another user's message, and the model then treats those instructions as if they came from the system operator. topics.title: Proxy
topics.summary: A proxy is an intermediary that receives a client request, applies policy, and forwards that request to the destination on the client's behalf, so the client never communicates directly with the remote server. topics.title: Pseudonymisation
topics.summary: Pseudonymisation is a data protection technique in which direct identifiers such as a name, account number or national identifier are replaced with artificial values, and the mapping that would restore them is kept separately and protected. It matters because it reduces exposure while keeping records useful: analysts can still follow one person's activity across many rows without knowing who that person is. The important distinction is that pseudonymised data is still personal data when re-ident

topics.title: Public Key Infrastructure
topics.summary: Public key infrastructure is the combination of certificate authorities, registration authorities, certificate repositories, revocation services and the policies that bind public keys to identities so that parties who have never met can authenticate each other. topics.title: Purdue Model
topics.summary: The Purdue Model, more precisely the Purdue Enterprise Reference Architecture, is a hierarchical reference model for industrial control networks that is widely reused in operational technology security as a way to describe zones and levels. topics.title: Purple Teaming
topics.summary: Purple teaming is collaborative adversary emulation in which offensive and defensive staff work the same scenario together, side by side or in tight cycles, so that each attack technique is tested against live telemetry and each detection gap is closed while the people who found it are still in the room. The colour term is descriptive rather than a formal standard: red team work emulates an adversary, blue team work defends and detects, and purple describes the joint activity that joins the two.

topics.title: Qualitative Risk Assessment
topics.summary: A qualitative risk assessment expresses likelihood and impact using ordered words or ranks, such as low, medium and high, rather than money or precise probabilities. Its inputs are a defined scenario, an agreed rating scale with written definitions for each level, and structured expert judgement, often combined in a matrix that maps the two ratings to an overall risk level used for prioritisation. topics.title: Quantitative Risk Assessment
topics.summary: A quantitative risk assessment expresses risk in numbers, typically as an annualised loss expectancy, which is the estimated frequency of an event in a year multiplied by the estimated loss when it occurs. topics.title: Ransomware
topics.summary: Ransomware is malicious software or an intrusion campaign whose objective is to deny an organisation access to its own data or systems and then sell that access back, typically by encrypting files, locking virtualisation or backup infrastructure, or threatening to publish stolen data. Modern incidents are rarely a single executable. topics.title: Reconnaissance
topics.summary: Reconnaissance is the disciplined collection and organisation of information about a target before and during an engagement, producing the map of systems, identities and technologies that every later phase depends on. Practitioners divide it into passive work, which draws on third-party and public sources and leaves no trace on the target, and active work, which sends traffic to target-owned infrastructure and is therefore visible to defenders. Passive sources include domain registration records

topics.title: Red Team Operations
topics.summary: Red team operations are authorised, goal oriented adversary emulation against an organisation's people, processes and technology, where the objective is a mission outcome rather than a list of vulnerabilities. The team is usually briefed to reach a defined target, such as a specific system or piece of data, and to do so while remaining undetected, because staying hidden tests detection and response instead of only testing whether a door opens. topics.title: Resilience Engineering
topics.summary: Resilience engineering is the study of how complex systems keep producing safe outcomes when conditions change, and it treats variability in human work as a resource rather than as a defect. Instead of asking only why a component failed, it examines how everyday performance usually succeeds and how that margin is slowly eroded. topics.title: Responsible Disclosure
topics.summary: Responsible disclosure is the coordinated process by which a person who finds a security weakness in someone else's product tells the vendor and gives them a reasonable window to fix it before any public detail appears. The mechanism is a private report, usually through a security contact, bug bounty platform or published disclosure policy, followed by triage, a fix, and only then a public advisory that credits the reporter. topics.title: Risk Appetite
topics.summary: Risk appetite is the amount and type of risk an organisation is willing to accept while pursuing its objectives, and it is a decision made by leadership rather than by the security team alone. It is usually expressed as a statement plus tolerances, for example which data classes may be processed on a public cloud, how long a critical service may stay down, or how many high severity findings may remain open at quarter end. topics.title: Risk Exception Management
topics.summary: Risk exception management is the governance process by which an organisation formally records that a specific control requirement cannot be met, for a defined period, and accepts the resulting risk with someone accountable for the decision. topics.title: Risk Register
topics.summary: A risk register is the controlled record of identified risks that an organisation has decided to track, each entry capturing the risk statement, the affected assets and business processes, the threat and vulnerability that make it credible, the existing controls, the assessed likelihood and impact, the resulting inherent and residual rating, the risk owner, the treatment decision and the target date. topics.title: Risk Treatment
topics.summary: Risk treatment is the decision and the action taken in response to an identified risk, and formal frameworks reduce it to four options: avoid the activity, reduce the risk with controls, transfer it to another party such as an insurer, or accept it with a named owner and a review date. topics.title: Risk-Based Prioritisation
topics.summary: Risk based prioritisation means ordering remediation work by the realistic harm a weakness can cause in this specific environment, rather than by severity score or by the order a scanner printed its output. topics.title: Rogue Access Point
topics.summary: A rogue access point is any wireless access point connected to an organisation's network without authorisation, whether it is a cheap router that a staff member plugged in for better coverage, a laptop sharing its connection, or a device an attacker planted to bridge wireless clients into the wired local area network. topics.title: Role-Based Access Control
topics.summary: Role-based access control (RBAC) is an access control model in which permissions are assigned to roles rather than directly to users, and users receive permissions only through the roles granted to them. topics.title: Rootkit
topics.summary: A rootkit is a set of techniques and components designed to keep malicious presence on a system hidden while retaining privileged control, typically by subverting the very mechanisms an administrator would use to observe the machine. topics.title: Routing Protocols
topics.summary: Routing protocols are the rules routers use to learn which paths exist to a destination and to choose one, and they fall into distance vector, link state and path vector families. A router running a link state protocol floods information about its own links so that every router can build the same map, while a distance vector protocol exchanges reachability and cost with its neighbours and largely trusts what they report. topics.title: RSA
topics.summary: RSA is a public-key cryptosystem whose security rests on the presumed hardness of factoring the product of two large primes, combined with modular exponentiation over that product. A key pair consists of a modulus derived from two secret primes, a public exponent usually 65537, and a private exponent derived through the extended Euclidean algorithm. topics.title: RTO and RPO
topics.summary: Recovery time objective and recovery point objective are the two commitments that translate continuity intent into engineering requirements. The recovery time objective is the targeted duration of time within which a business process, system or service must be restored after a disruption; it is a deadline, not a duration target, and it must sit inside the maximum tolerable period of disruption derived from the business impact analysis. topics.title: Rules of Engagement
topics.summary: Rules of engagement are the written agreement that defines the boundaries of an authorised security test: which systems and addresses are in scope, when testing may run, which techniques are forbidden, who may be contacted, and what happens if the test causes harm. topics.title: S3 Bucket Policy
topics.summary: An S3 bucket policy is a JSON resource-based policy attached directly to an object storage bucket that controls which principals may perform which actions against that bucket and the objects inside it, optionally under conditions. topics.title: Safety Instrumented System
topics.summary: A safety instrumented system is an independent control system that monitors an industrial process for dangerous conditions and drives it to a safe state, and its defining property is that it is separate from the basic process control system that runs normal production. topics.title: Salt
topics.summary: A salt is a unique, non-secret random value that is combined with an input before hashing so that identical inputs produce different digests, and it is a mandatory component of any password storage scheme. topics.title: SameSite Cookies
topics.summary: The SameSite attribute on a cookie tells the browser whether to attach that cookie to requests that originate from another site, and it is the mechanism behind a large part of modern cross site request forgery defence. topics.title: SAML
topics.summary: Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) is an XML-based standard for exchanging authentication and authorisation assertions between an identity provider and a service provider, and it remains the dominant federation protocol in enterprise and government environments. topics.title: SCADA
topics.summary: SCADA, short for supervisory control and data acquisition, is the layer of an industrial control environment that gives operators a consolidated view of many remote sites and lets them issue supervisory commands. topics.title: Scope and Rules of Engagement
topics.summary: Scope and rules of engagement are the written boundary that defines what may be tested, when, how, by whom, and what happens when something goes wrong; without documented authorisation from someone entitled to give it, the same activity is simply unauthorised access. topics.title: Secret Scanning
topics.summary: Secret scanning is the practice of detecting credentials, API keys, tokens, private keys and other sensitive material that has been committed to source control, embedded in build artifacts, written into logs, or left in configuration files and container layers. topics.title: Secrets Management
topics.summary: Secrets management is the discipline of storing, distributing, rotating and auditing the credentials that systems use to authenticate to each other, such as API keys, database passwords, certificates and signing keys. topics.title: Secrets Manager
topics.summary: A secrets manager is a managed service for storing, controlling access to, and automatically rotating credentials such as database passwords, API keys, tokens, certificates and private keys, so that applications retrieve them at runtime instead of embedding them in code, images or configuration files. topics.title: Secure Email Gateway
topics.summary: A secure email gateway is the control point that inspects mail as it crosses the boundary of an organisation, applying policy before messages reach user mailboxes and controlling outbound traffic as well. topics.title: Secure Software Development Lifecycle
topics.summary: Secure software development lifecycle means building security activities into each phase of how software is planned, written, tested, released and maintained, rather than adding them shortly before a release. topics.title: Secure Software Development Lifecycle
topics.summary: The Secure Software Development Lifecycle is a structured way of weaving security activities into every phase of how software is planned, built, tested, released and maintained, rather than bolting security on at the end. topics.title: Security Automation
topics.summary: Security automation is the use of scripts, playbooks and orchestration platforms to carry out security tasks that a human analyst would otherwise repeat by hand. It covers a wide band of work: collecting and normalising log data, enriching alerts with threat intelligence, matching indicators against assets, opening and updating tickets, isolating a host, disabling a session or blocking a domain. topics.title: Security Awareness Training
topics.summary: Security awareness training is a planned programme that changes what employees do when they meet a phishing email, a strange login prompt or a request to move money. topics.title: Security Misconfiguration
topics.summary: Security misconfiguration is the condition where a system is deployed and working, but one or more of its settings leaves a door open that nobody intended. It is not a flaw in the software code itself; the vendor shipped a safe default and a human changed it, skipped it, or left it untouched. topics.title: Security Policy
topics.summary: A security policy is a written management statement that says what the organisation requires of its people and systems, and who is accountable when those requirements are not met. Policy sits at the top of a hierarchy: policy states intent and mandatory rules, standards fix the specific technical values, procedures describe the step-by-step tasks, and guidelines offer advice that is not binding. topics.title: Security Steering Committee
topics.summary: A security steering committee is the standing governance forum where an organisation makes the security decisions that cannot legitimately be settled inside the security function: funding a control, accepting a residual risk, approving an exception to policy, or agreeing that a project will ship with a known weakness. topics.title: Separation of Duties
topics.summary: Separation of duties is a control principle that splits a sensitive process across two or more people so that no single individual can complete it alone. It is closely related to the principle of least privilege and to the two-person rule used for physical assets, but its focus is the workflow rather than the permission set: the request, the approval, the execution and the review belong to different roles. topics.title: Server-Side Request Forgery
topics.summary: Server-side request forgery is a flaw in which an application fetches a remote resource using a destination that an attacker controls, so the request is issued by the server itself with the server's network position and credentials. topics.title: Serverless Security
topics.summary: Serverless security covers the controls applied to code that runs on demand in a provider-managed platform, where the customer never patches a server, never chooses a host and often never sees a network. topics.title: Service Account Hygiene
topics.summary: Service account hygiene is the set of practices that keeps non-human identities controlled, accountable and minimal. A service account is an identity created for software rather than a person: a batch job, an integration, a monitoring agent or a scheduled report. topics.title: Service Mesh Security
topics.summary: Service mesh security is the practice of enforcing identity, encryption and access rules between workloads through a dedicated infrastructure layer that sits beside the application. topics.title: SHA-256
topics.summary: SHA-256 is a cryptographic hash function from the SHA-2 family that maps an arbitrary-length input to a fixed 256-bit digest, and it is specified in FIPS 180-4. topics.summary: The shared responsibility model is the contractual and architectural division of security duties between a cloud service provider and its customer, in which the provider secures the cloud itself while the customer secures what they put in the cloud. topics.title: Shift Handover
topics.summary: Shift handover is the structured transfer of operational context from one security operations shift to the next, and it is a control in its own right rather than an administrative courtesy. topics.title: SIEM
topics.summary: A Security Information and Event Management platform is a centralised system that ingests logs and telemetry from across an estate, normalises them into a common schema, correlates events over time, and evaluates detection rules to raise alerts that a security operations centre can triage. topics.title: SIEM Tuning

topics.title: Smishing
topics.summary: Smishing is phishing delivered over short message service or a comparable mobile messaging channel, and the delivery medium changes both the attacker's playbook and the defender's options. Text messages are short, arrive on a personal device, and are read within minutes, so urgency and brevity do the persuasive work that a longer email would need. topics.title: SOAR
topics.summary: Security Orchestration, Automation and Response is the discipline and tooling category concerned with turning detection output into repeatable action. topics.title: SOC 2

topics.title: SOC Metrics
topics.summary: SOC metrics are the quantitative measures a security operations centre uses to understand whether its detection and response work is effective. topics.title: Social Engineering
topics.summary: Social engineering is the deliberate use of psychological manipulation to persuade a person to take an action that helps an attacker, such as revealing a credential, approving a payment, granting access or holding a door. topics.title: Software Bill of Materials
topics.summary: A software bill of materials is a machine-readable inventory of the components that make up a piece of software, typically listing each package with its name, version, supplier, unique identifier and the relationships that describe how components nest. topics.title: SPF

topics.summary: SQL injection is a class of input handling flaw in which untrusted data reaches a database query as code rather than as a value. topics.title: Statement of Applicability
topics.summary: A Statement of Applicability is the document that records, for every control in the applicable catalogue, whether the organisation includes it, why that decision was made, and where the implementation lives. topics.title: Static Application Security Testing
topics.summary: Static application security testing is the automated analysis of source code, bytecode or binaries without executing the program, looking for patterns that indicate a security defect such as injection sinks reached by untrusted input, unsafe deserialisation, hard-coded cryptographic material or broken access control. topics.title: STRIDE
topics.summary: STRIDE is a threat enumeration mnemonic that groups threats into six categories: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege. topics.title: Subnetting
topics.summary: Subnetting is the practice of dividing one IP address range into smaller logical networks, each with its own broadcast domain and its own routing entry. topics.title: Supply Chain Attack
topics.summary: A supply chain attack is an intrusion that reaches a target indirectly by compromising something the target trusts: a software dependency, a build system, a package registry, an update mechanism, a managed service provider, or a hardware or firmware supplier. topics.title: Third-Party Risk Management
topics.summary: Third party risk management is the discipline of identifying, assessing and continuously monitoring the security and resilience exposure created by suppliers, contractors, software vendors and service providers. topics.title: Threat Actor Attribution

topics.title: Vishing

topics.title: Persistence
topics.summary: Persistence is the tactic that covers everything an adversary does to keep access across reboots, credential resets, and partial remediation, and it is the reason incidents that appear contained often resume weeks later. Behaviours in this tactic include modifying registry run keys and startup folders, installing services or daemons, creating scheduled tasks and cron entries, adding accounts or SSH authorised keys, abusing external remote services such as VPN or remote desktop gateways, planting

topics.title: Privilege Escalation
topics.summary: Privilege Escalation is the tactic covering the steps an adversary takes to move from a foothold with ordinary user rights to something far more powerful, whether that means local administrator on one host, domain-wide control, or an equivalent role in a cloud tenant. topics.title: Reconnaissance
topics.summary: Reconnaissance is the set of adversary activities that gather information about a target before and alongside intrusion attempts, and it is the one tactic where most of the work can happen entirely outside the victim's visibility. topics.title: Resource Development
topics.summary: Resource Development is the tactic covering the infrastructure, identities, and tooling an adversary establishes or acquires before and during a campaign, almost all of which sits on systems the victim does not own and therefore cannot monitor directly. topics.title: Stealth
topics.summary: Stealth is the ATT&CK tactic that groups the behaviours an adversary uses to keep their activity looking ordinary. It replaces what earlier versions of ATT&CK called Defense Evasion, and the rename matters: the tactic is defined by the goal of not being noticed rather than by a fixed list of tricks. topics.title: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism
topics.summary: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism describes adversary actions that subvert the way an operating system gates privilege rather than exploiting a memory-safety flaw to obtain it. topics.summary: This sub-technique covers adversaries abusing the macOS AuthorizationExecuteWithPrivileges application programming interface to obtain root without ever stealing a password. topics.title: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Setuid and Setgid
topics.shortTitle: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Setuid and Setgid
topics.summary: The setuid and setgid permission bits make a program run with the privileges of the file owner or group instead of the caller, and adversaries abuse them in two directions. They can set the bits on their own binary, so it keeps executing in an elevated context later, which is often used to escape a restricted execution environment such as a limited shell or a jailed session. topics.title: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Sudo and Sudo Caching
topics.shortTitle: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Sudo and Sudo Caching
topics.summary: Sudo delegates command execution to other users under a policy file, and its credential cache turns that delegation into a short window of password-free privilege. After a successful authentication sudo records a timestamp for the user and terminal, and for the configured timeout further commands run without a new password prompt; separate terminal sessions are tracked independently when ticket isolation is enabled. topics.title: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: TCC Manipulation
topics.shortTitle: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: TCC Manipulation
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers two related macOS behaviours: abusing an already trusted application so that malicious code inherits its privacy permissions, and directly altering the Transparency, Consent and Control database. In the first case the attacker injects into a process or script that the user previously approved, so the operating system attributes the file, camera or microphone access to the trusted parent and never prompts again. topics.shortTitle: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism: Temporary Elevated Clo...
topics.summary: This sub-technique describes adversaries abusing the permission structures that cloud providers build for short-term privilege, rather than granting themselves permanent roles. Just-in-time access requests, account impersonation, and role passing all create a token or session that carries rights the requesting identity does not normally hold. topics.title: Access Token Manipulation
topics.summary: Access token manipulation abuses the Windows object that carries a process identity and its group memberships. Every process runs with an access token, and that token decides which files, registry keys and services the process may touch. topics.shortTitle: Access Token Manipulation: Create Process with Token
topics.summary: Creating a process with a token means launching an entirely new program under an access token that was not issued to the caller, so the new process runs from its first instruction with the privileges and group memberships of a different account. Windows offers supported entry points for this, including process creation interfaces that accept an existing token and the interactive runas command, which builds a fresh logon session from credentials. topics.title: Access Token Manipulation: Make and Impersonate Token
topics.shortTitle: Access Token Manipulation: Make and Impersonate Token
topics.summary: Making and impersonating a token covers the case where the attacker builds a brand new access token instead of copying one that already exists in memory. With a valid username and password, a credential-carrying logon interface such as LogonUser creates a fresh logon session for that account and hands back the access token for it, which the attacker can then assign to a thread and use for the rest of the operation. topics.title: Access Token Manipulation: Parent PID Spoofing
topics.shortTitle: Access Token Manipulation: Parent PID Spoofing
topics.summary: Parent process identifier spoofing abuses the fact that the recorded parent of a Windows process is a value the creating code can choose rather than a fact Windows always derives. The process creation interface accepts a parameter that names the process to record as the parent, and specialised helper utilities exist that do the same from a command line. topics.title: Access Token Manipulation: SID-History Injection
topics.summary: SID-History injection abuses a directory attribute that exists so accounts can migrate between domains without losing access. A Windows security identifier, or SID, is the value that access checks actually compare, and every token carries the account SID plus the SIDs of its groups. The SID-History attribute on a directory account holds additional SIDs that are folded into the token at logon, so a trusted domain can keep honouring old identifiers. topics.title: Access Token Manipulation: Token Impersonation/Theft
topics.summary: Token impersonation or theft is the token-focused behaviour where an attacker duplicates an access token that already exists in memory and then attaches that copy to a thread inside a process they control. topics.title: Account Access Removal
topics.summary: Account Access Removal is the deliberate destruction of the accounts people need in order to work. The behaviour ranges from deleting a user, disabling an account or locking it out with failed attempts, to resetting a password, revoking a licence or stripping permissions in a hosted service so that the owner can no longer sign in. topics.title: Account Discovery
topics.summary: Account discovery is the enumeration of user, service and machine identities that exist in an environment, usually early in an intrusion, to identify accounts worth targeting for credential access or lateral movement. The mechanism is straightforward: the adversary queries whatever directory, database or operating system interface is reachable and returns identity information. On Windows systems this includes local account enumeration through command line utilities and remote procedure calls, do

topics.title: Account Discovery: Cloud Account
topics.summary: Cloud Account discovery enumerates identities inside a cloud provider or software-as-a-service tenant: users, groups, roles, service accounts, and the policies attached to them. Provider command-line interfaces and APIs return this data to any principal holding the right read permission, so one stolen token or access key can map every identity and its effective access level across a subscription, project, or tenant. topics.title: Account Discovery: Domain Account
topics.summary: Domain Account discovery queries the central directory for users, groups, and memberships across the whole environment. The adversary uses directory-aware utilities and scripting interfaces to pull lists of accounts, privileged groups, and group members, turning a single valid session into a map of who holds power in the organisation. topics.title: Account Discovery: Email Account
topics.summary: Email Account discovery collects addresses and mailbox identities, most often by dumping the global address list, the shared directory of everyone in an organisation, from an on-premises mail server or a hosted mail service. The output is a ready-made target list for phishing and for guessing login names on other systems, and it can also expose distribution groups that reveal teams, seniority, and reporting lines. topics.title: Account Discovery: Local Account
topics.summary: Local Account discovery enumerates the accounts and groups defined in a single host's own account database rather than in the central directory. The adversary lists local users, lists local groups, and inspects group membership to learn which names exist and which carry administrative rights, sometimes reading the account file directly on Linux or using the vendor account tool on a hypervisor. topics.title: Account Manipulation
topics.summary: Account manipulation covers any change an adversary makes to an account so that access survives, grows or becomes harder to remove. It includes setting a new password or adding credentials, changing group memberships and delegated rights, altering role or permission assignments in a directory or cloud tenant, and editing account properties that weaken policy. topics.title: Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Credentials
topics.summary: This sub-technique of account manipulation focuses on adding new authentication material to identities that live in a cloud directory or infrastructure platform, so the adversary keeps a way in that survives password resets. topics.title: Account Manipulation: Additional Cloud Roles
topics.summary: This sub-technique of account manipulation covers raising the privileges attached to a cloud identity so that the adversary keeps broad access to a tenant or subscription. In practice it means editing permission policies or attaching a new policy version, binding an existing policy to a compromised user or role, and assigning administrative directory roles such as a global administrator. topics.title: Account Manipulation: Additional Container Cluster Roles
topics.shortTitle: Account Manipulation: Additional Container Cluster Roles
topics.summary: This sub-technique of account manipulation covers granting extra permissions inside a container orchestration system, most often by binding an existing role to a user or service account. In Kubernetes, role based access control is expressed through Role and ClusterRole objects that list permissions, and through RoleBinding and ClusterRoleBinding objects that attach those roles to subjects. topics.title: Account Manipulation: Additional Email Delegate Permissions
topics.shortTitle: Account Manipulation: Additional Email Delegate Permissions
topics.summary: This sub-technique of account manipulation is about giving a second account the right to read or send mail as the first one. In on-premises Exchange and in the hosted Exchange service this is done with mailbox permission and delegation cmdlets, and it can also be done through administration consoles. topics.title: Account Manipulation: Additional Local or Domain Groups
topics.shortTitle: Account Manipulation: Additional Local or Domain Groups
topics.summary: This sub-technique of account manipulation is the plain group membership change: adding an account the adversary controls to a local group or a directory group that carries extra rights. On Windows this is usually done with the built-in net commands for local and domain groups, and on Linux with the user modification command that edits group membership. topics.title: Account Manipulation: Device Registration
topics.summary: This sub-technique of account manipulation covers enrolling a new device into a system that either proves identity or enforces device policy, so the adversary gains access that survives a password reset. In multifactor authentication services, which are the platforms that ask for a second proof of identity, an attacker holding a valid username and password can simply enroll their own phone or token. topics.title: Account Manipulation: SSH Authorized Keys
topics.summary: This sub-technique of account manipulation is about adding an attacker-owned public key to the SSH authorized keys file so that the holder of the matching private key can log in as that user without a password. The file normally sits in the user's home directory on Linux and macOS, and in a per-user location on ESXi hosts, where key authentication is the usual way to manage the system remotely. topics.title: Acquire Access
topics.summary: Acquire access is the purchase or transfer of an already compromised foothold rather than the creation of one. An adversary buys entry from an initial access broker, receives a planted backdoor or a set of working credentials, and skips the effort of finding and exploiting a weakness. The commodity being traded is quiet: access to a host that lacks monitoring, an account with high privileges, or a company in a chosen sector. topics.title: Acquire Infrastructure
topics.summary: Acquire Infrastructure covers the resource acquisition that happens before and around targeting, which is why it sits in the resource development tactic rather than in the intrusion itself. The adversary buys, rents, or otherwise obtains servers, domains, certificates, and third-party web services, and those assets become the staging points, redirectors, and command endpoints used later. topics.title: Acquire Infrastructure: Botnet
topics.summary: Under Acquire Infrastructure, this sub-technique focuses on obtaining an existing network of compromised machines rather than building one. The operator buys or subscribes to a botnet, often through a booter or stresser service that rents out attack capacity, and then uses it for follow-on activity such as large-scale phishing, distributed denial of service, or traffic relaying. topics.title: Acquire Infrastructure: DNS Server
topics.summary: Rather than hijacking someone else's name resolution, an adversary builds and operates a DNS server, the service that answers lookups of names to addresses, for their own operation. topics.title: Acquire Infrastructure: Domains
topics.summary: Adversaries register or otherwise obtain domain names so that later stages of an operation have a stable, trustworthy-looking place to send victims. A domain can be bought outright, obtained free from a low-cost registrar, or taken over after it expires. Attackers pick names that resemble a real brand through typosquatting, homoglyphs in other character sets, or a different top-level domain, and they may serve one-time hostnames so each victim sees a unique URL. topics.title: Acquire Infrastructure: Malvertising
topics.summary: Malvertising is the purchase of online advertising space that is then used to deliver malicious content to selected victims. Under Acquire Infrastructure, the acquired asset is an ad placement and its audience targeting, not a machine or a domain. Ads are bought to sit prominently in search results or on popular sites, often spoofing well-known brands, and clicks may lead to cloned download pages offering trojanised installers. topics.title: Acquire Infrastructure: Server
topics.summary: In this sub-technique an adversary buys, leases, or otherwise obtains a server, meaning a real machine or a dedicated cloud instance that they configure and run, instead of hijacking someone else's box. The parent technique covers infrastructure acquisition broadly; here the asset is a stand-alone server that is fully under the operator's control. topics.title: Acquire Infrastructure: Serverless
topics.summary: Serverless computing, in which a provider runs small functions on demand without the customer managing a machine, is acquired in this sub-technique as disposable operational infrastructure. The parent technique covers acquisition generally; here the asset is a function, worker, or script hosted under a provider's shared domain. topics.title: Acquire Infrastructure: Virtual Private Server
topics.summary: An adversary rents a virtual private server, a virtual machine or container sold by a cloud provider, and uses it as operational infrastructure. This sub-technique sits under Acquire Infrastructure and is narrower than the parent: the acquired asset is a rented, provider-hosted machine rather than a domain, a physical server, or a service account. topics.title: Acquire Infrastructure: Web Services
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers registering ordinary third-party web services, such as code repositories, cloud storage, paste sites, or social platforms, and using them as operational infrastructure. Unlike buying a server or a domain, the operator never owns the hosting, so the traffic destination is a legitimate, widely used provider that most organisations already permit. topics.title: Active Scanning
topics.summary: Active scanning is the reconnaissance category where the adversary sends traffic directly to victim infrastructure instead of reading third party sources, accepting that the traffic may be logged in exchange for fresher and more certain results. The family includes sweeping address ranges for live hosts, probing services for software and version detail, and enumerating content through brute force requests. topics.title: Active Scanning: Scanning IP Blocks
topics.summary: This sub-technique is the address range sweep: systematic probing of the publicly routed addresses an organisation holds, whether allocated as a contiguous block or as several ranges. topics.title: Active Scanning: Vulnerability Scanning
topics.summary: This sub-technique is scanning with the intent to match a target against known weaknesses, rather than merely listing open ports. A typical run fingerprints the service, harvests version banners, then consults a vulnerability database or a local set of checks to decide whether a specific flaw is likely present, sometimes verifying with a safe probe. topics.title: Active Scanning: Wordlist Scanning
topics.summary: Wordlist scanning tries thousands of guessed names against a service to discover content and infrastructure that was never advertised. topics.title: Adversary-in-the-Middle
topics.summary: Adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) describes an attacker who positions themselves on the network path between two parties that believe they talk directly. Instead of defeating encryption head on, the attacker abuses the protocols that decide where traffic goes, such as ARP, DNS, LLMNR, NBT-NS or DHCP, so a victim host hands its traffic to an attacker-controlled system. topics.summary: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) maps an Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) address to a link layer address such as a Media Access Control (MAC) address, and it does so without any authentication. topics.summary: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) lets a client obtain an IPv4 address and other network settings from a server it has not authenticated. The exchange is a broadcast discovery, an offer, a request and an acknowledgement, and the client accepts the first suitable offer it receives. topics.title: Adversary-in-the-Middle: Evil Twin
topics.summary: An evil twin is a fraudulent wireless access point that copies the Service Set Identifier (SSID) of a legitimate network so that devices and users connect to it voluntarily. The attacker may broadcast a stronger signal, jam clients away from the real access point, or wait for probe requests that name previously known networks and answer them, so automatic reconnection does the work. topics.title: Application Layer Protocol
topics.summary: Application layer protocol abuse is the embedding of command and control inside protocols that networks and users expect to see, so the traffic resembles ordinary application use. The mechanism is protocol mimicry. topics.title: Application Layer Protocol: DNS
topics.summary: DNS command and control describes adversary use of the Domain Name System to carry instructions and data between an implant and its controller, usually by encoding information into the queried name itself and receiving instructions in resource records returned by the authoritative server. topics.title: Application Layer Protocol: File Transfer Protocols
topics.shortTitle: Application Layer Protocol: File Transfer Protocols
topics.summary: File transfer protocols are an attractive command channel because they are already trusted, already permitted, and already noisy. topics.title: Application Layer Protocol: Publish/Subscribe Protocols
topics.summary: Publish and subscribe protocols give an attacker a message broker as a middle layer, so the malware never speaks directly to attacker infrastructure. topics.title: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
topics.summary: Web protocols command and control describes adversary use of HTTP and HTTPS to carry instructions and exfiltrated data between an implant and its controller. topics.title: Application Window Discovery
topics.summary: Application window discovery is the enumeration of the windows currently open on a host, normally through a scripting environment or native operating system functions that return window titles along with the process that owns each window. topics.title: Archive Collected Data
topics.summary: Archiving collected data is the packing step that sits between collection and exfiltration. The adversary takes files or records already gathered on a host, compresses them to shrink the total size, and often encrypts the result so that content inspection on the way out yields nothing readable. topics.shortTitle: Archive Collected Data: Archive via Custom Method
topics.summary: Archiving via custom method is the least observable of the three archive sub-techniques, because the attacker implements compression or encryption directly in their own code with no dependency on an external utility or a named library. topics.shortTitle: Archive Collected Data: Archive via Library

Libraries such as rarfile for Python, libzip, and zlib provide the same functions a utility would, but they are called as functions inside the running program instead of being launched as a separate child process. topics.shortTitle: Archive Collected Data: Archive via Utility
topics.summary: This sub-technique narrows archive collection to the use of preinstalled or third party archiving programs rather than libraries or custom code. topics.title: Audio Capture
topics.summary: Audio capture is the recording of sound through a host microphone or through a voice and video calling application that already holds the device. Malware reaches the hardware either by calling the operating system media interfaces or by attaching to a conferencing process, and the second route is quieter because no new device access event is generated. topics.title: Automated Collection
topics.summary: Automated collection is the use of scripts, interpreters or cloud interfaces to gather data across a host or an estate without a human doing the copying. Instead of opening folders by hand, the adversary runs a loop that selects files by extension, name, path or date and stages the copies in one location for later exfiltration.
