topics.title: Automated Exfiltration
topics.summary: Automated exfiltration is the use of scripted or scheduled processing to move collected data out of a network without a human driving each transfer. Collection still happens first; automation then handles packaging, compression, optional encryption, transfer, and in many cases the deletion of the local copy. topics.title: Automated Exfiltration: Traffic Duplication
topics.summary: Traffic duplication is the sub-technique of abusing a device's built-in traffic mirroring feature so that a copy of network traffic is forwarded to infrastructure the adversary controls. topics.title: Compromise Infrastructure: Server
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers taking over third-party servers, rather than buying or renting them, and using them to stage, launch, and sustain an operation. Under the parent technique, the compromised asset here is a server with an established role, and that role shapes how the intrusion is used: a web server may host a watering hole that serves exploits to selected visitors, while a mail server may be used to send phishing messages that pass the recipient's checks because the sending host has real

topics.title: Compromise Infrastructure: Serverless
topics.summary: Instead of renting a server, the adversary gains control of a serverless function, a small piece of code that a cloud provider runs on demand, and lets the provider's own network carry the traffic. A tampered function can answer infected hosts directly or forward their requests to an adversary-controlled backend, so the client only ever talks to a familiar cloud hostname. The artefacts live in the control plane and in execution logs: unexpected function deployments, edited environment variables,

topics.title: Compromise Infrastructure: Virtual Private Server
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers seizing a virtual private server, meaning a rented machine or container at a cloud provider, that belongs to somebody else and using it as operational infrastructure. The parent technique covers compromising third-party assets in general; here the asset is a hosted virtual machine. The operator gains not only a machine but also the provider's reputation and the legitimate customer's history, so outbound traffic originates from a host that may already appear in allowlist

topics.title: Compromise Infrastructure: Web Services
topics.summary: Rather than building new infrastructure, the adversary takes over an existing account on a third-party web service such as a code host, social platform, file-sharing site or bulk email provider, and reuses that provider's reputation as a launch point. Because the traffic flows to and from subdomains of well-known services, it blends into the noise defenders already tolerate. Detection depends on account-level telemetry rather than destination reputation: authentication events from unusual locati

topics.title: Container Administration Command
topics.summary: Container administration command abuse means using the management interface of a container platform to run code inside a container instead of on the host. The Docker daemon, the Kubernetes API server, and the kubelet all expose APIs that legitimately allow remote management, and anyone who obtains suitable credentials, a service account token, or reachability to an unauthenticated socket can turn those APIs into an execution channel. Documented mechanisms include specifying a command or entrypoi

topics.title: Container and Resource Discovery
topics.summary: Container and resource discovery is the enumeration of a container environment to learn what is running, which images exist, and how the platform is arranged. Attackers query the Docker or Kubernetes APIs, read platform logs, or use a web dashboard to list containers, pods, deployments, nodes, namespaces, and overall cluster status. Docker logs in particular can disclose configuration details, which services are reachable, and even which cloud provider hosts the workload. Kubernetes API response

topics.title: Content Injection
topics.summary: Content injection is the manipulation of network traffic in transit so the victim receives adversary supplied content instead of, or alongside, the genuine response. Two patterns are described. In a from the middle position the adversary sits between a client and a server and rewrites what passes in either direction. In a from the side position the adversary races the real server and delivers a forged response first. Because the manipulation happens upstream, often at an internet service provide

topics.title: Create Account
topics.summary: Create Account describes adversary creation of new accounts to maintain access after an initial foothold is lost or remediated. The accounts involved can be local or domain user accounts, accounts holding administrative rights, cloud and SaaS identities, service principals, or machine accounts created through directory APIs, and they can be created on a single host, in the enterprise directory, or in a hosted tenant the organisation only partially monitors. The technique is favoured because a fr

topics.title: Create Account: Cloud Account
topics.summary: Cloud account creation is the persistence variant in a hosted identity service, where the intruder adds a user, service principal or role based identity instead of a machine or directory account. Providers differ in how they model this: one directory service offers user objects plus service principals and managed identities that can be attached to applications, functions or virtual machines; another offers service accounts that can be linked to resources and impersonated; and a third has no serv

topics.title: Create Account: Domain Account
topics.summary: Domain account creation is the persistence variant where the intruder adds an account to the central directory rather than to a single host, so one credential unlocks every system and service that trusts that domain. With enough rights, the command that adds a user in Active Directory Domain Services can be run against the domain controller, which produces a directory object with organisation wide reach. The advantage for the attacker is scale and cover: the new account authenticates normally on

topics.title: Create Account: Local Account
topics.summary: Local account creation is a persistence behaviour in which an intruder with sufficient rights adds a user account that exists only on one machine or device, so future access needs no malware to remain installed. On Windows the built in account management command can add a user and then place it in a privileged local group, on Linux the user creation utility does the same, on macOS the directory services command line tool can create the entry, and appliances, ESXi hosts and Kubernetes clusters ea

topics.title: Create or Modify System Process
topics.summary: Creating or modifying a system-level process means registering the payload with the component that the operating system already starts at boot and keeps alive afterwards. On Windows that component is the Service Control Manager with service entries under the registry key HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services; on Linux it is the init system, usually systemd; on macOS it is launchd, which reads property list files. The shared property that makes this attractive is the second execution context: th

topics.title: Create or Modify System Process: Container Service
topics.shortTitle: Create or Modify System Process: Container Service
topics.summary: Container platforms run their own long-lived services on the host, and those services can be configured to start workloads automatically. On a single host, Docker and Podman run as daemons, and a container started with a restart policy such as restart=always is brought back by the daemon after a reboot or a crash, so the container becomes a persistent process that no login triggers. Where the parent technique installs a service, this sub-technique instead configures the container platform, so th

topics.title: Create or Modify System Process: Launch Agent
topics.shortTitle: Create or Modify System Process: Launch Agent
topics.summary: A Launch Agent is the per-user half of launchd persistence on macOS. The artifact is a property list file, a plist, placed in /System/Library/LaunchAgents, /Library/LaunchAgents, or ~/Library/LaunchAgents, and it is loaded by the per-user launchd instance when that user logs in. The keys that matter for detection are Label, which names the task, ProgramArguments, which holds the executable path and its arguments, and RunAtLoad or KeepAlive, which decide whether the job runs at login and whether

topics.title: Create or Modify System Process: Launch Daemon
topics.shortTitle: Create or Modify System Process: Launch Daemon
topics.summary: Launch Daemons are the system-wide counterpart to Launch Agents. They are property list files read by launchd from /System/Library/LaunchDaemons and /Library/LaunchDaemons, and unlike agents they are loaded before anyone logs in and run on behalf of every user. Installing one requires elevated privileges, and the program it names inherits administrative rights, which is exactly why the technique appears in macOS malware that wants a durable, unprivileged-looking foothold with powerful execution.

topics.title: Create or Modify System Process: Systemd Service
topics.shortTitle: Create or Modify System Process: Systemd Service
topics.summary: Systemd is the service manager and init system on most modern Linux distributions, and it is driven entirely by unit configuration files, most of them ending in .service. System level units live under the system directories below /, typically /etc/systemd/system and /usr/lib/systemd/system, while user units live under the user's home directory. Within a unit, ExecStart, ExecStartPre, and ExecStartPost run when the service starts, whether that is at boot or from systemctl start; ExecReload runs o

topics.title: Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service
topics.shortTitle: Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service
topics.summary: A Windows service is a background process started by the Service Control Manager, and its configuration lives in the registry, primarily under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services. Each service key holds an ImagePath that names the executable, plus optional failure recovery commands, a start type that decides whether it loads at boot, and an ObjectName that decides which account the process runs as. An attacker with administrative rights can add a new service, repoint an existing ImagePath, or

topics.title: Credentials from Password Stores
topics.summary: Credentials from Password Stores is the parent behaviour of taking secrets from the places designed to hold them rather than from memory, network traffic or plain files. The locations differ by platform and product: browser password databases, macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager and Credential Locker, Linux keyring services, application configuration vaults and cloud secret managers. Because each store uses its own protection, the technique varies from decrypting a local database with a k

topics.title: Credentials from Password Stores: Cloud Secrets Management Stores
topics.shortTitle: Credentials from Password Stores: Cloud Secrets Managemen...
topics.summary: Cloud secrets managers are central services that hold API keys, database passwords and tokens so that applications no longer keep them in plain text files or environment variables. Because the service is designed to hand out secrets to authorised consumers, an attacker with the right permissions does not need to break any encryption. They call the same interface that legitimate workloads use, for example a get-secret-value operation in AWS, a secrets describe command in GCP, or a key vault secre

topics.title: Credentials from Password Stores: Credentials from Web Browsers
topics.shortTitle: Credentials from Password Stores: Credentials from Web Br...
topics.summary: Adversaries harvest saved website logins from the local credential stores that browsers keep for user convenience. On Windows the Chromium family writes a database file named Login Data, and the password column holds ciphertext protected by a key that is itself wrapped with the signed-in user's secrets, so copying the file alone is not enough. The attacker also reads the browser's local state file or asks the Data Protection API (DPAPI) to unwrap that key, then decrypts each stored row in memory

topics.title: Credentials from Password Stores: Keychain
topics.summary: The macOS Keychain Services system stores account names, passwords, private keys, certificates, payment data and secure notes across three collections: the login keychain for the user, the system keychain for items shared by the host, and the local items keychain used for iCloud synchronisation. It is a sub-technique of Credentials from Password Stores because the target is this specific store, and the accessible paths are the database files under the user, system and network library directories

topics.title: Credentials from Password Stores: Password Managers
topics.shortTitle: Credentials from Password Stores: Password Managers
topics.summary: Third-party password managers hold a user's entire credential set inside one encrypted database that is unlocked with a master password. While the vault is open, the plaintext entries and often the derived master key exist in the process memory, because the application needs them to fill forms and copy secrets to the clipboard. Attackers therefore rarely attack the file encryption directly. They read the memory of the running password manager, inject code into it, or abuse a documented software

topics.title: Credentials from Password Stores: Securityd Memory
topics.shortTitle: Credentials from Password Stores: Securityd Memory
topics.summary: Rather than reading the keychain database directly, this sub-technique reads the memory of securityd, the macOS service that implements security protocols such as encryption and authorisation. An adversary with root access can scan the process memory for the derived master key that protects a logged-in user's keychain, and once that key is found the remaining encrypted values can be unlocked in turn, yielding plaintext passwords for accounts, Wi-Fi, mail, browsers, certificates and secure notes.

topics.title: Credentials from Password Stores: Windows Credential Manager
topics.shortTitle: Credentials from Password Stores: Windows Credential Manager
topics.summary: Windows Credential Manager keeps saved sign-ins for websites, applications and network resources in containers called Credential Lockers, which older documentation described as Vaults. Entries for Internet Explorer and Edge live in the Web Credentials locker, while application and network entries sit in the Windows Credentials locker. Each locker is a folder of encrypted files inside the user profile, and the key that protects them is stored beside them, itself wrapped with the user's own logon

topics.title: Data Destruction
topics.summary: Data destruction is the deliberate overwriting of file contents rather than the removal of directory entries. Simple deletion unlinks a name from its data, and the blocks usually remain readable to forensic tools, so wipers write over the data with random bytes, fixed patterns or even image files before removing the name. The scope can be a single host or an entire estate, and destructive tooling frequently borrows lateral movement and credential access behaviour so it can spread before it strik

topics.title: Data Destruction: Lifecycle-Triggered Deletion
topics.summary: Lifecycle triggered deletion is a cloud native form of data destruction. Object storage services let an owner attach a lifecycle policy to a bucket so objects are transitioned, archived or expired after a set number of days. An adversary holding the right permission simply rewrites that policy so every object expires almost immediately, and the provider service performs the deletion on its own schedule. The attacker never issues a bulk delete call, which makes the event look like routine houseke

topics.title: Data Encoding
topics.summary: Data encoding is the reformatting of command and control traffic with a standard scheme so that the payload does not read as instructions. It is not encryption: the transformation follows published rules such as hexadecimal, Base64, MIME or a character encoding, and anyone who knows the scheme can reverse it. The operational purpose is to break up signatures, defeat keyword matching, and blend into protocols that already carry encoded content, such as web form fields, mail attachments or structu

topics.title: Data Encoding: Non-Standard Encoding
topics.summary: Non-standard encoding hides command and control (C2) content by changing how bytes are represented before they travel over a protocol such as HTTP or DNS, rather than by encrypting them. The operator and the implant share a private scheme, which may be a lightly modified Base64 alphabet, a custom byte-to-text mapping, or a wrapper that reorders and mixes the payload with plausible-looking fields. Because the scheme departs from the published specification, signature and protocol-parsing tools th

topics.title: Data Encoding: Standard Encoding
topics.summary: Standard encoding is the specific case of data encoding in which the adversary uses a published, widely implemented scheme that already fits the protocol in use. ASCII, Unicode, hexadecimal, Base64 and MIME are the documented examples, and some schemes reduce size as well, as gzip compression does when combined with a text conversion. The important property is that the resulting blob is valid for the protocol, so a mail gateway or web proxy parsing the message sees nothing out of specification a

topics.title: Data Encrypted for Impact
topics.summary: Data encrypted for impact is the technique of rendering data unusable to its owner by encrypting it in place, typically to extort payment or to degrade an organisation's ability to operate. The mechanism relies on the same cryptographic primitives that protect data legitimately: a symmetric cipher such as AES with a randomly generated key for bulk file content, and asymmetric or hybrid wrapping of that key so the victim cannot recover it without the adversary's secret. Implementations vary. Some

topics.title: Data from Cloud Storage
topics.summary: Data from Cloud Storage describes collection of objects held in managed storage rather than through a normal business application. The targets are object stores such as Amazon S3, Azure Storage and Google Cloud Storage, and the document or file services that sit behind office suites and chat platforms, including OneDrive, Google Drive, Dropbox, Slack, Confluence and Salesforce. Where no front end application exists, the objects are listed and downloaded directly with provider programming interfa

topics.title: Data from Configuration Repository
topics.summary: Data from Configuration Repository covers collection aimed at the central systems that hold configuration and management data for many devices at once, rather than at the devices themselves. These repositories are the memory of a management platform: they store device configuration files, software inventories, interface and address details, routing information, and frequently the credentials or keys the platform uses to log in to everything it manages. An adversary who reads from them obtains, i

topics.title: Data from Configuration Repository: Network Device Configuration Dump
topics.shortTitle: Data from Configuration Repository: Network Device Config...
topics.summary: Network Device Configuration Dump is the sub-technique of Data from Configuration Repository in which the adversary retrieves complete configuration files from network devices rather than walking individual management variables. Device configuration holds the parameters that decide how the device operates: interface addressing, routing and access control rules, logging destinations, device identity for authentication services, and very often reusable secrets such as service account names, encryp

topics.title: Data from Configuration Repository: SNMP (MIB Dump)
topics.shortTitle: Data from Configuration Repository: SNMP (MIB Dump)
topics.summary: SNMP MIB Dump is the sub-technique of Data from Configuration Repository in which the adversary reads the Management Information Base of network devices over Simple Network Management Protocol. The Management Information Base is a structured repository: every manageable variable has an object identifier, a numeric address in a tree, and holds values such as the system description, hardware model, physical location, installed software, interface counters, address resolution entries, routing infor

topics.title: Data from Information Repositories
topics.summary: Data from information repositories is the collection stage in which an adversary mines the collaboration and storage systems a business already uses, instead of hunting for files on a single endpoint. These platforms hold policies, network and architecture diagrams, technical documentation, test credentials left in notes or code, project schedules, source snippets and customer records, and most of them are reachable from any authenticated account. The behaviour is largely ordinary search and rea

topics.title: Data from Information Repositories: Code Repositories
topics.shortTitle: Data from Information Repositories: Code Repositories
topics.summary: Code repositories are version controlled stores of source code, usually with build pipelines, issue tracking and package registries attached, and this sub-technique is the parent behaviour aimed at them. The valuable material is not only the current product source: commit history, configuration files, infrastructure definitions, build scripts, pipeline variables and developer notes frequently contain credentials, internal host names and architectural detail that shortens an adversary's next step

topics.title: Data from Information Repositories: Confluence
topics.summary: Confluence is a wiki style information repository, so this sub-technique is the parent behaviour narrowed to one product family and its search, space and page model. It is usually deployed beside issue tracking tools in development teams, which means its content skews towards engineering: runbooks, design documents, environment details, source snippets and credentials pasted into pages for convenience. An adversary holding any valid account can use the built in search for words such as password,

topics.title: Data from Information Repositories: Customer Relationship Management Software
topics.shortTitle: Data from Information Repositories: Customer Relationship...
topics.summary: Customer relationship management software is the system of record for customer interactions, so this sub-technique is the parent behaviour directed at the data a business holds about the people it serves. Records typically include names, email addresses, phone numbers, postal addresses, purchase history, support conversations and sometimes partial payment details, and the platform usually offers reporting, export and integration features that move data in bulk. An adversary with a valid account,

topics.title: Data from Information Repositories: Databases
topics.summary: Databases concentrate the records an organisation depends on, so this sub-technique is the parent behaviour aimed at structured data stores, whether self hosted or delivered as a managed cloud service. Targets range from relational systems to document and analytics platforms, and the data of interest includes usernames, hashed passwords, personal information and financial records. Collection can happen through the normal database protocol with a valid account, through an application that already

topics.title: Data from Information Repositories: Messaging Applications
topics.shortTitle: Data from Information Repositories: Messaging Applications
topics.summary: Messaging applications are where much day to day business conversation happens, so this sub-technique is the parent behaviour applied to chat platforms such as Microsoft Teams, Slack and Google Chat. The material of interest is informal and often more revealing than formal documentation: credentials and connection strings pasted into channels, source code snippets, links to internal shares, product plans, and discussions about an incident that is still being handled. That last category makes cha

topics.title: Data from Information Repositories: Sharepoint
topics.summary: SharePoint is a document and collaboration platform, so this sub-technique is the parent behaviour applied to one product whose content and permission model differ from a wiki. Sites and document libraries usually hold the files an organisation actually works from: policies, network and architecture diagrams, project plans, spreadsheets, contracts, and the occasional test credential. Adversaries tend to use the same client interfaces as employees, including the web application, the desktop sync

topics.title: Data from Local System
topics.summary: Data from Local System describes collecting files and information that already exist on a compromised host before exfiltration. The adversary searches the local file system, stored configuration, embedded databases, virtual machine disk images and process memory for documents, key material and records of interest, often driven by a command interpreter or by a network device command line that can read local storage. The activity is broad and mostly indistinguishable from ordinary administrator wo

topics.title: Data from Network Shared Drive
topics.summary: Network shared drives are a collection source rather than an intrusion method: an adversary who already holds an account or a session on a host browses file shares reachable from it and copies whatever looks valuable. Shares are commonly mounted by the operating system as drive letters or mount points and are accessed with built-in tooling, so the intruder issues ordinary directory listings and file copies instead of deploying a custom collector. The resulting artefacts live mostly on the server

topics.title: Data from Removable Media
topics.summary: Data from removable media describes collecting information from storage that is attached to or inserted in a compromised computer, such as optical discs, memory cards, and Universal Serial Bus drives. The intruder needs no malware for this: ordinary shell commands list drives, enumerate files, and copy interesting items to a staging location before exfiltration. Because the media is local, the collection can avoid network-based monitoring entirely, and the strongest evidence therefore sits at th

topics.title: Data Manipulation
topics.summary: Data Manipulation covers adversary changes to information that affect what a person, process or system concludes from it. The goal is not to steal the data or make it unavailable, but to make it wrong in a way that serves the attacker, whether that shifts a business outcome, misleads analysts or covers the traces of other activity. The technique spans stored records, data moving between systems, and data that exists only in memory, and the practical impact depends entirely on which process consu

topics.title: Data Manipulation: Runtime Data Manipulation
topics.summary: Runtime Data Manipulation changes what a user or a process sees when data is read, without altering the stored record itself. The adversary normally edits the application that presents the information: a patched binary, a swapped dynamic library, a replaced reporting script, or a shim loaded ahead of the real component. A related route is changing file associations so that opening a data file launches a different program, or masquerading a tool under a trusted name. The stored value stays truthf

topics.title: Data Manipulation: Stored Data Manipulation
topics.summary: Stored Data Manipulation narrows the parent technique to data at rest, meaning records sitting in databases, documents on file shares, archived mail and proprietary file formats. The adversary edits those records directly rather than intercepting data as it moves between systems or while it exists only in memory, so the change persists until somebody notices and corrects it. Because the edit is made through normal file or database access, the application may never log a suspicious transaction, a

topics.title: Data Manipulation: Transmitted Data Manipulation
topics.summary: Transmitted Data Manipulation covers tampering with information while it moves between systems rather than after it is written to storage. The adversary places itself on the path, for example on a compromised network device, a malicious forward proxy, an injected library inside a data pipeline, or a middle position on an internal link, and rewrites fields inside the stream. Because the receiving side builds its stored record from the tampered stream, that record looks internally consistent, and

topics.title: Data Obfuscation
topics.summary: Data Obfuscation covers the tricks an adversary uses to make command and control traffic hard to recognise rather than hard to read. The channel may stay plaintext, be partly encoded, or be wrapped in something that looks ordinary, but the aim is to break signature matching, protocol parsers and content inspection. Defenders see this as anomalies inside otherwise familiar traffic: unusual byte distributions, protocol fields that ignore the specification, or conversations whose content never deco

topics.title: Data Obfuscation: Junk Data
topics.summary: Junk Data is the simplest form of data obfuscation: the adversary keeps a normal-looking protocol conversation but pads it with random or meaningless bytes. Junk may be prepended, appended, or interleaved between the meaningful characters, so a parser that expects a clean structure either fails or returns garbage. Because the wrapper protocol is unchanged, the traffic still passes firewalls and still resembles the protocol it mimics at connection level. Defenders notice sessions whose payload si

topics.title: Data Obfuscation: Protocol or Service Impersonation
topics.shortTitle: Data Obfuscation: Protocol or Service Impersonation
topics.summary: Protocol or Service Impersonation makes command and control traffic pass as a trusted protocol or a well-known cloud service. The adversary may fake a TLS handshake so later bytes appear encrypted, or shape HTTP headers, URI paths and certificates to resemble Gmail, Google Drive, or an internal business application. The traffic usually reaches infrastructure the adversary controls, or abuses a legitimate service as a relay, so reputation based blocking is weak on its own. The distinguishing arte

topics.title: Data Obfuscation: Steganography
topics.summary: Steganography hides command and control data inside another file or message so the carrier looks innocent. The adversary embeds bytes in image pixels, document structure, audio samples, or unused protocol header fields, then moves the carrier through a normal channel such as a web upload or a mail attachment. Unlike encryption, the goal is to hide that a secret message exists at all, so a defender must detect the carrier rather than decrypt its payload. Artefacts include media files whose size o

topics.title: Data Staged
topics.summary: Data staging is the consolidation step that sits between collection and exfiltration. Rather than sending each stolen file out as it is found, an attacker gathers material into a central location or directory, either as many separate files or combined through archiving, and then removes it in fewer, larger transfers. The reason is operational rather than technical: every outbound connection is an opportunity for a network sensor, a proxy log, or a data loss prevention rule to fire, so reducing t

topics.title: Data Staged: Local Data Staging
topics.summary: Local data staging keeps the collected material on the machine where it was found, which makes it the quietest form of consolidation because no network traffic is generated until the very end. The parent technique describes gathering data centrally before exfiltration; this sub-technique is the same pattern confined to one host. After searching the file system, a mail client cache, or a database, the attacker copies or moves the selected files into a single directory, often a temporary path, a u

topics.title: Data Staged: Remote Data Staging
topics.summary: Remote data staging concentrates material taken from several machines onto one host before it leaves the network. It is the same consolidation idea as the parent technique, but the collection point is a different system from the source of the data, which means the staging host becomes a visible hub: it receives files from many internal peers in a short period and then pushes a much larger volume outward. Attackers reach the collection point through the same mechanisms already used for lateral mo

topics.title: Data Transfer Size Limits
topics.summary: Data transfer size limits split exfiltration into fixed size chunks or cap packet sizes so that no single transfer crosses the thresholds defenders use to flag large outbound movements. The adversary's motive is economical rather than technical: many monitoring rules and data loss prevention policies are built around volume, so keeping each request small means the individual event looks like ordinary browsing or update traffic while the total over days may exceed everything the organisation sent

topics.title: Debugger Evasion
topics.summary: Debugger evasion covers the checks a program performs to work out whether a human analyst is watching it, together with the change in behaviour that follows. On Windows the classic signals are the IsDebuggerPresent and NtQueryInformationProcess functions and the BeingDebugged flag inside the Process Environment Block; on Linux a process can read the TracerPID field in its own status file under the proc filesystem. Malware may also look for hardware breakpoints, watch for interrupt instructions,

topics.title: Defacement
topics.summary: Defacement is the unauthorised alteration of content that people see, used to deliver a message, intimidate an audience, or claim credit for an intrusion. The change itself is usually small, such as replacing a home page, a login banner or a desktop background, but the purpose is psychological and reputational rather than purely technical. The mechanism is ordinary content modification: editing a file in a web root, publishing through a content management system, changing a wallpaper setting in

topics.title: Defacement: External Defacement
topics.summary: External defacement changes content that people outside the organisation can see, most often a public website, and is used to deliver a political message, embarrass the victim, or claim credit for the intrusion. The delivery mechanism varies: a compromised content management account, a web application weakness that allows file writes, a publishing pipeline that accepts attacker content, or redirection of traffic so a different page is served. Significant cases are treated as public events, so th

topics.title: Defacement: Internal Defacement
topics.summary: Internal defacement targets content that only the organisation can see: intranet pages, internal portals, server login banners, and the desktop background on user workstations. The purpose is intimidation and doubt rather than public messaging, because the audience is staff who already believe the network is protected. Typical mechanics are replacing a web page inside the corporate network, editing the text shown on a logon screen, or changing the wallpaper setting through the registry or a poli

topics.title: Delay Execution
topics.summary: Delay execution is a set of timing tricks used to keep malicious activity away from the moment of inspection and to separate events that a correlation rule would otherwise link. The simplest form is a programmatic sleep, pausing before the payload acts. A second form borrows legitimate scheduling: the actor registers the work with the operating system's task scheduler so it runs later, which also makes the trigger look like ordinary maintenance. A third form uses benign commands as filler, such

topics.title: Deobfuscate/Decode Files or Information
topics.summary: Deobfuscation is the step in which an attacker converts deliberately hidden data back into something usable on the victim system. The initial file, script or registry value is not the real payload; it is a container holding encoded, compressed, encrypted or split content, and the real behaviour only appears once the container is unpacked. Attackers rarely ship a decoder of their own, because the operating system already offers one: the certificate utility can decode a base64 blob hidden inside a

topics.title: Deploy Container
topics.summary: Adversaries deploy containers to run code and to sidestep controls that watch for malicious processes on a host. The deployment may use a malicious image that already contains the payload, or a benign public image that downloads and executes code at start up, which keeps the image itself unremarkable. Attackers also deliberately deploy containers configured without the network policies, resource limits, or user restrictions that normally apply, so they obtain a permissive environment inside an o

topics.title: Develop Capabilities
topics.summary: Developing capabilities is the in-house engineering stage of resource development: the adversary identifies a requirement, builds the tool that meets it, and keeps the result exclusive rather than buying or downloading something defenders may already recognise. Outputs range from malware and loaders to exploits, command and control protocols, and self-signed certificates that lend apparent authenticity to a payload. Work may be contracted out, yet it still counts as adversary development when th

topics.title: Develop Capabilities: Code Signing Certificates
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers creation of code signing certificates, usually self-signed, before a payload is signed. Code signing attaches a cryptographic signature to an executable or script so that a recipient can check the stated author and confirm the file has not changed since it was signed. The trust decision is the weak point: many users, and some tools, treat any valid signature as a positive signal without checking whether the issuing authority is one the organisation recognises. A self-si

topics.title: Develop Capabilities: Digital Certificates
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers an adversary generating their own self-signed SSL/TLS (Secure Sockets Layer / Transport Layer Security) certificates while building out infrastructure, before any victim is touched. The attacker runs a key generation and certificate signing tool, so the same private key that the certificate describes is also the key that signs the certificate. The resulting files contain a public key, a subject identity, and a signature made without approval from any external certificat

topics.title: Develop Capabilities: Exploits
topics.summary: This sub-technique describes an adversary writing their own exploit code to attack a bug in software or hardware, rather than downloading or buying one. The work starts from a known vulnerability, often found through vulnerability intelligence, patch analysis of a vendor update, or fuzzing, which means feeding malformed input to a program until it crashes in an interesting way. The result is a reliable trigger that drives the target into unintended behaviour such as memory corruption or command

topics.title: Develop Capabilities: Malware
topics.summary: This sub-technique is the malware engineering side of capability development: writing payloads, droppers, loaders, backdoors, packers and command and control protocols, and sometimes preparing infected removable media. The emphasis falls on purpose-built code the adversary controls and can update, which is why one family may share configuration formats and protocol quirks across separate intrusions even when the compiled binaries differ. Some builders deliberately plant artefacts associated with

topics.title: Device Driver Discovery
topics.summary: Device driver discovery is the enumeration of the drivers and kernel modules present on a host, usually as a step before choosing an escalation path. A driver list reveals what hardware the machine has, which security products are installed through their filter drivers, whether the host is a real workstation or a virtual machine, and which third party drivers might carry a known vulnerability. On Windows the work is done with the driverquery command line tool, the EnumDeviceDrivers interface, or

topics.title: Direct Volume Access
topics.summary: Direct volume access means opening a raw handle to a whole logical volume rather than to a file inside it, so a program reads and writes the underlying file system structures itself. Because the read does not travel through the normal file path, file level permissions, access checks and the file system filter drivers that record file activity may never see the operation. Attackers use it to copy registry hives, locked database files or the contents of an entire drive, and they often reach for bu

topics.title: Disable or Modify System Firewall
topics.summary: Disable or Modify System Firewall covers tampering with host-based and network firewall policy to remove restrictions on traffic and open paths for later action. Once sufficient privileges are held, the adversary turns off firewall profiles, edits existing rules so previously blocked ports or protocols are permitted, or adds rules that create covert channels, for example allowing a remote desktop protocol on an unusual port that is less scrutinised than the standard one. Platform specifics vary:

topics.title: Disable or Modify System Firewall: Cloud Firewall
topics.shortTitle: Disable or Modify System Firewall: Cloud Firewall
topics.summary: Cloud firewall controls live in the provider control plane rather than on the guest host, so an attacker who holds valid cloud credentials rarely needs to touch the operating system to open a path in. They call the provider interface to add an ingress rule to an existing security group, create a permissive group, or attach a new rule set to a running instance, often widening a single port to every address or allowing all protocols. Because the change happens in the management plane, the artefact

topics.title: Disable or Modify System Firewall: Network Device Firewall
topics.shortTitle: Disable or Modify System Firewall: Network Device Firewall
topics.summary: Here the target is the filtering function inside network hardware such as routers, switches, and dedicated edge appliances, not a host or a cloud tenant. An attacker who reaches a management interface, either with valid device accounts or by exploiting a public-facing service, edits access control lists, security zones, or policy rules so that traffic which was previously blocked is now permitted, often by adding a broad permit for internal subnets. The evidence lives in the device configuration

topics.title: Disable or Modify System Firewall: Windows Host Firewall
topics.shortTitle: Disable or Modify System Firewall: Windows Host Firewall
topics.summary: On Windows the firewall is a host service with three profiles, named domain, private, and public, and its state and rules can be changed from several places. An attacker holding local administrator rights can turn a profile off, or add a rule that opens a port for remote access or command and control, using built-in tools such as netsh advfirewall or the PowerShell firewall cmdlets, by editing the relevant registry keys directly, or through the Windows Security interface. topics.title: Disable or Modify Tools
topics.summary: Disable or Modify Tools is the broad degradation of defensive controls and of the sensors that feed detection. Adversaries stop security services, kill their processes, edit configuration files and registry keys, block product updates, and tamper with logging pipelines such as Event Tracing for Windows (ETW), audit policy, and central log forwarding. topics.title: Disable or Modify Tools: Clear Linux or Mac System Logs
topics.shortTitle: Disable or Modify Tools: Clear Linux or Mac System Logs
topics.summary: Clearing Linux or Mac System Logs is the Unix-family counterpart to deleting evidence already written, and it covers the text logs that most native services keep under the shared system log directory. On Linux the targets are the general message log, the authentication logs, the login records, kernel, scheduled job, mail, and web server logs; on macOS the same directory holds system, install, and application logs alongside the unified logging store. topics.title: Disable or Modify Tools: Clear Windows Event Logs
topics.shortTitle: Disable or Modify Tools: Clear Windows Event Logs
topics.summary: Clearing Windows Event Logs removes evidence that has already been written, in contrast to the sibling behaviours that stop collection. The adversary runs a built-in utility, a scripting command, or uses the graphical viewer to delete the contents of the System, Application, or Security log, or deletes the stored log files directly from the directory where Windows keeps them. Because Windows records the act of clearing in the very log being cleared, a single deletion produces a distinctive pair

topics.title: Disable or Modify Tools: Disable or Modify Cloud Log
topics.shortTitle: Disable or Modify Tools: Disable or Modify Cloud Log
topics.summary: Cloud Log tampering degrades the audit record in a cloud tenant or subscription, where visibility is a product feature rather than a fixed property of the host. Adversaries with sufficient permissions reconfigure the collection plane itself: disabling or trimming a multi-region trail, removing the notification topics that deliver findings, turning off log file validation or encryption settings, or excluding services and regions from capture. In productivity suites the equivalent is per-user audi

topics.title: Disable or Modify Tools: Disable or Modify Linux Audit System Log
topics.shortTitle: Disable or Modify Tools: Disable or Modify Linux Audit Sy...
topics.summary: This sub-technique degrades the Linux Audit system, the kernel-level facility that produces the host's security-relevant record of process, file, network, and login activity. Where the Windows counterpart targets a service and a policy store, here the adversary aims at the audit daemon, its rule definitions, and sometimes the library functions the daemon calls. topics.title: Disable or Modify Tools: Disable or Modify Windows Event Log
topics.shortTitle: Disable or Modify Tools: Disable or Modify Windows Event Log
topics.summary: This sub-technique targets the Windows Event Log service, the component that writes the records analysts depend on for authentication and process activity. Unlike clearing existing logs, the objective here is to stop or reconfigure collection, so the service no longer starts, no longer writes, or no longer receives the audit categories of interest. Behaviours include changing the service startup type, modifying the Start value under the service and WMI autologger registry keys, and adjusting aud

topics.title: Disable or Modify Tools: Modify or Spoof Tool UI
topics.shortTitle: Disable or Modify Tools: Modify or Spoof Tool UI
topics.summary: Modify or Spoof Tool UI is the deception layer of Disable or Modify Tools. Rather than removing a defence, the adversary misrepresents its state so that the humans who rely on its console, tray icon, or dashboard believe protection is active. Typical behaviour is a stand-in interface that reports a healthy status, a completed update, or no threats while the underlying service, driver, or agent has already been disabled or degraded. It is usually paired with the impairment it conceals, which is w

topics.title: Disk Wipe
topics.summary: Disk wipe is an impact technique in which the adversary destroys raw disk data to remove availability rather than to steal anything. Instead of deleting files through the operating system, the attacker writes directly to the storage device and overwrites sectors, either across arbitrary regions of the volume or at the specific on disk structures that are needed to boot. topics.title: Disk Wipe: Disk Content Wipe
topics.summary: Disk content wipe is the half of disk wiping that destroys data itself rather than the structures that describe it. The adversary obtains direct access to the storage device and overwrites arbitrary regions of it, often with random bytes, so that whole areas of the volume become meaningless even though the disk is still readable by the hardware. Because the file system metadata may survive in places, a victim can be left with a volume that mounts and reports files that no longer contain anything

topics.title: Disk Wipe: Disk Structure Wipe
topics.summary: Disk structure wipe targets the small, critical regions of storage that a computer needs in order to start, rather than the bulk of the data. The master boot record holds the first code the firmware runs and the table describing where partitions begin, and if those bytes are overwritten the machine has nothing valid to hand over to an operating system. topics.title: Domain or Tenant Policy Modification
topics.summary: Domain or tenant policy modification abuses the central control plane of a managed identity environment. Instead of attacking each machine, an adversary with delegated rights edits the settings that every machine or user obeys: Group Policy Objects in Active Directory, domain trust and federation configuration, or tenant settings in a cloud identity service. The direct cost of the edit is trivial, but the effect is multiplied because the setting is applied automatically and at scale. Changes are

topics.title: Domain or Tenant Policy Modification: Group Policy Modification
topics.shortTitle: Domain or Tenant Policy Modification: Group Policy Modifi...
topics.summary: Group Policy modification is the Active Directory branch of policy abuse. A Group Policy Object is a directory object linked to sites, domains or organisational units, and its settings are stored as files under the domain share in the SYSVOL folder. Any principal with write permission on the object or on the policy template files can add a preference, a logon script, a service setting or a scheduled task that the affected computers apply on their next policy refresh. Detection rests on the fact

topics.title: Domain or Tenant Policy Modification: Trust Modification
topics.shortTitle: Domain or Tenant Policy Modification: Trust Modification
topics.summary: Trust modification changes the relationships that let one domain or identity tenant accept authentication from another. In Active Directory this means editing existing trust objects, adding a new trust, or converting a domain to a federated one so that tokens signed by a certificate the attacker controls are accepted. In a cloud identity service it means registering an external identity provider or changing federation and claim rules so an attacker chosen identity maps to a privileged user. The

topics.title: Domain Trust Discovery
topics.summary: Domain trust discovery maps the relationships that let one Windows domain or forest accept identities from another. An attacker who already holds one valid account queries that graph from inside, because trusts reveal which domains will accept a Kerberos referral or an access token issued elsewhere. The work is done through directory queries or through the Windows directory service trust enumeration interface, and it is frequently wrapped in the built in nltest utility using its trust listing op

topics.title: Downgrade Attack
topics.summary: Downgrade attacks abuse backward compatibility: instead of breaking a control, the attacker makes the system use an older component or protocol version that never had the control in the first place. topics.title: Drive-by Compromise
topics.summary: A drive by compromise needs no attachment and no convincing message: the user is infected while browsing, because content the browser loads on a page the user chose to visit has been placed there by an attacker. Delivery has several shapes. The site itself may be legitimate but compromised, with an injected script or frame that loads attacker content. The page may pull a script from a cloud storage bucket that was left publicly writable, so the operator can change the script without touching the

topics.title: Dynamic Resolution
topics.summary: Dynamic Resolution is the umbrella for techniques in which malware does not carry a fixed destination but computes one at run time. The implant and the adversary's infrastructure share an algorithm, so the same inputs produce the same domain, address or port on both sides, leaving no hard coded indicator for defenders to block. topics.title: Dynamic Resolution: DNS Calculation
topics.summary: DNS Calculation derives the command and control port from values inside an ordinary Domain Name System (DNS) answer rather than using a fixed port or the returned address itself. topics.title: Dynamic Resolution: Domain Generation Algorithms
topics.summary: Domain Generation Algorithms (DGAs) are routines that deterministically produce large lists of candidate domains from changing inputs such as the date, a counter or a seed value. The implant queries the candidates until one resolves, and the adversary pre registers only the few names for the current period, so the rendezvous point is cheap to maintain and impossible to block with a static list. topics.title: Dynamic Resolution: Fast Flux DNS
topics.summary: Fast Flux DNS hides command and control behind a domain that resolves to a large, constantly changing pool of addresses. Two variants exist. In single flux, many address records are published for one name with very short Time To Live (TTL) values, so the answer changes between queries and each query may return a different host. topics.title: Email Bombing
topics.summary: Email bombing is a volumetric technique against a human inbox rather than a service. The adversary subscribes the target address to large numbers of newsletters, signup forms and mailing lists that do not use confirmed opt-in, so the victim receives thousands of messages within minutes. Some variants simply send bulk mail directly. topics.title: Email Collection
topics.summary: Email collection targets the mailbox, which concentrates business detail, personal data, password resets, shared documents and, in an incident, the plans and coordination of the responders themselves. Adversaries gather it in two broad ways: from the client side, by reading local mail store files or taking over an open session on a workstation, and from the server side, by authenticating to a mail platform with stolen credentials or tokens and querying it directly. Server side collection is attr

topics.title: Email Collection: Email Forwarding Rule
topics.summary: Email forwarding rule abuse is the creation of a mailbox level rule so that incoming mail is copied or redirected to an address the adversary controls. The rule is stored in the mailbox on the server, not on the endpoint, so it keeps working after a password reset, after session tokens are revoked, and after the user's laptop is rebuilt. Rules can be created from the desktop mail client, from the web interface, by command line tooling, or by an administrator acting on many mailboxes at once. The

topics.title: Email Collection: Local Email Collection
topics.summary: Local email collection is the client side half of email theft: the adversary reads mailbox data that already sits on a compromised workstation rather than querying a mail server. Outlook keeps messages in local database files, with .ost files backing cached and IMAP accounts and .pst files used for personal stores such as POP accounts or exports, and both typically live under the user profile in the Outlook Files folder or a local application data path. Because these files are ordinary user docu

topics.title: Email Collection: Remote Email Collection
topics.summary: Remote email collection is the server side half of email theft. Instead of reading files on a workstation, the adversary authenticates to a mail platform, whether an on premises Exchange deployment, a hosted mail service or a cloud productivity suite, and retrieves messages from there. Access may use stolen user credentials, an application or OAuth style token, a service account, or an existing mail protocol session such as a direct client connection that avoids the web interface entirely. Becau

topics.title: Encrypted Channel
topics.summary: An encrypted channel is command and control traffic that the malware itself encrypts, rather than relying only on whatever protection the carrier protocol already provides. The operator selects an algorithm, generates or embeds a key, and encrypts the payload before it is placed inside the transport. The plaintext instruction therefore never appears on the wire, so content inspection and simple signatures fail. What remains observable is metadata: the destination, the timing and regularity of th

topics.title: Encrypted Channel: Asymmetric Cryptography
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers command and control traffic that uses a public key algorithm, where each party holds a key pair made of one public key and one private key. The sender encrypts with the receiver's public key, and only the matching private key can decrypt, so the operator can distribute a key openly without giving away the ability to read messages. Common algorithms here are RSA and ElGamal. Public key operations are much slower than symmetric ones, so most real protocols use them only t

topics.title: Encrypted Channel: Symmetric Cryptography
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers command and control traffic protected with a symmetric algorithm, where one secret key both encrypts the plaintext and decrypts the ciphertext. Common choices seen in the field include the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES), the Data Encryption Standard (DES), triple DES (3DES), Blowfish and RC4. topics.title: Endpoint Denial of Service
topics.summary: Endpoint denial of service attacks the host and the software stack on it rather than the path to the host. Traffic may be modest in volume, but it is shaped to consume a resource the service cannot do without: connection state tables, worker threads, memory pools, name resolution caches, or processor cycles spent on expensive operations. topics.title: Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
topics.shortTitle: Endpoint Denial of Service: Application Exhaustion Flood
topics.summary: Application exhaustion floods push on the most expensive features an application offers rather than on the platform beneath it. Every non trivial application contains operations whose cost is far higher than the cost of asking for them: generating a report, running a wide database query, reindexing a search, rendering a large image, converting a document, or computing a password hash. Repeated requests to those paths consume processor time, memory, database connections, or temporary storage, and

topics.title: Endpoint Denial of Service: Application or System Exploitation
topics.shortTitle: Endpoint Denial of Service: Application or System Exploit...
topics.summary: Application or System Exploitation is the availability-impact variant of denial of service in which the adversary abuses a software vulnerability rather than sheer traffic volume. A single crafted request, malformed file, or protocol message can terminate a process, panic a kernel, or exhaust a resource inside a service. topics.title: Endpoint Denial of Service: OS Exhaustion Flood
topics.shortTitle: Endpoint Denial of Service: OS Exhaustion Flood
topics.summary: Operating system exhaustion targets the kernel layer, where finite tables and self imposed limits sit. The defining property is that the machine does not need to run out of real capacity; it only needs to reach the maximum number of concurrent connections, backlog entries, or state lookups the operating system allows. topics.title: Endpoint Denial of Service: Service Exhaustion Flood
topics.shortTitle: Endpoint Denial of Service: Service Exhaustion Flood
topics.summary: Service exhaustion floods aim at the software that answers requests rather than at the kernel's connection tables. The target is a specific daemon with its own practical ceiling: a web server with a limited worker pool, a name server with a bounded request queue, a database with a connection cap, or a mail gateway with a fixed number of concurrent sessions. topics.title: Escape to Host
topics.summary: Escape to host describes breaking out of a container or virtual machine to reach the system underneath. Isolation is enforced by kernel namespaces, control groups, hypervisor boundaries, and mandatory access control profiles, and an escape normally abuses a configuration mistake or a flaw in that boundary rather than the application inside it. topics.title: Establish Accounts
topics.summary: Establishing accounts is the deliberate construction of identities the adversary will use later, and it sits in resource development because the work happens before any victim is touched. A usable persona needs more than a registration: a plausible name, a work history, a profile photo, posts, and connections to other accounts, so a target who searches for the sender finds corroboration rather than an empty shell. Email accounts are the most reusable asset, because nearly every other service, in

topics.title: Establish Accounts: Cloud Accounts
topics.summary: Cloud accounts give an adversary storage, compute and messaging capacity without owning a single server, and they are usually obtained through a self-service sign-up that needs only a mailbox and a payment method. The same tenant can stage exfiltration in object storage, serve tooling, run virtual machines or serverless functions, and send bulk mail through notification or email services whose domains carry strong sender reputation. topics.title: Establish Accounts: Email Accounts
topics.summary: Email accounts are the hinge of persona work, because almost every other service, including domain registration, cloud tenancy, code hosting and trial subscriptions, verifies identity through a mailbox. The adversary therefore creates mailboxes meant to survive scrutiny: mainstream providers when a plausible corporate identity is needed, disposable services when anonymity matters more, and addresses shaped to resemble a person or a brand. topics.title: Establish Accounts: Social Media Accounts
topics.summary: This sub-technique narrows account establishment to social platforms, where a persona has to survive being looked up by the very people it approaches. The work is mostly cultivation: naming the profile after a plausible real or invented person, borrowing a photo, listing employers and schools that exist, then gradually connecting with genuine users so mutual contacts appear. topics.title: ESXi Administration Command
topics.summary: This technique abuses the guest management services that virtualisation platforms install inside virtual machines so the host can look after them. A background agent runs in each guest and exposes remote operations, which on Windows guests appears as a tools daemon process, with equivalent daemons on Linux and macOS. topics.title: Event Triggered Execution
topics.summary: Event triggered execution covers persistence that is driven by a subscription rather than by a startup list or a schedule. The host, the shell, or the cloud platform is asked to watch for a condition, and when that condition appears the watched code runs. topics.title: Event Triggered Execution: Accessibility Features
topics.summary: The Windows logon screen starts accessibility helpers such as sethc.exe, the Sticky Keys program, and utilman.exe, the Utility Manager, inside the winlogon session before any user has authenticated. An adversary abuses the keyboard shortcut that starts those helpers, either by overwriting the helper binary in the system folder or by repointing the registry references that name it, so the shortcut launches attacker code instead. topics.title: Event Triggered Execution: AppCert DLLs
topics.summary: The AppCertDLLs value under the Session Manager area of the registry holds a list of libraries that Windows loads into every process which calls one of the process creation interfaces, such as CreateProcess, CreateProcessAsUser, CreateProcessWithTokenW or WinExec. topics.title: Event Triggered Execution: AppInit DLLs
topics.summary: The AppInit_DLLs value under the Windows NT key, and its Wow6432Node twin for 32-bit code, tells the user32 library which extra modules to load. Since user32 is loaded by almost every graphical program, an entry there reaches an extremely large number of processes and gives the adversary persistence and a route into processes that hold higher rights. topics.title: Event Triggered Execution: Application Shimming
topics.summary: The Application Compatibility Infrastructure sits between a program's import table and the operating system, so that old software keeps working on a new build. Shims are grouped into databases with the sdb extension, held in the AppPatch folder, and the installed and custom sets are registered under the compatibility flags area of the registry; administrators install custom databases with the sdbinst utility. topics.title: Event Triggered Execution: Change Default File Association
topics.shortTitle: Event Triggered Execution: Change Default File Association
topics.summary: Windows decides which program opens a file from the file name extension, and those mappings live in the registry. An extension such as .txt is listed under HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT, and its default value names a handler class; the handler class then holds one or more action keys under its shell subkey, and each action has a command subkey whose value is the command line Windows runs. topics.title: Event Triggered Execution: Component Object Model Hijacking
topics.shortTitle: Event Triggered Execution: Component Object Model Hijacking
topics.summary: Component Object Model is the Windows mechanism that lets software components interact through the operating system, and each component is named by a class identifier that the registry maps to a library or a server. Because the registry lookup checks the current user's classes area before the machine-wide area, a component can be redirected with a write to a user-writable key and no administrator rights. topics.title: Event Triggered Execution: Emond
topics.summary: The Event Monitor Daemon on macOS, called emond, is a launch daemon that accepts events from other services, passes them through a simple rules engine and performs the matching action. It loads rule files in the property list format from the rules directory under the etc folder, and its launch daemon configuration names a queue directory that must contain at least one file, otherwise the service does not start. topics.title: Event Triggered Execution: Image File Execution Options Injection
topics.shortTitle: Event Triggered Execution: Image File Execution Options I...
topics.summary: Image File Execution Options is a registry area that lets a developer attach a debugger to a program. Each targeted executable has a subkey, and a Debugger string value inside it is prepended to the image name when the process is created, so the debugger runs and the real binary becomes its argument. topics.title: Event Triggered Execution: Installer Packages
topics.summary: Installer packages bundle the files and the instructions an operating system needs to place software on a host, and those instructions include scripts that run before and after the copy step. On macOS a package uses preinstall and postinstall scripts that execute as root, on Linux the deb and rpm formats use maintainer scripts named preinst, postinst, prerm and postrm that also run as root, and on Windows the installer service runs custom actions described inside the package. topics.title: Event Triggered Execution: LC_LOAD_DYLIB Addition
topics.summary: Mach-O is the executable format used by macOS and OS X, and a Mach-O file begins with a series of load commands that tell the kernel and the dynamic linker how to build the process. One of those commands, the load dynamic library command, records a library that must be loaded when the binary starts. Attackers can add one of these commands to an existing binary, pointing at a malicious dynamic library, so the payload executes inside the process every time that binary is run. topics.title: Event Triggered Execution: Netsh Helper DLL
topics.shortTitle: Event Triggered Execution: Netsh Helper DLL
topics.summary: Netsh is the command line utility Windows uses to inspect and change network configuration, and it is extensible: it loads helper dynamic link libraries that add functionality. The list of helper libraries is stored in the registry under the Netsh key in the local machine software hive, which means registering a helper is a registry change rather than a file placed in a startup folder. topics.title: Event Triggered Execution: PowerShell Profile
topics.summary: PowerShell reads profile scripts at the start of every session, unless the interpreter is launched with the NoProfile switch. There is a profile for all users and all hosts, one for all users of a single host program, one for the current user across hosts, and one for the current user in a specific host such as the console, the integrated scripting environment or an editor. topics.title: Event Triggered Execution: Python Startup Hooks
topics.shortTitle: Event Triggered Execution: Python Startup Hooks
topics.summary: The Python interpreter performs site initialisation before it runs any user script. During that step it processes path configuration files, which are text files with the pth extension found in the site-packages or dist-packages directories: a line that begins with import is executed, not merely added to the search path. topics.title: Event Triggered Execution: Screensaver
topics.summary: A Windows screensaver is an executable with the .scr extension that the desktop starts after a configured period of user inactivity, and the settings that control it live in the registry under the current user's Control Panel desktop key. topics.title: Event Triggered Execution: Trap
topics.summary: The trap builtin in Unix shells registers a command list that the shell runs when it receives a specified signal. Signals are the operating system's way of telling a process that something happened, and the keyboard interrupt from control and C, the terminal end signal, and the shell exit signal are the ones users meet most often. topics.title: Exclusive Control
topics.summary: Exclusive control describes an adversary hardening a host it already owns so that rival actors cannot use the same foothold. The mechanism is anything that removes an entry path after the attacker is inside: applying the vendor patch for the vulnerability that was originally exploited, stopping or uninstalling the affected service, resetting or stripping privileges from the accounts that provided access, closing administrative shares, or deleting other malware families found on the host. topics.title: Execution Guardrails
topics.summary: Execution guardrails are conditions the operator embeds in their own tooling so that it acts only where they intend. Before doing anything useful, the code inspects something about the host or its surroundings, such as the name of a mapped network share, the presence of a particular attached device, a file that exists only on the target, the Active Directory domain the machine is joined to, or a local and external address range, and it proceeds only when the observed value matches the expected o

topics.summary: Environmental keying is the cryptographic form of an execution guardrail. Rather than comparing a value and branching, the payload is stored encrypted and the decryption key is derived from a value that exists only in the intended environment, such as a network share name, a hardware or device identifier, an installed software version, the contents of a specific file, the Active Directory domain, the system time, or a local or external address. topics.title: Execution Guardrails: Mutual Exclusion
topics.summary: Mutual exclusion guardrails use a named system object, normally a mutex, as a marker that a host has already been infected. The loader creates the mutex with a fixed or algorithmically derived name and checks the creation result: a fresh handle tells it that no other copy is running, while an already-existing object tells it to exit quietly. topics.title: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol
topics.summary: Exfiltration over an alternative protocol covers theft in which the data leaves through a protocol other than the one carrying the command and control channel, and often to a different network destination than the main control server. topics.title: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
topics.summary: Exfiltration over a command and control channel is the transfer of collected data out of a victim environment using the same communication path the adversary already uses to task and control implanted tooling. topics.title: Exfiltration Over Other Network Medium
topics.summary: Exfiltration over another network medium means moving collected data out of a target through a path that is not the primary command and control route, for example a wireless connection, a mobile data link, a modem line, a Bluetooth pairing or another radio channel. topics.summary: Exfiltration over Bluetooth is the sub-technique of using a short range radio pairing to move collected data off a host. It differs from its parent only in the medium: the transfer travels over Bluetooth instead of a wireless, cellular or modem link, and the practical consequence is proximity. topics.title: Exfiltration Over Physical Medium
topics.summary: Exfiltration over a physical medium is theft in which data leaves on hardware instead of over the network: a removable drive, an external disk, a phone, a media player, or any other portable device that can store or forward files. It is the natural choice where the network offers no way out, most obviously on an air-gapped estate, and it can serve either as the final exit point or as a bridge that moves data between systems that are not connected to each other. topics.shortTitle: Exfiltration Over Physical Medium: Exfiltration over USB
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers data leaving an environment on removable USB storage rather than over a network path. It is the variant defenders meet in air-gapped or heavily segmented estates, where the adversary either brings a device in, plugs it into a host, stages the collected files onto it, and carries it out, or uses the device as a bridge between two systems that never talk to each other. topics.title: Exfiltration Over Web Service
topics.summary: Exfiltration over a web service moves data out of an environment through legitimate, publicly available or tenant sanctioned online services rather than through adversary controlled infrastructure. The mechanism sidesteps the assumption that egress to unknown destinations is the thing worth blocking. topics.shortTitle: Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration Over Webhook
topics.summary: Exfiltration Over Webhook abuses the outbound webhook feature of software as a service (SaaS) platforms to push data out of the tenant. A webhook is a URL that a service calls automatically when something changes, so an adversary who can create or edit a webhook in a victim tenant points it at an endpoint they control and lets the platform deliver the content. topics.shortTitle: Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
topics.summary: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage moves collected data into a consumer or enterprise file service such as Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive or Box instead of sending it over the primary command and control channel. Many clients synchronise automatically, so a file copied into a synced folder leaves the network without any explicit upload command, and the resulting traffic is HTTPS to a well known domain. topics.shortTitle: Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Code Repos...
topics.summary: Exfiltration to Code Repository hides stolen data inside ordinary developer traffic. The adversary uses a code hosting service such as GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket as the destination, normally through the service's application programming interface (API) over HTTPS, so the transfer appears as a routine push, commit, gist or release upload. topics.summary: Exfiltration to Text Storage Sites uses public paste services to park stolen data as plain text. The adversary posts content to a site such as pastebin[.]com through a web form or the site's application programming interface (API), often receiving a short URL that can be fetched later from anywhere. topics.title: Exploit Public-Facing Application
topics.summary: Exploit Public-Facing Application covers adversary exploitation of weaknesses in internet-reachable software to obtain code execution, data access or a foothold inside a network. topics.title: Exploitation for Client Execution
topics.summary: Exploitation for client execution is the abuse of a software flaw in an application that the victim runs locally, in order to obtain code execution in that application's context. The targets are the programs people use constantly: browsers and their rendering engines, office and productivity suites, document readers, media players, messaging clients and chat add-ons. topics.title: Exploitation for Credential Access
topics.summary: Exploitation for credential access means using a software flaw in an authentication or credential handling component to obtain usable credentials, or to bypass the check that would normally be required. topics.title: Exploitation for Defense Impairment
topics.summary: This technique is not tied to one product. It describes using a software flaw in a security control as the way to weaken or remove that control. The vulnerable component is the defense itself, such as endpoint detection and response agents, antivirus drivers, edge firewall appliances, or cloud and software as a service security boundaries, and attackers commonly run discovery first to learn which of those products is present in the environment. topics.title: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
topics.summary: Exploitation for privilege escalation is the use of a programming flaw in software the victim already runs to gain rights the attacker was not granted. The target is chosen for its privilege level: a service running as system or root, a kernel component, a setuid program on Linux, or a driver that runs in the most trusted processor mode. topics.title: Exploitation for Stealth
topics.summary: Exploitation for stealth covers the use of a software flaw not to gain more access but to keep existing access hidden. An adversary abuses a bug in a logging pipeline, a monitoring agent, a security product or a cloud control plane so that activity stops producing records, alerts are dropped, or work happens inside a component that telemetry does not cover.
