topics.title: Exploitation of Remote Services
topics.summary: Exploitation of remote services is the use of a software flaw in a network facing service to run attacker controlled code on another host, most often to move laterally inside a network that is already partly compromised. The target may be an operating system component, a file sharing service, a remote desktop service, a database listener or a management appliance, and the injected code runs with the privileges of that service. topics.title: External Remote Services
topics.summary: External Remote Services describes adversary use of legitimate remote access services to gain an initial foothold or to re-enter an environment from outside the perimeter. The services involved are ones the organisation exposes deliberately for business reasons: virtual private network concentrators, remote desktop gateways, remote shell and file transfer services, and hosted remote management or desktop-as-a-service platforms. topics.title: Fallback Channels
topics.summary: Fallback channels are reserve communication paths that malicious software keeps in case the primary path fails, is blocked or starts drawing attention. A typical implant carries a list of destinations, protocols or mediums and walks down that list when a connection fails, when a domain is blocked or sinkholed, or when traffic volume crosses a threshold the operator wants to stay below. topics.title: File and Directory Discovery
topics.summary: File and Directory Discovery is the enumeration of a file system: listing directory contents, walking folder trees, and searching filenames or file contents for terms such as password, backup, or key. topics.title: File and Directory Permissions Modification
topics.summary: File and directory permissions modification covers the deliberate rewriting of access control rules so that an adversary gains rights the operating system would otherwise refuse. Every mainstream platform expresses these rules differently, but the shape of the abuse is consistent: the attacker either grants themselves access to an object they cannot currently touch, or removes access from others so that defenders cannot read, replace or clean the file. Extended access control lists can add finer entries on top of that model in supported filesystems, but the two everyday commands that change how access is decided are the one that changes ownership and the one that changes the mode bits and any extended list.

topics.title: Financial Theft
topics.summary: Financial theft covers adversary activity whose purpose is to take money, whether by direct transfer, fraud, extortion, or manipulation of cryptocurrency systems. It is rarely a single technique; it is a goal reached through chains such as compromising an account and impersonating a trusted party to authorise a payment, or encrypting and exfiltrating data and then demanding payment to restore access and prevent publication. topics.title: Firmware Corruption
topics.summary: Firmware corruption targets the software stored in non volatile memory on hardware: the motherboard firmware that starts the machine, drive controller firmware, network adapter firmware, and the management controller used for remote administration. topics.title: Forced Authentication
topics.summary: Forced authentication turns a victim machine into the client of an attacker controlled service, so that the machine volunteers its own credentials instead of the attacker having to guess them. The mechanism depends on a design choice in Windows networking: when a system is asked to open a network resource, it authenticates automatically as the current user rather than waiting for a prompt. topics.title: Forge Web Credentials
topics.summary: Forge Web Credentials covers the creation of new authentication material for web applications and internet services, rather than the theft or interception of material that already belongs to a user. topics.title: Forge Web Credentials: SAML Tokens
topics.summary: SAML Tokens is the sub-technique of Forge Web Credentials in which the adversary creates Security Assertion Markup Language assertions and signs them with a token signing certificate they control, so that federated services accept them as issued by the trusted identity provider. topics.title: Forge Web Credentials: Web Cookies
topics.summary: Web Cookies is the sub-technique of Forge Web Credentials in which the adversary manufactures session cookies rather than collecting them from a victim browser. Many web applications keep a user signed in with a cookie whose contents are structured and signed: a user or session identifier, an issue and expiry time, sometimes roles or other attributes, and a signature or message authentication code produced with a server side secret. topics.title: Gather Victim Host Information
topics.summary: Gathering victim host information is collection about individual systems rather than networks: administrative attributes such as host name and assigned address, and configuration specifics such as operating system, language, browser, and running software versions. topics.shortTitle: Gather Victim Host Information: Client Configurations
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers collection of client side configuration detail rather than installed applications: operating system family and build, processor architecture, virtualisation platform, system language, locale and time zone. topics.summary: This sub-technique of Gather Victim Host Information narrows the focus from applications to firmware, the low level software stored on device chips such as basic input output systems, network switch images, router code and baseboard controllers. topics.summary: This sub-technique narrows host information gathering to physical equipment: the make, model, and version of servers, workstations, laptops, and network devices on specific hosts, plus the presence of additional components that signal stronger protection, such as card or biometric readers and dedicated encryption hardware. topics.title: Gather Victim Host Information: Software
topics.summary: Adversaries map the software running on victim hosts so they can pick exploits that are known to work and avoid wasting effort on hardened systems. Collection is usually passive or semi-passive: reading version banners from exposed services, capturing user agent strings from a planted web page, mining file metadata such as PDF producer fields, or simply reading job adverts and purchase invoices that name products. topics.title: Gather Victim Identity Information
topics.summary: Gather Victim Identity Information is the reconnaissance behaviour of collecting facts about the people inside a target organisation before contact. The material includes ordinary personal detail such as names, job titles, work email addresses, and answers to security questions, and it extends to sensitive authentication material such as passwords, session tokens, and the multi-factor authentication methods registered to an account. topics.summary: This sub-technique is the credential focused branch of victim identity gathering, and it is the one that most directly enables access. Credentials reach an adversary by three main routes. topics.shortTitle: Gather Victim Identity Information: Email Addresses
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers collecting the email addresses of a target organisation's staff, which is the step that converts a company name into a working target list. topics.shortTitle: Gather Victim Identity Information: Employee Names
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers collecting the names of a target organisation's employees, which is the raw material for everything that follows in a social engineering campaign. topics.title: Gather Victim Network Information
topics.summary: Gathering victim network information is the broad collection of network-level facts an adversary assembles before touching a target: allocated address ranges, owned domain names, routing structure, and the services exposed to the internet. topics.title: Gather Victim Network Information: DNS
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers the Domain Name System records that describe a victim's naming and mail estate. topics.shortTitle: Gather Victim Network Information: Domain Properties
topics.summary: This sub-technique narrows the parent activity to the registration and administrative facts attached to a victim's domain names, rather than the network itself. topics.shortTitle: Gather Victim Network Information: IP Addresses
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers the collection of the Internet Protocol addresses allocated to a victim, typically as contiguous blocks rather than individual hosts. topics.summary: This sub-technique covers reconnaissance aimed specifically at the defensive network devices guarding a victim: firewalls, content filters, proxies and bastion hosts, network-based intrusion detection systems (NIDS), and related security appliances. topics.shortTitle: Gather Victim Network Information: Network Topology
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers the physical and logical arrangement of a victim's networks, both the internet-facing edge and the internal segments behind it, including gateways, routers, and other infrastructure that defines how traffic flows. topics.title: Gather Victim Org Information
topics.summary: Gathering victim organisation information is collection about how a target business is structured and operated: divisions and departments, the nature of its daily business, and the roles and responsibilities of key employees. topics.title: Gather Victim Org Information: Business Relationships
topics.shortTitle: Gather Victim Org Information: Business Relationships
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers collection about the organisations a victim depends on and is depended on by: managed service providers, contractors, and partners that hold connected and often privileged network access, plus the supply chains and shipment paths that deliver hardware and software. topics.shortTitle: Gather Victim Org Information: Determine Physical Locations
topics.summary: This sub-technique narrows organisation gathering to physical geography: where a victim's offices, data centres, warehouses, and key infrastructure sit, and which legal jurisdiction and authorities govern each site. topics.title: Gather Victim Org Information: Identify Business Tempo
topics.shortTitle: Gather Victim Org Information: Identify Business Tempo
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers collection about when a victim organisation is active and when it is not: operational hours, working days, holiday shutdowns, and the timing of purchases and shipments. topics.title: Gather Victim Org Information: Identify Roles
topics.shortTitle: Gather Victim Org Information: Identify Roles
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers collection about the identities inside a victim organisation and what each person is able to reach. Adversaries map names to job titles, teams, and responsibilities, then infer access: who approves payments, who administers directory or cloud systems, who handles sensitive projects or executive support. topics.title: Generate Content
topics.summary: Generate Content covers the adversary work of producing written, audio, visual, or multimedia material that supports targeting and operations, rather than producing code. The material itself is the payload of persuasion: personas, impersonated organisations, pretexts, forged documents, and influence narratives tailored to a specific victim or region. topics.title: Generate Content: Audio-Visual Content
topics.summary: Audio-Visual Content is the media-focused part of Generate Content. Adversaries produce synthetic voice recordings, manipulate audio or video during live calls, fabricate profile photographs and identity documents, and create video showing people who never said or did those things. Production ranges from manual editing through AI-assisted generation to paid synthetic media services, and the goal is often a single convincing moment during a voice or video interaction rather than a mass campaign.

topics.title: Generate Content: Written Content
topics.summary: Written Content is the text-focused part of Generate Content: phishing lures, fraudulent financial communications, fabricated job adverts, forged employment credentials, decoy documents, and the persona text that sustains a false identity over weeks or months. topics.title: Group Policy Discovery
topics.summary: Group Policy discovery is the enumeration of centrally managed configuration in an Active Directory domain. Group Policy Objects are the containers that hold these settings, and their files sit under a predictable path inside the SYSVOL share on domain controllers, which any authenticated domain user can usually read by default. topics.title: Hardware Additions
topics.summary: Hardware additions are the introduction of physical computing or networking devices into an environment to create access that did not exist before. The category covers more than a USB stick carrying files: it includes single board computers hidden behind a desk, rogue wireless access points, network taps, inline devices that rewrite traffic, keystroke injectors that present themselves as keyboards, and expansion cards that read memory directly. topics.title: Hide Artifacts
topics.summary: Hide artifacts is a defensive evasion technique that covers the many ways an adversary conceals the traces of their activity instead of removing the activity itself. Operating systems provide legitimate concealment features so that system files, administrative execution, and management accounts do not clutter or disrupt the user environment, and those same features can be turned against the defender. topics.title: Hide Artifacts: Bind Mounts
topics.summary: Bind Mounts abuse a Linux feature that maps a directory or file onto another location in the same file system. An adversary with root privileges can overlay the process directory of a benign process onto the process directory belonging to a malicious one. Utilities such as ps and top read process information through the file system, so the kernel follows the mount and reports the benign details instead of the real ones. topics.title: Hide Artifacts: Email Hiding Rules
topics.summary: Email Hiding Rules abuse the rule engine inside a mailbox or a mail transport to divert messages the adversary does not want read. Rules can move mail into low visibility folders, mark it as read, forward it elsewhere or delete it, and they commonly filter on ordinary message content such as keywords, senders or subjects. They can be created from a mail client or remotely through mailbox management cmdlets and interfaces. Mailbox audit records capture rule creation and modification, folder moves

topics.title: Hide Artifacts: Extended Attributes
topics.summary: Extended Attributes describes hiding payloads inside the key and value metadata that macOS and Linux attach to files and directories. These attributes are not shown by ordinary tools such as Finder, ls or cat, and they persist because they are stored beside the file rather than inside its content. On Linux they are grouped into namespaces with different permission rules, and on macOS they appear as flat strings, many of them under the com.apple prefix and used by Gatekeeper and Spotlight. topics.title: Hide Artifacts: File/Path Exclusions
topics.summary: File and Path Exclusions describes placing malicious files in locations that antivirus and other scanners are configured not to read. Scanning products exclude folders and file names to cut performance cost and to avoid breaking legitimate applications, and those exclusions are often hardcoded defaults rather than decisions made by the local administrator. topics.title: Hide Artifacts: Hidden File System
topics.summary: Hidden File System describes an adversary maintaining a private storage structure that the operating system never mounts or presents. Payloads and working data live inside it, so directory listings, indexing services and file-based scanners never see the contents. Implementations range from a small volume embedded in unused disk space, to a portable partition image dropped as an ordinary file, to content fragments scattered across the disk in ways the resident file system does not describe. topics.title: Hide Artifacts: Hidden Files and Directories
topics.shortTitle: Hide Artifacts: Hidden Files and Directories
topics.summary: Hidden files and directories is the file system half of artifact hiding, and it exploits conventions that every major operating system uses to keep the user's workspace tidy. topics.title: Hide Artifacts: Hidden Users
topics.summary: Hidden users is the account focused branch of artifact hiding, and it matters because attacker created accounts are one of the most durable forms of persistence. Operating systems and desktop environments offer several ways to keep an account out of the place where people normally look, which is the logon screen and the graphical user management interface. topics.title: Hide Artifacts: Hidden Window
topics.summary: Hidden Window describes adversaries suppressing the visible interface of a program so that nothing appears on screen while it runs. On Windows this is usually done with interpreter flags such as the hidden window style in PowerShell, or by writing Registry values that place console windows off screen. topics.title: Hide Artifacts: Ignore Process Interrupts
topics.summary: Ignore Process Interrupts describes running commands in a way that survives the signals normally used to stop them. Operating systems deliver signals to control process behaviour, and a terminal session sends a hangup signal when it closes or the user logs off. Utilities such as nohup detach a command from that terminal and ignore the hangup, while interpreter options can suppress the error handling that would otherwise end a script. topics.title: Hide Artifacts: NTFS File Attributes
topics.summary: NTFS File Attributes abuses the metadata structures of the New Technology File System, the Master File Table that holds one record for every file and directory on a volume. A payload can be written into Extended Attributes or into an extra Data attribute, commonly called an alternate data stream, instead of the visible file body. topics.title: Hide Artifacts: Process Argument Spoofing
topics.summary: Process Argument Spoofing hides what a process was actually asked to do by rewriting its command line after the process has been created. Windows keeps a command line in the process environment block, and many sensors read it from there when they log a process start. An adversary can create a process suspended with harmless arguments, allow the creation event to be recorded, then overwrite the stored command line in memory before resuming execution. topics.title: Hide Artifacts: Resource Forking
topics.summary: Resource Forking hides payloads in the resource fork, a secondary stream that classic Mac file systems attached to a file beside its normal data. The fork existed for structured items such as icons, dialogs, menus and code, and on modern macOS it appears as an extended attribute that ordinary file views rarely show. topics.title: Hide Artifacts: Run Virtual Instance
topics.summary: Run Virtual Instance covers adversaries executing their tooling inside a virtual machine, emulator or sandbox on an already compromised host, so that host-based sensors observe only the virtualisation process. Native hypervisors, lightweight emulators and portable hypervisor binaries all serve this purpose, and temporary sandboxes defined by small configuration files are especially quick to stand up. topics.title: Hide Artifacts: VBA Stomping
topics.summary: VBA Stomping hides a malicious macro by removing or replacing the macro source code stored inside an Office document while leaving the compiled version that Office actually executes. Macro source lives in module streams, and each module stream carries a PerformanceCache holding compiled p-code. A separate project stream records which Office build the macro project targets. topics.title: Hide Infrastructure
topics.summary: Hide infrastructure is the collection of tricks used to keep command and control systems alive and hard to attribute. Rather than hiding the channel once it is in use, the adversary hides the infrastructure itself, so that scanners, researchers, and defenders cannot easily find, block, or take it down. topics.title: Hijack Execution Flow
topics.summary: Hijack execution flow is the family of tricks that change which code the operating system actually runs when a program or a library is requested. Rather than breaking a program, the attacker interferes with the lookup or loading step: the directory that is searched first, the order of library paths, a registry value that redirects a load, or an environment variable that names a library to preload. topics.title: Hijack Execution Flow: AppDomainManager
topics.summary: This sub-technique hijacks assembly loading inside the .NET runtime by abusing the application domain manager. Every managed process creates application domains, and the AppDomainManager class decides how those domains are set up and which assemblies are loaded into them. topics.title: Hijack Execution Flow: COR_PROFILER
topics.summary: This sub-technique abuses the .NET Framework profiling feature rather than a Windows service or path. When the CLR starts inside a process, it reads the COR_PROFILER setting and loads the named profiling component, with the DLL location supplied separately in COR_PROFILER_PATH from .NET Framework 4 onward. topics.title: Hijack Execution Flow: DLL
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers abuse of dynamic link libraries (DLLs), the shared code files that Windows programs load at run time, and several distinct behaviours sit under the same label. topics.title: Hijack Execution Flow: Dylib Hijacking
topics.summary: Dylib hijacking is the macOS form of library hijacking: a malicious dynamic library (dylib) is placed where an application will look for it at run time. The dynamic loader walks a list of search paths in order, and entries written with the @rpath prefix let an application resolve libraries relative to its own location, which gives an attacker a predictable place to plant a file. topics.title: Hijack Execution Flow: Dynamic Linker Hijacking
topics.shortTitle: Hijack Execution Flow: Dynamic Linker Hijacking
topics.summary: Dynamic linker hijacking abuses the environment variables that a loader reads before a program starts, such as LD_PRELOAD on Linux and DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES on macOS. Libraries named in those variables are mapped first and take precedence over the system library that provides the same symbols, so the attacker's version of a common function runs instead of the real one. topics.summary: This sub-technique abuses weak permissions around installer processes. topics.title: Hijack Execution Flow: KernelCallbackTable
topics.summary: This sub-technique hijacks a graphical process from inside by rewriting one entry of its KernelCallbackTable, a structure in the PEB that user32.dll fills with the callback routines Windows calls when it delivers certain messages. topics.shortTitle: Hijack Execution Flow: Path Interception by PATH Environm...
topics.summary: This sub-technique intercepts execution by abusing the PATH environment variable, the ordered list of directories the operating system searches when a program is called without a full path. If the attacker can write to a directory that appears earlier in that list than the real binary's directory, a file with the same name is found and run first. topics.shortTitle: Hijack Execution Flow: Path Interception by Search Order ...
topics.summary: This sub-technique abuses the order in which Windows resolves a program name that is given without a full path. When one program starts another by name alone, the operating system checks a sequence of locations, and the directory of the calling program is commonly examined before the system directories. topics.shortTitle: Hijack Execution Flow: Path Interception by Unquoted Path
topics.summary: This sub-technique abuses ambiguity in how Windows resolves an executable path that contains spaces but is not enclosed in quotation marks. topics.shortTitle: Hijack Execution Flow: Services File Permissions Weakness
topics.summary: This sub-technique targets weak filesystem permissions rather than path parsing. When the folder holding a service binary, or the binary file itself, allows an ordinary user to write, an adversary can overwrite or replace that executable and let the service mechanism run it. topics.title: Impair Defenses
topics.summary: Impairing defenses is the deliberate degradation, misconfiguration or removal of security controls so that subsequent activity is neither observed nor blocked. The mechanism exploits the fact that defenders administer their own tools through the same operating system, directory and cloud control planes the adversary is trying to reach. topics.title: Implant Internal Image
topics.summary: Implant Internal Image is persistence that lives in the templates an organisation uses to build workloads. Cloud providers distribute machine images, containers start from base images, and internal registries hold the approved versions of both. topics.title: Indicator Removal
topics.summary: Indicator removal is the deliberate editing or deletion of the records that show what an intruder did, and the defining feature in current reporting is selectivity rather than wholesale wiping. Rather than destroying a whole log, which is loud and obvious, an attacker targets the artefacts that look anomalous and leaves enough ordinary data behind that the system still appears to be behaving normally. topics.title: Indicator Removal: Clear Command History
topics.summary: Clear command history is the narrow form of indicator removal that targets only the record of commands typed into an interactive interpreter. The parent technique covers every kind of artefact, while this sub-technique covers the shell's own memory of a session. The affected storage differs by platform, and so does the attacker's approach. topics.title: Indicator Removal: Clear Mailbox Data
topics.summary: Clearing mailbox data covers the deletion or rewriting of email and mail application records that would otherwise prove how an intrusion began and what was taken. topics.shortTitle: Indicator Removal: Clear Network Connection History and C...

topics.title: Indicator Removal: Clear Persistence
topics.summary: Clear Persistence is the removal of the mechanisms and artefacts an intruder installed to keep access, performed so that investigators cannot describe how the foothold worked. topics.title: Indicator Removal: File Deletion
topics.summary: File Deletion is the cleanup half of an intrusion: once a payload, script, or tool has done its work, the attacker removes it so that responders cannot recover the binary, read its strings, or trace where it came from. topics.shortTitle: Indicator Removal: Network Share Connection Removal
topics.summary: Network Share Connection Removal is the deliberate disconnection of mapped drives and administrative share sessions that an intruder no longer needs. After using Server Message Block (SMB) shares to read files, drop tools, or reach another host, the attacker tears the connection down so that a later review of open sessions and stored credentials shows nothing unusual. topics.title: Indicator Removal: Relocate Malware
topics.summary: Relocate Malware is the copying of a payload to new paths on the same host, or to further hosts, followed by cleanup of the original, so that the file an analyst first identified stops existing and the surviving copy has no obvious history. topics.title: Indicator Removal: Timestomp
topics.summary: Timestomping is the alteration of a file's recorded times so that a hostile file looks older, or at least looks like its neighbours. File systems store several times, typically creation, modification, last access, and a metadata change time, and an attacker can rewrite them with ordinary utilities, a short script, or library calls inside malware, commonly setting a dropped payload to match the dates of signed system binaries in the same folder. topics.title: Indirect Command Execution
topics.summary: Indirect command execution covers the use of legitimate utilities that launch other programs, so that the command line interpreter most commonly watched by defenders is never the parent process. topics.title: Ingress Tool Transfer
topics.summary: Ingress tool transfer covers bringing files and utilities from outside into a compromised environment so later stages have something to work with. The carrier, not the tool, is the technique: files can arrive over an existing command and control session, over alternate protocols such as file transfer and remote copy services, through cloud storage clients that sync automatically once an account is accessed, or through built in download utilities already present on the host. topics.title: Inhibit System Recovery
topics.summary: Inhibiting system recovery is the removal or disablement of the mechanisms that would let an organisation restore systems and data after destructive activity. It is the step that converts a recoverable outage into an existential one, and it is usually executed shortly before or alongside mass encryption or wiping activity. topics.title: Input Capture
topics.summary: Input capture covers the methods used to collect what a person types or submits rather than what a system stores. Credentials are entered constantly at login portals, password dialogs, mail clients and remote access gateways, so intercepting that entry can yield valid accounts that never need to be cracked. topics.title: Input Capture: Credential API Hooking
topics.summary: Credential API hooking intercepts the programming interfaces that handle authentication so that the parameters carrying usernames, passwords or tokens are copied as they pass through. topics.title: Input Capture: GUI Input Capture
topics.summary: Graphical user interface input capture uses believable imitations of operating system and application prompts to make a person type credentials into attacker controlled code. The canonical case is a fake elevation dialog, which copies the look of the prompt Windows shows when a task needs administrator rights, but the same idea appears as fake installers asking for a licence key or password, fake malware removal tools, and lookalike browser or mail client sign in windows. topics.title: Input Capture: Keylogging
topics.summary: Keylogging records the keystrokes a user produces so that credentials can be recovered as they are typed, which is valuable when stored secrets are unavailable or strongly protected and may require long term interception before anything useful is captured. topics.title: Input Capture: Web Portal Capture
topics.summary: Web portal capture plants credential recording code on an externally facing login page so that usernames and passwords are saved or forwarded before the service authenticates the user. The page normally keeps working, which is why the compromise can survive for a long time: users sign in successfully and see nothing wrong. topics.title: Input Injection
topics.summary: Input injection covers any mechanism that manufactures keystrokes, mouse movement or other user input on a victim machine so that actions appear to come from the person at the keyboard. topics.title: Inter-Process Communication
topics.summary: Inter-process communication (IPC) is the set of mechanisms an operating system provides so that processes can exchange data, coordinate work and avoid deadlock, and those same mechanisms can be repurposed to run code. topics.title: Inter-Process Communication: Component Object Model
topics.summary: The Component Object Model (COM) is the native Windows mechanism that lets software components call each other through defined interfaces, without the caller knowing how the server is implemented. topics.title: Inter-Process Communication: Dynamic Data Exchange
topics.summary: Dynamic Data Exchange (DDE) is an older Windows client-server protocol that lets applications exchange strings and data links and, importantly, ask each other to run commands. It was the original transport behind Object Linking and Embedding (OLE) and was later superseded by the Component Object Model (COM), yet it remains registered in many Windows installations and can be switched on by registry settings. topics.title: Inter-Process Communication: XPC Services
topics.summary: On macOS, XPC services carry structured messages between applications and helper daemons, and many of those daemons run as root so that a normal user process can request a privileged task such as a network connection or a file operation. topics.title: Internal Spearphishing
topics.summary: Internal Spearphishing is targeted phishing sent from a trusted account inside the victim organisation instead of from an outside address. The pattern is multi stage: the attacker first controls either a device or the credentials of a real user, then uses that mailbox, calendar or chat identity to reach colleagues, partners or privileged staff. topics.title: Lateral Tool Transfer
topics.summary: Lateral tool transfer covers the copying of tools, payloads or collected files from one compromised host to another inside the same environment. topics.title: Local Storage Discovery
topics.summary: Local storage discovery is the enumeration of drives, volumes and partitions on a host or hypervisor, together with their attributes: capacity, free space, file system type, mount path, device type and volume serial number. topics.title: Log Enumeration
topics.summary: Log enumeration is the reading, exporting, or continuous monitoring of logs on a compromised host or logging platform in order to learn about the environment and about the defenders. An adversary may query the Windows event log with wevtutil or through PowerShell, export security events to a file, or, in cloud environments, pull guest logs through an agent utility, and may then send the collection to their own infrastructure for offline review. topics.title: Masquerading
topics.summary: Masquerading is the manipulation of an artefact's name, path or metadata so that it is mistaken for something legitimate, whether by a person, an automated control or an analyst reviewing evidence. topics.summary: Double file extension masquerading exploits the gap between the file name a user sees and the extension the operating system acts on. topics.title: Masquerading: Masquerade Account Name

topics.title: Masquerading: Masquerade Task or Service
topics.summary: Masquerading a task or service means giving a persistence object a name, display name or description that copies or closely resembles a legitimate one, so that a reviewer scanning a list of scheduled tasks or services sees nothing that stands out. The technique only changes labels and descriptive text; the executable that the object actually launches is what performs the malicious work, which is why name-based review is a weak control. topics.title: Masquerading: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location
topics.shortTitle: Masquerading: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location
topics.summary: Matching a legitimate resource name or location means placing a malicious file, registry key or container object where its name and path are already associated with something trusted. Typical forms are an unsigned executable dropped into a system directory, a payload named after a well-known Windows process, and a registry key whose name is a close approximation of one written by legitimate software, including subtle spelling changes and trailing spaces. topics.title: Masquerading: Overwrite Process Arguments
topics.summary: Overwriting process arguments is a Linux-oriented hiding technique in which a running program rewrites its own command-line memory so that process listings show something benign. The kernel stores the argument strings in the process address space and exposes them through the proc filesystem, and ordinary tools read that same region, so a program that clears the strings and writes a fake first argument changes what an analyst sees without needing elevated privilege. topics.title: Masquerading: Rename Legitimate Utilities
topics.summary: Renaming legitimate utilities covers two related behaviours: giving a trusted system or administration tool a different file name, and moving or copying that tool into a non-standard directory under a new name. Both target controls that key on the tool's name or its usual path rather than on what the binary does. topics.title: Masquerading: Right-to-Left Override
topics.summary: Right-to-left override is a defence evasion sub-technique that abuses the Unicode formatting character U+202E, which reverses the display order of everything that follows it inside a string, file name or registry key. The bytes on disk are unchanged, so the real extension still decides how the operating system handles the file, while the rendered name in a file listing, mail client or document viewer reads backwards and appears harmless. topics.title: Masquerading: Space after Filename
topics.summary: The space after filename sub-technique hides a program's true type by adding a trailing space to the file name. On platforms where the extended attribute that marks an executable is what decides how a file is handled, the trailing space makes the operating system treat the file by its real type, while the extension shown in a file listing suggests a harmless document. The result is that a double click executes code instead of opening a viewer, and the label on screen still shows a document or te

topics.title: Modify Authentication Process
topics.summary: Authentication on every platform is handled by dedicated components: the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service and the Security Accounts Manager on Windows, pluggable authentication modules on Unix-like systems, and authorization plug-ins on macOS. This technique covers any adversary change to those components with one of two goals, either harvesting credentials as they are validated or bypassing validation so that no valid password is needed. The change may be a binary patch in memory, an

topics.title: Modify Authentication Process: Conditional Access Policies
topics.shortTitle: Modify Authentication Process: Conditional Access Policies
topics.summary: Conditional access policies are the rules an identity provider applies before it grants a session: they can require a second factor, demand a managed device, restrict source addresses, or refuse sign-ins that look risky. Cloud platforms express the same idea through policy conditions in their identity and access management rules, checking attributes such as the caller address, the request date, or the region and resource involved. Because these rules are configuration rather than code, this sub-

topics.title: Modify Authentication Process: Domain Controller Authentication
topics.shortTitle: Modify Authentication Process: Domain Controller Authenti...
topics.summary: This sub-technique narrows authentication tampering to the domain controller, the server that validates logons for an entire Windows domain, instead of a component on a single host. A widely documented example injects a master password into the running Local Security Authority Subsystem Service, so the patched service accepts that value for any domain account while still validating genuine passwords normally. Because the patch lives only in memory, a reboot clears it, which is why the technique

topics.title: Modify Authentication Process: Hybrid Identity
topics.summary: Many organisations keep one identity for each user across an on-premises directory and a cloud identity provider, and the glue between them is a set of synchronisation and authentication components. Microsoft environments, for example, can share identities through password hash synchronisation, pass-through authentication, or Active Directory Federation Services, and other cloud platforms also hand authentication to a federation service and receive a token describing the user and their privilege

topics.title: Modify Authentication Process: Multi-Factor Authentication
topics.summary: Multi-factor authentication raises the cost of a stolen password by requiring a second proof, so attackers who already hold working credentials often weaken or remove that second check rather than breaking it. The work is usually administrative rather than technical: an intruder with enough rights edits the identity provider, removes a user or group from the policy that enforces the second factor, or registers an authentication method they control, such as a new phone number or application enrol

topics.title: Modify Authentication Process: Network Device Authentication
topics.shortTitle: Modify Authentication Process: Network Device Authentication
topics.summary: Routers, switches and firewalls run their own operating systems and verify administrator logons locally, often against a small set of configured accounts. This sub-technique covers changes to that system image or its authentication logic so that a password known to the attacker is accepted. Rather than attacking a remote service, the adversary modifies the device firmware or image and installs it, and the inserted code sits in front of the normal checking routine. When a sign-in is attempted, th

topics.title: Modify Authentication Process: Network Provider DLL
topics.shortTitle: Modify Authentication Process: Network Provider DLL
topics.summary: Windows supports add-on network provider libraries so that third-party software can extend network authentication and credential management. During an interactive logon, the Winlogon module passes the user's credentials to the local notification process over a remote procedure call, and that process then distributes them in cleartext to each registered credential manager so the manager can react to the logon event. A library registered as a credential manager therefore receives the account name

topics.title: Modify Authentication Process: Password Filter DLL
topics.shortTitle: Modify Authentication Process: Password Filter DLL
topics.summary: Windows password filters are dynamic libraries that the Local Security Authority loads in order to enforce password policy before a new password is accepted into the Security Accounts Manager. Because a filter must judge the candidate password itself, the operating system hands it the real plaintext value during every password set or reset. An adversary can register a malicious filter by placing a library on the host and adding its name to the notification packages value in the registry, after w

topics.title: Modify Authentication Process: Pluggable Authentication Modules
topics.shortTitle: Modify Authentication Process: Pluggable Authentication M...
topics.summary: On Linux, Unix and macOS, authentication is assembled from pluggable authentication modules, a modular set of configuration files, shared libraries and helper binaries that services call when a user signs in. A service names its configuration, that configuration lists modules in order, and the modules consult files such as the password and shadow files to verify the supplied secret. An adversary who can write to these paths can replace or patch a module so that it accepts a value of their choosi

topics.title: Modify Authentication Process: Reversible Encryption
topics.summary: Active Directory normally stores account passwords as the output of a one-way function, so the stored value cannot be turned back into the original password. The AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption account property changes that behaviour and keeps a recoverable copy of the password, a feature that exists only for legacy protocols needing the original secret. When the property is enabled and the user then sets or changes the password, the directory keeps an encrypted value in the account parameters

topics.title: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure
topics.summary: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure is the parent technique for a family of actions that change the compute layer of a cloud account rather than reading it. The controlled API surface is the resource lifecycle itself: creating and terminating virtual machines, volumes and snapshots, reverting resources to earlier points in time, and adjusting the quotas, policies and regional settings that govern what can be deployed. The defensive problem is that every one of these calls is an authorised manage

topics.title: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure: Create Cloud Instance
topics.shortTitle: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure: Create Cloud Instance
topics.summary: Creating a cloud instance is the compute-side counterpart to snapshot creation, and the two are usually seen together. The adversary provisions a new virtual machine inside the victim account, often from an image they supply or from a snapshot of an existing volume, and deliberately selects a network placement, security group, or identity role that is less restrictive than what guards the existing estate. The new machine has no history, no endpoint agent baseline, and often no logging pipeline,

topics.title: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure: Create Snapshot
topics.shortTitle: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure: Create Snapshot
topics.summary: Creating a snapshot is the storage-side move in cloud compute evasion. A snapshot is a point-in-time copy of a virtual machine, volume, or virtual hard drive, and it is created through an ordinary authorised API call that leaves a clear audit record but no running workload to inspect. The value to an adversary is that the copy can be attached to a different instance under a policy the adversary controls, so data that was protected by the original instance permissions, network rules, or endpoint

topics.title: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure: Delete Cloud Instance
topics.shortTitle: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure: Delete Cloud Instance
topics.summary: Deleting a cloud instance is a destructive cleanup step rather than a stealth one. Once the adversary has finished with a machine, terminating it removes the guest operating system, its event logs, its memory contents, and any files staged on its disks, unless those disks are detached or snapshots exist elsewhere. The same reasoning applies to attacker-created instances that were only ever a temporary workbench. In practice this behaviour produces a distinctive audit trail: an instance creation,

topics.title: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure: Modify Cloud Compute Configurations
topics.shortTitle: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure: Modify Cloud Compute...
topics.summary: This sub-technique targets the settings that acting as guard rails around cloud compute: service quotas, subscription associations, tenant-wide policies, and the regional or size constraints that determine what a subscription is allowed to deploy. Rather than touching a running machine, the adversary changes what the platform will permit, which can be far quieter. topics.title: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure: Revert Cloud Instance
topics.shortTitle: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure: Revert Cloud Instance
topics.summary: Reverting a cloud instance restores a machine or its attached storage to an earlier point in time, typically by applying a snapshot through the provider console or an API call. Where deletion destroys a resource, reversion rewinds one, which is a different defensive problem: the machine keeps running and keeps its identity, but the recent contents that recorded malicious activity are gone. The same effect can be achieved less visibly with ephemeral storage that providers reset on stop or start,

topics.title: Modify Cloud Resource Hierarchy
topics.summary: Cloud providers organise tenants, accounts, subscriptions and resource groups in a hierarchy so that policy and billing can be applied to whole groups at once. This technique describes adversaries editing that hierarchy rather than the workloads inside it. In Azure, an actor holding a Global Administrator role may create new subscriptions or move a pay-as-you-go subscription into a tenant they control, which lets them consume the victim's compute while the activity is logged only on the attacker

topics.title: Modify Registry
topics.summary: The Windows Registry is a hierarchical configuration store, and modifying it is rarely an end in itself: it is how an adversary makes another technique survive, hide or take effect. Values can be written locally with the built in reg utility, through the Windows API from a remote access tool, or over the network when the remote registry service and administrative access are available. Common aims include establishing autostart persistence, weakening defences such as macro restrictions, adjusting

topics.title: Modify System Image
topics.summary: Modify System Image describes adversary changes to the operating system of an embedded network device, such as a router, switch or firewall, in order to weaken defences and add capabilities. These devices normally use a monolithic design: the operating system and nearly all device functionality live inside a single image file, which the boot process loads and runs. That concentration is what makes the technique powerful and what shapes its artefacts. Instead of installing separate programs, the

topics.title: Modify System Image: Downgrade System Image
topics.shortTitle: Modify System Image: Downgrade System Image
topics.summary: Downgrade System Image is the sub-technique of Modify System Image in which the adversary installs an older release of the device operating system instead of altering the current one. Older releases of network device firmware commonly ship weaker default ciphers, fewer hardening options, known and already fixed vulnerabilities, and less mature logging, so the adversary regains ground the vendor had closed. On embedded devices the swap usually means replacing the operating system file in storage,

topics.title: Modify System Image: Patch System Image
topics.shortTitle: Modify System Image: Patch System Image
topics.summary: Patch System Image is the sub-technique of Modify System Image in which the adversary changes the device operating system itself, either in storage so the change appears on the next boot, or in live memory so it takes effect immediately. Embedded network devices are usually monolithic: the operating system and most of the device functionality live in a single file or image, so one edit can alter routing, authentication, encryption and management at once. For the stored case the adversary uses or

topics.title: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
topics.summary: Multi factor authentication interception attacks the second proof of identity rather than the password. An adversary who already holds valid credentials may use a keylogger to capture a token generated code or a smart card personal identification number as the user types it, proxy authentication through an infected host that has the hardware token inserted, or read codes that arrive out of band by email or text message. Codes delivered to phones can also be taken by compromising the handset or t

topics.title: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
topics.summary: Multi-factor authentication request generation describes an adversary who already holds a valid password and then attacks the second factor by making the system send approval prompts to the real user. Push authenticators, one-time codes sent by text message, and automated phone calls can all be triggered simply by attempting a login, so an attacker can repeat the attempt until the user gives in. This pressure is commonly called MFA fatigue. The telemetry is far from subtle: identity providers re

topics.title: Multi-Stage Channels
topics.summary: Multi stage channels split command and control into successive layers rather than using one endpoint for the whole operation. A lightweight first stage beacon checks in, reports basic host details and can pull down additional files; it then hands the host over to a second tool that talks to a completely separate server and offers richer interaction such as a shell. Because each stage uses different hosting and usually different domains or providers, blocking or sinkholing one layer leaves the ot

topics.title: Native API
topics.summary: Native API execution means malware drives the operating system through its own programming interfaces instead of running a separate attacker supplied binary. Applications call documented entry points such as process creation and memory allocation routines, which in turn reach kernel services; the same end result can also be requested by invoking system calls directly from assembly, skipping the user mode libraries that many security products hook. Code can be injected into an already running pro

topics.title: Network Boundary Bridging
topics.summary: Boundary bridging means an adversary takes control of the device that enforces separation between two networks and then changes its policy so traffic that should never cross now does. The target is usually a router or firewall at the perimeter, or an internal segmentation device such as a switch or a virtual firewall sitting between server tiers. The change is configuration rather than code: access control lists, routing entries, address translation rules, or virtual local area network assignmen

topics.title: Network Boundary Bridging: Network Address Translation Traversal
topics.shortTitle: Network Boundary Bridging: Network Address Translation Tr...
topics.summary: This sub-technique is the address translation variant of boundary bridging. A device that performs network address translation rewrites the source or destination address in the IP header as packets cross it, which is how privately addressed networks reach the internet and how external requests find internal services. An adversary with control of that device edits the translation table or its rules so the two separated networks can exchange traffic directly. In designs where translation is mandat

topics.title: Network Denial of Service
topics.summary: Network denial of service attacks attack availability by consuming the transport capacity that a service depends on, rather than the resources of the server itself. The mechanism is saturation: when offered traffic exceeds the bandwidth of the target link, or the capacity of the network devices in front of it, legitimate packets are dropped and users cannot reach the service even though the server is healthy. topics.title: Network Denial of Service: Direct Network Flood
topics.shortTitle: Network Denial of Service: Direct Network Flood
topics.summary: A direct network flood is the simplest shape of denial of service: one or more systems send high volumes of packets straight at the victim's network, with no reflector or third party in the path. topics.title: Network Denial of Service: Reflection Amplification
topics.shortTitle: Network Denial of Service: Reflection Amplification
topics.summary: Reflection amplification is denial of service in which the adversary never sends the bulk of the traffic; innocent third party servers do. The attacker sends a request to a reflector service with the victim's address forged as the source, so the reflector's reply is delivered to the victim. When the response is much larger than the request, the technique amplifies the attacker's bandwidth by orders of magnitude, and well known amplification vectors have historically included domain name system,

topics.title: Network Service Discovery
topics.summary: Network service discovery is the mapping step in which an adversary enumerates listening services on remote hosts and network devices to find something worth attacking or moving toward. The work is done with port scans, service and version probes, and wordlist scans that reach every address in a range and record which ports answer, which are filtered, and what banner or response each one returns. Because the probes are read-only and never complete a real session, the activity produces no authent

topics.title: Network Share Discovery
topics.summary: Network share discovery is the enumeration step where an intruder lists the folders and drives that other machines expose over the network, in order to find where data lives and which hosts are worth moving into. On Windows networks this rides on the SMB protocol, and the usual tools are the built in net command for querying a remote host share list or the local share list, along with equivalents on other platforms such as the sharing listing command on macOS. topics.title: Network Sniffing
topics.summary: Network sniffing is the passive capture of traffic from a network interface so the adversary can read data in transit. The interface is placed into promiscuous mode so the network card accepts frames not addressed to it, or traffic is copied to a monitoring port and captured there, which enlarges the visible traffic without touching the endpoints. The payoff is reconnaissance and credential theft: protocols that carry authentication material in the clear, such as older file sharing or directory

topics.title: Non-Application Layer Protocol
topics.summary: Non-application layer protocol command and control carries attacker traffic inside protocols that sit below the application layer of the OSI model, that is, beneath HTTP, DNS and similar services. Documented examples include network layer options such as ICMP echo requests, transport layer options such as raw UDP or TCP handled directly by a socket, session layer mechanisms such as SOCKS, and tunnelled or redirected protocols such as serial over LAN. Because ICMP support is mandatory on IP hosts

topics.title: Non-Standard Port
topics.summary: Non-standard port describes command and control traffic that carries a protocol on a port number it would not normally use. The operator keeps the protocol, often TLS (Transport Layer Security), but changes the port, so the packet no longer matches the protocol and port pairing that many firewalls, proxies and parsers assume. topics.title: Obfuscated Files or Information
topics.summary: Obfuscation is the deliberate reshaping of a payload or its data so that static inspection, signatures, and content filters cannot describe it, while the code still runs as intended. Common mechanisms include compressing or encrypting a file, encoding embedded strings, splitting a payload across several innocent-looking files, and encoding the commands a scripting interpreter will later run. topics.title: Obfuscated Files or Information: Binary Padding
topics.shortTitle: Obfuscated Files or Information: Binary Padding
topics.summary: Binary padding adds generated junk bytes to an executable so its on-disk form changes while its behaviour does not. Padding is usually appended at the end of the file or inserted into existing sections, and it is often produced by a small routine rather than a fixed block. The immediate effect is a new cryptographic hash, which defeats hash-based blocklists without any change to the code that executes. A secondary effect is size: some analysis pipelines, mail gateways, and public scanning servic

topics.title: Obfuscated Files or Information: Command Obfuscation
topics.shortTitle: Obfuscated Files or Information: Command Obfuscation
topics.summary: Command obfuscation rewrites a command so that its text no longer matches known bad strings, while the interpreter still performs the original action. Because command lines are one of the richest detection sources on a host, appearing in process creation events such as Windows Security 4688 and Sysmon 1 as well as shell history and endpoint telemetry, an attacker who can change the wording of a command without changing its effect defeats signature matching and complicates triage. Common forms in

topics.title: Obfuscated Files or Information: Compile After Delivery
topics.shortTitle: Obfuscated Files or Information: Compile After Delivery
topics.summary: Compile after delivery means the payload arrives as source code or an intermediate form rather than as a finished executable, and the target system builds it before running it. Text files, scripts, and bytecode are far less likely to be flagged than a binary, because many controls and reviewers concentrate on executable formats. The build usually relies on tools already present on the host, such as the .NET compilers or the GNU compiler collection, and sometimes a compiler is bundled with the de

topics.title: Obfuscated Files or Information: Compression
topics.summary: Compression reduces the size of a payload and packs several files into one container, which gives an attacker a delivery format that antivirus engines cannot read without unpacking it first. Common choices include ZIP, gzip, 7z and RAR archives, and self extracting archives that carry their own unpacking stub, so a single double click both extracts and launches the content without asking the user for a separate action. topics.title: Obfuscated Files or Information: Dynamic API Resolution
topics.shortTitle: Obfuscated Files or Information: Dynamic API Resolution
topics.summary: Dynamic API resolution means a program does not declare the operating system functions it needs in its import table, but looks them up at runtime instead. Static review of the import address table is a cheap way to guess what a binary does, because an import of a process creation or memory writing function is revealing. topics.title: Obfuscated Files or Information: Embedded Payloads
topics.shortTitle: Obfuscated Files or Information: Embedded Payloads
topics.summary: Embedded payloads hide the real malicious content inside a second, apparently harmless file. The carrier is usually a document, script, installer or signed binary that already looks normal on the endpoint, while the code that matters sits in an overlay appended past the end of the carrier, in an unused metadata field, or nestled inside a file of the same type. topics.title: Obfuscated Files or Information: Encrypted/Encoded File
topics.shortTitle: Obfuscated Files or Information: Encrypted/Encoded File
topics.summary: Encrypting or encoding file content hides strings, byte patterns and configuration values so that signature and static analysis tools have nothing distinctive to match. The transformation may cover an entire file or only selected regions such as embedded command and control addresses, and it is frequently layered, for example a compressed archive that is also encrypted or a script whose sensitive strings are Base64 encoded. Because the protected content only becomes readable at the moment of use

topics.title: Obfuscated Files or Information: Fileless Storage
topics.shortTitle: Obfuscated Files or Information: Fileless Storage
topics.summary: Fileless storage means holding attacker data somewhere other than an ordinary file on disk, so that file scanning and integrity checking have nothing to inspect. Typical locations include the Windows Registry, the WMI repository, event logs, and memory mounted directories on Linux and network devices such as the directories for shared memory or temporary runtime data. Because these stores are built into the operating system, data placed there can survive reboots while generating no conventional

topics.title: Obfuscated Files or Information: HTML Smuggling
topics.shortTitle: Obfuscated Files or Information: HTML Smuggling
topics.summary: HTML smuggling builds the payload inside the victim's browser instead of sending it across the network as a file. The delivery page carries the harmful bytes as encoded text, commonly a base64 string inside a script, a JavaScript blob, or a data URL, and the browser turns that text back into a file-like object on the fly. Because the response is ordinary HTML and JavaScript, content filters that inspect download names, file types, or known malicious binaries have nothing to block. A download is

topics.title: Obfuscated Files or Information: Indicator Removal from Tools
topics.shortTitle: Obfuscated Files or Information: Indicator Removal from T...
topics.summary: Indicator removal from tools describes an intruder revising their own tooling after learning that a defensive product detected it. The trigger is usually feedback: a quarantined file, a blocked execution, a killed process, or simple knowledge that a target runs a particular security product. The revision is narrow and deliberate, aimed at the specific signature that fired, whether that is a unique byte string, a file hash, a tool name, or a recognised code pattern. For the defender the consequen

topics.title: Obfuscated Files or Information: Invisible Unicode
topics.shortTitle: Obfuscated Files or Information: Invisible Unicode
topics.summary: Invisible Unicode characters let an attacker put content into a file or script that a human reader cannot see. Unicode assigns a code point to every character, and some valid code points render as nothing at all: zero width spaces and joiners, variation selectors, bidirectional formatting controls, and undefined Private Use Area characters that a font draws as blank. topics.title: Obfuscated Files or Information: Junk Code Insertion
topics.shortTitle: Obfuscated Files or Information: Junk Code Insertion
topics.summary: Junk code is functional looking but unnecessary code inserted into a program to slow down analysis and to dilute the small distinctive fragments that static detection depends on. topics.title: Obfuscated Files or Information: LNK Icon Smuggling
topics.shortTitle: Obfuscated Files or Information: LNK Icon Smuggling
topics.summary: LNK icon smuggling abuses a Windows shortcut file so that a remote address rides along inside what looks like a harmless image path. A shortcut is a small metadata container with several data blocks, and one of them, the icon location block, tells Explorer where to fetch a picture to display for the file. topics.title: Obfuscated Files or Information: Polymorphic Code
topics.shortTitle: Obfuscated Files or Information: Polymorphic Code
topics.summary: Polymorphic code changes its own runtime footprint every time it executes, so the byte sequence a scanner learns from one sample does not describe the next run. Implementations range from mutation engines that rewrite instructions, reorder functions and swap equivalent instructions, to code that builds its working form at run time from an encrypted or encoded template. The functional behaviour stays the same while the representation shifts, which is precisely the weakness of hash and static sign

topics.title: Obfuscated Files or Information: Software Packing
topics.shortTitle: Obfuscated Files or Information: Software Packing
topics.summary: Software packing compresses or encrypts an executable so its real code is not readable or statically recognisable until it runs. A packer performs the transformation, and well-known examples include UPX and MPRESS, though custom packers are common because they avoid the artefacts popular tools leave behind. topics.title: Obfuscated Files or Information: Steganography
topics.summary: Steganography hides data inside another file so the carrier still looks and usually still works like an ordinary image, audio clip, video, or text document. Unlike encryption, which makes content unreadable but obvious, steganography aims to hide that anything is concealed at all, and the two are often combined so the embedded payload is also encrypted. topics.title: Obfuscated Files or Information: Stripped Payloads
topics.shortTitle: Obfuscated Files or Information: Stripped Payloads
topics.summary: Stripped payloads are executables or scripts from which the human readable scaffolding has been removed before delivery. Compilers and linkers normally leave function names, symbol tables, section headers, and debug references that tell an analyst what the code is called and how it is arranged; strip options and build flags delete that material, leaving machine instructions with almost no labels. Interpreted payloads receive the equivalent treatment when variable names are shortened and strings

topics.title: Obfuscated Files or Information: SVG Smuggling
topics.shortTitle: Obfuscated Files or Information: SVG Smuggling
topics.summary: SVG smuggling hides script inside Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) files, which are vector images written in Extensible Markup Language (XML). Because script tags are a legitimate part of the format, a crafted image can carry JavaScript that the rendering context executes, and SVG content is frequently treated as an image by mail gateways, web filters and users, so it receives less scrutiny than a script or executable. topics.title: Obtain Capabilities
topics.summary: Obtain Capabilities is the resource development behaviour of acquiring the tools of an intrusion from outside the adversary's own team, instead of building them in house. The acquisition channels are buying, downloading, and stealing. Purchases flow through criminal marketplaces, exploit brokers, malware developers, and commercial software vendors, including licences for red team frameworks. Free downloads come from open repositories and public proof-of-concept code. Theft targets capability ins

topics.title: Obtain Capabilities: Artificial Intelligence
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers an adversary using publicly accessible generative artificial intelligence tools, typically large language models, to support an operation instead of building capability in house. The model is treated as rented capability: the adversary outsources text generation, code drafting, translation, and summarisation to a service anyone can reach. topics.title: Obtain Capabilities: Code Signing Certificates
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers buying or stealing a code signing certificate, which is a certificate used to put a verifiable digital signature on software and scripts. The purpose is attribution of trust: a valid signature tells the operating system and the user that a named publisher produced the code and that nobody altered it afterwards. topics.summary: This sub-technique covers buying or stealing an SSL/TLS certificate issued by a real certificate authority, so the resulting chain of trust validates on any normal client. topics.title: Obtain Capabilities: Exploits
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers buying, downloading, or stealing exploit code instead of writing it. topics.title: Obtain Capabilities: Malware
topics.summary: This sub-technique describes acquiring malicious software rather than writing it, covering the full range of payloads, droppers, packers, backdoors, and command and control protocols. topics.title: Obtain Capabilities: Tool
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers acquiring legitimate software tools for malicious use. The defining property is intent, not capability: the software was written for administration, testing, or remote management, and the adversary simply points it at a victim. topics.title: Obtain Capabilities: Vulnerabilities
topics.summary: This sub-technique is about acquiring knowledge of a vulnerability rather than acquiring working exploit code. The object of the behaviour is information: which weakness exists, in which product and version, how severe it is, and whether a fix exists. topics.title: Office Application Startup
topics.summary: Office application startup covers the persistence mechanisms that live inside the configuration the Office suite loads when one of its programs opens. topics.title: Office Application Startup: Add-ins
topics.summary: Office add-ins are loadable components that the Office applications pull in at startup to extend their features, and because they are loaded automatically and run inside the trusted Office process, they are an attractive persistence slot for an attacker who already has write access to a user profile or the registry. topics.shortTitle: Office Application Startup: Office Template Macros
topics.summary: Office template macros is the variant of Office persistence that plants attacker code in a template file which Office loads when the application starts. Word keeps a base template in the user profile that supplies styles and settings for every new document, and Excel can load a personal workbook from a startup folder in the same way; because these files are read automatically at launch, a macro stored in one runs without any document being opened. topics.summary: Office Test is the registry based variant of Office persistence, and it works by creating a key that Office does not write during a normal installation. topics.summary: Outlook forms are the message templates that define the layout and the behaviour of items in a mailbox, and they are stored inside the mailbox itself rather than as loose files on disk. topics.shortTitle: Office Application Startup: Outlook Home Page

topics.title: Office Application Startup: Outlook Rules
topics.summary: Outlook rules are server side instructions that the mailbox applies to incoming mail automatically, such as moving a message to a folder or running a script when a message matches a condition. topics.title: OS Credential Dumping
topics.summary: OS Credential Dumping is the parent behaviour of extracting account secrets from an operating system, usually as password hashes or clear text passwords. topics.title: OS Credential Dumping: LSA Secrets
topics.summary: LSA Secrets covers credential material that Windows stores in the SECURITY registry hive for the Local Security Authority, most often passwords belonging to service accounts and scheduled tasks, plus keys used by other system components. topics.title: OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory

topics.summary: NTDS targets the Active Directory database file held on Windows domain controllers, which contains password hashes and account information for every user and computer in the domain. topics.summary: Proc Filesystem dumping uses the Linux proc pseudo-filesystem to read the virtual memory of running processes. topics.shortTitle: OS Credential Dumping: Security Account Manager
topics.summary: The Security Account Manager sub-technique targets the local account database on a Windows host, which stores password hashes for accounts that exist only on that machine, such as the built-in administrator and locally created users. topics.title: Password Policy Discovery
topics.summary: Password policy discovery is the collection of the rules that govern credentials in a network or cloud environment: minimum length, character complexity, history depth, maximum age and account lockout thresholds. topics.title: Peripheral Device Discovery
topics.summary: Peripheral device discovery is the enumeration of hardware attached to, or reachable from, a compromised host: keyboards, printers, cameras, smart card readers and removable storage. topics.summary: Local groups discovery is the narrow version of permission group enumeration: it reads only the account and group database stored on the host the attacker already controls, with no query to a central directory. topics.title: Phishing

topics.summary: Phishing for information is social engineering delivered by message, where the objective is data rather than code execution. topics.summary: Voice phishing replaces the written message with a phone call. topics.summary: Spearphishing Voice, usually called vishing, uses a telephone call or voice message instead of email to move a person into an action that grants access. topics.summary: Property list files, usually called plists, are the key-value configuration files that macOS and its applications read at runtime. topics.title: Query Public AI Services
topics.summary: Query public AI services covers using hosted artificial intelligence tools, particularly large language models, as an analysis layer on top of public information. Where classic open source research means reading pages and databases by hand, this technique uses a model to synthesise, aggregate and summarise material at scale, and to turn scattered facts into a usable picture. topics.title: Query Registry
topics.summary: Query registry is the reading of the Windows registry to learn how a host is built, configured and protected. The registry holds operating system settings, installed software, security policy, service configuration and traces of past user activity, so a handful of reads answers questions that would otherwise need many separate commands. topics.title: Reflective Code Loading
topics.summary: Reflective code loading places executable content directly into the memory of an already running process instead of writing a file to disk and starting it as a normal thread or shared library. The payload may be a compiled binary, an anonymous file that exists only in RAM, or position-independent shellcode. topics.title: Remote Access Tools
topics.summary: Remote access tools are legitimate products that create an interactive session between two hosts, and they span a wide range of shapes: graphical desktop support suites, command-line remote management agents, protocol tunnels provided by development or management software, and hardware devices that present keyboard, video and mouse over the network. topics.title: Remote Access Tools: IDE Tunneling
topics.summary: IDE tunneling is the narrow case of the remote access parent where the channel is provided by an integrated development environment. Modern editors bundle secure shell connectivity, port forwarding, file synchronisation and remote debugging into one session, and several of them also ship a command-line tunnel command that registers the machine with the vendor's relay and returns a public web address for it. topics.title: Remote Access Tools: Remote Access Hardware
topics.shortTitle: Remote Access Tools: Remote Access Hardware
topics.summary: Remote access hardware covers small physical devices that sit between a computer's keyboard, video and mouse connections and provide a network-accessible session, with IP-based keyboard, video and mouse appliances such as TinyPilot and PiKVM as the typical examples. Unlike the other remote access branches, nothing needs to run on the target operating system. topics.title: Remote Access Tools: Remote Desktop Software
topics.shortTitle: Remote Access Tools: Remote Desktop Software
topics.summary: This sub-technique is the graphical branch of remote access: desktop support and remote monitoring and management software that carries screen output, keyboard input and mouse control between two machines. Well-known examples include VNC, TeamViewer, AnyDesk, ScreenConnect and LogMeIn, along with the remote control modules that ship inside products you would not normally classify as remote access, such as video meeting clients and browser-based remote desktop features. topics.title: Remote Service Session Hijacking
topics.summary: Remote service session hijacking is lateral movement that takes over a session which is already open instead of creating a new one. When a user logs into a remote service such as Secure Shell (SSH), Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP), or telnet, the service creates a session object that represents that authenticated interaction, and the session carries the user's identity and permissions for as long as it lives.
