topics.title: Remote Service Session Hijacking: RDP Hijacking
topics.shortTitle: Remote Service Session Hijacking: RDP Hijacking
topics.summary: Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) hijacking takes over a remote desktop session that already exists on a Windows host. Remote Desktop Services keeps each interactive session addressable by a numeric session identifier, and an account whose context has System level privileges can reconnect an existing session to a different connection without presenting that user's credentials and without generating a prompt. topics.title: Remote Service Session Hijacking: SSH Hijacking
topics.shortTitle: Remote Service Session Hijacking: SSH Hijacking
topics.summary: Secure Shell (SSH) hijacking attacks the trust that public key authentication creates between machines. When a user connects with key based authentication, an agent process holds the private key in memory and signs authentication requests on the user's behalf, and the resulting session on the remote host keeps that authenticated identity for as long as it stays open. topics.title: Remote Services
topics.summary: Remote services is the use of legitimate remote access protocols and their native authentication to log on to another host and act there, rather than exploiting a vulnerability to gain a foothold. The technique exploits trust that already exists: domain credentials, SSH keys, administrative shares or a management plane that accepts connections from an internal network segment. topics.title: Remote Services: Cloud Services
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers using valid, synchronised, or federated identities to sign in to a cloud control plane rather than to a server on the corporate network. Because the same directory account may be federated to the provider, an intruder who steals one set of credentials can authenticate to the web console, the command line interface, or the provider's API, then manage resources, read storage, or create new identities. topics.title: Remote Services: Direct Cloud VM Connections
topics.shortTitle: Remote Services: Direct Cloud VM Connections
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers logging straight into a cloud-hosted virtual machine through the provider's own console or connection service, instead of running scripts through the cloud API. Providers offer serial console access, instance connection helpers, and session managers that place an operator at a virtual keyboard or an equivalent shell. Authentication may use a password, a Secure Shell key, or an application token, and these paths often land with root or system level rights because they we

topics.title: Remote Services: Distributed Component Object Model
topics.shortTitle: Remote Services: Distributed Component Object Model
topics.summary: Distributed Component Object Model is the remote extension of the Windows Component Object Model, and this sub-technique covers its use with valid accounts to act on another host. Component Object Model lets a client object call methods on a server object, which is typically a dynamic link library or an executable; the distributed form adds a remote procedure call transport so those calls cross the network. Permissions to activate and launch objects remotely are held in registry access control l

topics.title: Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
topics.summary: Remote Desktop Protocol is a Microsoft protocol that provides graphical remote access to a Windows session, and it is one of the most common lateral movement mechanisms because it is enabled by default on many server builds and requires only valid credentials and reachable network access. An adversary who has obtained credentials or a session token can authenticate to a target host, interact with the desktop as the compromised identity, and from that host repeat the process toward further system

topics.title: Remote Services: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
topics.summary: SMB and Windows administrative shares provide file and named pipe access over the Server Message Block protocol, and the administrative shares that exist on Windows systems by default can be used both to move files to a remote host and to request remote execution of a service or scheduled task. An adversary with administrative credentials can copy a payload to a target, then trigger execution through a remote service control or task scheduling interface, and finally clean up the staged file. topics.title: Remote Services: SSH
topics.summary: Secure Shell is the standard encrypted remote login and command execution protocol on Unix-like systems, and it is also widely enabled on network devices, hypervisors, and appliances. It supports interactive sessions, single command execution, port forwarding, and agent-based authentication, all of which an adversary can use after obtaining valid credentials or private keys. Lateral movement commonly begins from a host the adversary already controls, using either a stolen key or a replayed passw

topics.title: Remote Services: VNC
topics.summary: VNC, or Virtual Network Computing, is a screen-sharing service that relays a remote computer's display, mouse, and keyboard over the network using the RFB protocol. Unlike Remote Desktop Protocol, which shares a whole session and its resources, VNC mirrors the existing console, so a remote operator sees and acts as whoever is already logged on. An intruder holding valid credentials can therefore open documents, pull files, run commands, and pivot to further hosts. Defenders spot it through inbou

topics.title: Remote Services: Windows Remote Management
topics.summary: Windows Remote Management, usually shortened to WinRM, is Microsoft's implementation of the WS-Management protocol. It lets an operator run commands, read the registry, or change services on a remote host, and it normally listens on TCP 5985 for HTTP and 5986 for HTTPS. It can be reached with the winrm command, PowerShell remoting, or tooling that drives Windows Management Instrumentation over it. topics.title: Remote System Discovery
topics.summary: Remote system discovery is the mapping of hosts, addresses and services reachable from a compromised position, producing the target list that later lateral movement and exploitation depend on. The mechanism varies with access level. From an endpoint, an adversary can use address resolution and name resolution traffic, broadcast name service queries, connection attempts to common ports, and management interfaces that enumerate peers. From a domain joined host, directory and network browsing inter

topics.title: Replication Through Removable Media
topics.summary: Replication through removable media moves code onto new systems by writing malicious files to USB flash drives, external disks, memory cards or mobile devices and relying on the media being inserted somewhere else. Attackers either drop an executable with a convincing document-like name or icon and wait for a curious user, or they replace an existing file on the drive so an authorised operator carries the payload across a boundary. Older systems may still honour Autorun or Autoplay entries that

topics.title: Resource Hijacking
topics.summary: Resource hijacking converts a victim estate into a source of profit. The attacker does not steal data so much as rent out capacity that belongs to someone else: processor and graphics cycles for cryptocurrency mining, network bandwidth resold through residential proxy networks, or messaging and cloud service quotas used to send bulk spam or generate paid traffic. The operations are economically motivated, so persistence and quiet operation matter more than speed, and the tell is usually a resour

topics.title: Resource Hijacking: Bandwidth Hijacking
topics.summary: Bandwidth hijacking turns a compromised endpoint into a network resource that the adversary sells or spends elsewhere. The implant does not need to steal files; it only needs outbound capacity, so the visible effect is sustained egress traffic that competes with legitimate business flows and with the connection limits of local networking equipment. topics.title: Resource Hijacking: Cloud Service Hijacking
topics.summary: Cloud service hijacking is resource theft performed through software as a service rather than through malware on a host. After gaining access to a company's cloud tenant, an adversary reuses the platform's own capabilities: messaging and email APIs such as AWS SES, SNS, SendGrid, or Twilio become a bulk spam and phishing delivery engine, and hosted artificial intelligence services are reached through reverse proxies so the victim account pays for model inference. Where the abused service is part

topics.title: Resource Hijacking: Compute Hijacking
topics.summary: Compute hijacking is the processing power branch of resource hijacking. The attacker installs code that consumes processor or graphics cycles for their own benefit, most often to mine cryptocurrency, and it runs alongside legitimate workloads until saturation degrades service. Servers and cloud instances are favourite targets because they are powerful and lightly watched, while containers are attractive because a stolen interface credential lets an attacker start many short lived workers at once

topics.title: Resource Hijacking: SMS Pumping
topics.summary: SMS pumping is telecommunications fraud that abuses a victim's messaging spend rather than the victim's computers. The adversary first acquires blocks of phone numbers from carriers on revenue-sharing ranges, then drives the victim's messaging infrastructure to send large volumes of messages at those numbers, collecting a share of the carrier payout. The preferred entry point is any publicly reachable form that triggers a message, such as one-time password delivery or account verification, usual

topics.title: Rogue Domain Controller
topics.summary: A rogue domain controller is a machine that an adversary registers in Active Directory so that it appears to be a legitimate replica of the domain directory. The machine is added by creating new server and directory service agent objects in the Configuration partition of the directory schema, which requires domain administrator rights, local administrator rights on a controller, or the KRBTGT password hash. topics.title: Rootkit
topics.summary: A rootkit is software whose main purpose is concealment: it intercepts or modifies the operating system calls that report system state, so tools asking about files, processes, services, drivers, network connections or registry keys receive a filtered answer. The hiding logic can live in user space through library or application programming interface hooks, in kernel space through drivers or kernel modules, in a hypervisor beneath the operating system, or in system firmware and boot code. topics.title: Safe Mode Boot
topics.summary: Safe mode starts Windows with a minimal driver and service set, and many third party endpoint agents are configured not to load in that state, so rebooting a host into safe mode is an effective way to run without them. topics.title: Scheduled Task/Job
topics.summary: Scheduled task abuse is the practice of registering work with the operating system's own scheduler so that attacker code runs at a chosen time, at start-up, or repeatedly without further interaction. Every mainstream platform ships such a service: the Windows Task Scheduler driven by schtasks, the task XML store and the Task Scheduler service; the cron daemon on Unix-like systems reading per-user crontab files and system directories; systemd timers on modern Linux; and orchestration job objects

topics.title: Scheduled Task/Job: At
topics.summary: This sub-technique is scheduled execution through the at command, the queue-based scheduler that predates richer job systems on Windows, Linux and macOS. Its character is one-shot: a job is queued for a specific clock time or a delay, runs once, and then is gone, which makes it attractive when an operator wants execution at an inconvenient hour without leaving a permanent entry. topics.title: Scheduled Task/Job: Container Orchestration Job
topics.summary: This sub-technique is scheduled execution inside a container orchestration platform, where the scheduler is an object in the cluster's own database rather than a file on one host. In Kubernetes an operator writes a CronJob, which the controller turns into Job objects on a timetable, and each Job creates one or more pods that the scheduler places on nodes; a workload object with a replica count can also be used to keep a chosen number of containers running indefinitely. The effect is persistence

topics.title: Scheduled Task/Job: Cron
topics.summary: This sub-technique is persistence and recurring execution through cron, the long-standing time-based scheduler on Unix-like systems. An operator adds an entry to a crontab whose five leading fields describe minute, hour, day of month, month and day of week, followed by the command to run; a short form can also express intervals, and a keyword can replace the fields entirely with a named period such as a reboot. topics.title: Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task
topics.summary: This sub-technique is abuse of the Windows Task Scheduler, the richest of the platform schedulers and the one with the most ways to reach it. A task can be registered from the command line with schtasks, through the graphical Task Scheduler console, through a scripting wrapper around the scheduling interfaces, or through remote procedure calls that allow a privileged account on another host to register work without logging on interactively. topics.title: Scheduled Task/Job: Systemd Timers
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers recurring execution through systemd timers, the modern alternative to cron on Linux distributions that use systemd as their service manager. A timer is a unit file whose name ends in .timer, and it does not contain the command itself: it activates a service unit of the same base name, so a unit pair of a timer and a service is really two files, often installed together by whoever wants the work to run. topics.title: Scheduled Transfer
topics.summary: Scheduled transfer is the timing half of exfiltration: rather than dumping data the moment it is collected, the adversary constrains when traffic leaves so that the pattern of activity resembles something the environment already produces. Two variants are common. Time of day scheduling places transfers inside busy business hours, where they hide among ordinary cloud and backup traffic, or deliberately inside quiet windows such as nights and weekends when analyst coverage is thin. topics.title: Screen Capture
topics.summary: Screen capture takes images of what is displayed on a compromised desktop, giving an adversary a view of information that may never be written to a file or a log. Capability comes either from the remote access tool the attacker already runs or from native interfaces and utilities, such as the Windows graphics copy routine, the X window dump tool on Linux, or the screenshot utility on macOS. topics.title: Search Closed Sources
topics.summary: Closed sources are information collections that are not freely available: commercial threat intelligence subscriptions, paid data aggregation services, and criminal marketplaces. An adversary uses them because the same facts that help a defender also help an attacker, and because the material is often more current or more specific than anything published openly. Purchases of leaked credential sets, employee contact lists, and infrastructure detail are the typical goods. The activity happens off

topics.title: Search Closed Sources: Purchase Technical Data
topics.shortTitle: Search Closed Sources: Purchase Technical Data
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers buying technical facts about a specific target rather than reading analysis about a sector. The goods are concrete: employee contact lists, credential dumps taken from unrelated breaches, network diagrams, remote access details, and scan output for a chosen address range. Sellers range from legitimate paid aggregation services to criminal marketplaces that specialise in stolen data. The purchase happens outside the victim estate, so the trails are payment records, marke

topics.title: Search Closed Sources: Threat Intel Vendors
topics.shortTitle: Search Closed Sources: Threat Intel Vendors
topics.summary: Commercial threat intelligence vendors publish paid reports, indicator feeds, and customer portals. The material is written for defenders, so it describes which industries are currently targeted, which tradecraft succeeds, and which countermeasures the vendor observed defeating it. An adversary who obtains access learns the same lessons, and because the reports are dated and tied to real incidents, they also show which sectors are under active focus. topics.title: Search Open Technical Databases
topics.summary: Rather than sending a single packet, this technique consults third party collections of technical facts about the victim: domain registration records, certificate transparency logs, historical and passive domain name system records, routing data, internet wide scan datasets and internet of things search services. topics.title: Search Open Technical Databases: CDNs
topics.summary: A content delivery network keeps copies of a site's content on many edge servers and answers each request from the location nearest the user. That arrangement hides the origin server address, but it also creates a second copy of the site on infrastructure the organisation does not fully control. An adversary studies the delivery network by resolving host names, reading response headers, and testing whether the origin address still accepts direct connections that skip the delivery layer. Typical

topics.title: Search Open Technical Databases: Digital Certificates
topics.shortTitle: Search Open Technical Databases: Digital Certificates
topics.summary: The Transport Layer Security certificate that a service presents is public by design, and since certificate transparency logs became standard for publicly trusted authorities, every issued certificate is recorded in append-only logs that anyone can query. Each entry carries the subject organisation, the common name, often a list of extra hostnames in the subject alternative name field, plus validity dates and the issuing authority. topics.title: Search Open Technical Databases: DNS/Passive DNS
topics.shortTitle: Search Open Technical Databases: DNS/Passive DNS
topics.summary: This sub-technique is reconnaissance through the domain name system, either by querying a target's authoritative servers directly or by reading passive collections that record historical query and response pairs observed around the internet. Direct queries against records for mail, text verification, service and name server entries expose which third parties handle mail and identity, where services are hosted, and which subdomains exist. topics.title: Search Open Technical Databases: Scan Databases
topics.shortTitle: Search Open Technical Databases: Scan Databases
topics.summary: Internet-wide scanning services probe the routable address space on a schedule and publish the results as a searchable database. A typical record holds the address, the port, the service banner, the certificate offered, and sometimes a screenshot of the login page. An adversary queries those databases by organisation name, address block, or product string, so they can find exposed services without sending a single packet to the victim. topics.title: Search Open Technical Databases: WHOIS
topics.summary: WHOIS is a public lookup service operated by registrars and the regional internet registries that allocate domain names and address blocks. A query returns the registration record for a domain or an address range: the registrant organisation, contact details, name servers, registrar identity, and creation and expiry dates. topics.title: Search Open Websites/Domains
topics.summary: This technique describes open source collection from public websites and domains, where the adversary never touches victim infrastructure. Social profiles, press releases, tender portals, conference agendas, support forums and job adverts are mined for organisational structure, technology choices, supplier relationships and named staff. The output feeds later stages: a believable pretext for phishing, a target list for account creation, or a supplier relationship worth abusing for trusted access

topics.title: Search Open Websites/Domains: Code Repositories
topics.summary: This sub-technique is public source code discovery, where adversaries mine hosted repositories for what a victim's engineering culture and history reveal. Useful material includes programming languages and frameworks in use, third party dependencies with known flaws, internal hostnames and service names appearing in configuration samples, contributor names and email addresses, and secrets committed by accident such as application programming interface tokens or database connection strings. topics.title: Search Open Websites/Domains: Search Engines
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers the use of search engine indexing and advanced query syntax to find victim information that was published but never meant to be found. Adversaries combine ordinary keyword searches with operators that restrict results by site, file type or URL pattern, which surfaces exposed directories, configuration backups, log files, spreadsheet exports and administrative pages that were left reachable. topics.title: Search Open Websites/Domains: Social Media
topics.summary: This sub-technique narrows open website collection to social platforms, where employees describe their employer, tools, projects and daily frustrations in their own words. Adversaries passively harvest this material to build target lists with real names, job titles and reporting lines, then move to active variants such as fake recruiter profiles or interest groups that convince a target to volunteer further detail. topics.title: Search Threat Vendor Data
topics.summary: Search threat vendor data describes adversaries reading the reporting written about them. Instead of gathering information about a victim, the actor studies threat intelligence publications, vendor blogs, indicator feeds and incident write-ups that describe their own campaigns or those of groups working the same industries. topics.title: Search Victim-Owned Websites
topics.summary: This technique covers reconnaissance against websites the victim owns, from the home page and staff directory through to support portals and legacy subsites. The target is content that the organisation published deliberately, such as department names, physical sites, named employees with contact details, and partner relationships that hint at who holds trusted access. topics.title: Selective Exclusion
topics.summary: Selective exclusion is the deliberate choice to leave parts of a system untouched while damaging the rest. In a ransomware context the actor avoids file types such as libraries, executables and shortcuts, and steers clear of directories and components whose corruption would immediately destabilise the host. topics.title: Server Software Component
topics.summary: Server Software Component describes persistence achieved by abusing the extension mechanisms that enterprise servers deliberately provide for developers and administrators. Web servers, mail servers, database engines, and hypervisors all accept third-party plug-ins, modules, filters, or stored code so that organisations can add features without rebuilding the product. topics.title: Server Software Component: IIS Components
topics.summary: IIS Components is the Windows web server branch of Server Software Component persistence. Internet Information Services supports three extension surfaces: ISAPI extensions, which handle requests mapped to them; ISAPI filters, which observe or alter every request and response passing through the worker process; and IIS modules, introduced with IIS 7.0, which are native dynamic link libraries that register themselves or managed code that hooks the request pipeline. topics.title: Server Software Component: SQL Stored Procedures
topics.shortTitle: Server Software Component: SQL Stored Procedures
topics.summary: SQL Stored Procedures is the database form of persistence under the Server Software Component parent. A stored procedure is a named block of database code that users call by name, and database engines store these blocks inside system catalog tables. Because the engine loads and runs them on request, a procedure that an administrator does not expect becomes durable code execution inside the database service. topics.title: Server Software Component: Terminal Services DLL
topics.shortTitle: Server Software Component: Terminal Services DLL
topics.summary: Terminal Services DLL persistence abuses the service loader on Windows hosts that accept Remote Desktop connections. Services that run inside a shared generic host process are configured by a ServiceDll value in the Registry, which names the library the host loads on behalf of the service. For Terminal Services, now also called Remote Desktop Services, that value normally points to termsrv.dll in the system directory. topics.title: Server Software Component: Transport Agent
topics.summary: Transport Agent persistence targets Microsoft Exchange mail flow. Exchange lets developers write compiled transport agents that the server invokes at defined stages of the transport pipeline, the code path every message follows on its way to a mailbox. Legitimate agents perform filtering, journaling, attachment handling, or signature stamping. topics.title: Server Software Component: vSphere Installation Bundles
topics.shortTitle: Server Software Component: vSphere Installation Bundles
topics.summary: vSphere Installation Bundles are the package format VMware uses to add or update software on ESXi hypervisors. A bundle contains a compressed payload archive that places files on the host, an XML descriptor that names the bundle and its dependencies, and a signature that determines the host acceptance level, the trust threshold that ESXi enforces before installation. topics.title: Server Software Component: Web Shell
topics.summary: A web shell is a server-side script planted in a web-accessible location so that ordinary HTTP requests become a remote control channel. The adversary typically arrives through a vulnerable web application, a file upload feature, or stolen administrative access, then writes a small script in the language the server already executes, such as PHP, ASP, ASP.NET, or Java. topics.title: Serverless Execution
topics.summary: Serverless execution describes abuse of cloud functions, workflow automation, and integration services to run attacker controlled code without managing a server. The code is submitted as a function, an automation flow, or a script inside a cloud office suite, and the provider runs it on demand. topics.title: Service Stop
topics.summary: Service stop is the deliberate shutdown or disabling of a service or process so that the function it provides becomes unavailable. Attackers use it for three related reasons: to interrupt incident response by taking security and monitoring agents offline, to free locked data stores so they can be encrypted or overwritten, and purely to deny a business function such as mail or database access. topics.title: Shared Modules
topics.summary: Shared modules are reusable executable libraries that a process loads at run time: dynamic link libraries on Windows, and shared objects or dynamic libraries on Linux and macOS. The technique covers the use of that loading mechanism to bring attacker code into a process, either to add functionality to malware or to have a legitimate process load a library the adversary supplied. topics.title: Social Engineering
topics.summary: Social Engineering is the use of persuasion, trust building, and emotional pressure to make a person perform an action that grants access, approves a change, discloses information, or runs adversary-supplied instructions. The defining property is that the adversary seeks a legitimate user action instead of a technical flaw, so the resulting authentication and approval events look authorised in most audit data. topics.title: Social Engineering: Email Spoofing
topics.summary: Email Spoofing is the header-manipulation form of Social Engineering, in which the adversary falsifies sender fields so that mail appears to originate from a domain the sender does not control. Unlike general impersonation, which may rely on a lookalike address or a compromised mailbox, spoofing forges the envelope and From values themselves, and it succeeds wherever domain authentication is missing or unenforced. topics.title: Social Engineering: Impersonation
topics.summary: Impersonation is the identity layer of Social Engineering: the adversary adopts the identity of a trusted person or organisation so that a request is judged against the wrong actor. Typical cases are an executive, a colleague, or a third-party vendor whose mailbox is either spoofed or genuinely compromised, which is why attacker-sent mail can arrive from a real, previously reputable address with valid authentication results. topics.title: Software Deployment Tools
topics.summary: Software deployment tools are the enterprise's own remote execution machinery, and an intruder who obtains the right account inherits it. topics.title: Software Discovery
topics.summary: Software Discovery is the reconnaissance step in which an adversary builds an inventory of installed applications and their versions on hosts or in cloud tenants. The value is decision support: knowing which endpoint agent is present tells the attacker what to avoid, and knowing which product and patch level is installed tells them whether a local privilege escalation or remote exploit is worth trying. topics.summary: Backup Software Discovery is a targeted form of software enumeration aimed at the tools and configurations an organisation relies on to recover data. The adversary wants to know whether backups exist, where they are stored, whether they are currently reachable, and which product manages them, because that determines how much damage a destructive or encrypting payload can do. Typical products of interest include enterprise backup suites and popular consumer and small business tools, and enumerati

topics.title: Software Discovery: Security Software Discovery
topics.summary: Security Software Discovery narrows the discovery phase to defensive tooling: endpoint protection, endpoint detection and response agents, host firewalls, logging shippers, and cloud monitoring agents such as provider-native metric and log collectors. The adversary wants to know what can see them and what cannot, so they enumerate installed products, running services, driver names, registry keys, and configuration files. topics.title: Software Extensions
topics.summary: Software extensions are the modular add-on components that browsers, code editors, chat clients and similar platforms load to gain extra features, and they matter to attackers because the host application loads them automatically and hands them a share of its own permissions. The parent technique covers the whole family; the abuse can be split into three behaviours. The first is installation by deception, where a fake or typosquatted extension in a public marketplace convinces a user to add it.

topics.title: Software Extensions: Browser Extensions
topics.summary: Browser extensions are small programs loaded into the browser itself, and they are the most common member of the software extension family because they follow the browser everywhere, including onto personal and unmanaged machines. What makes the sub-technique distinct is the reach of the host: an extension added to a browser profile can read and modify pages the user visits, reach stored cookies and saved form data, observe downloads and, with the right permission, talk to any address on the net

topics.title: Software Extensions: IDE Extensions
topics.summary: Integrated development environment extensions are plugins that add features to a code editor or full development suite, and they deserve their own entry because the host grants them a different and in some ways richer level of access than a browser does. topics.title: Stage Capabilities
topics.summary: Stage Capabilities covers the adversary work that happens before an intrusion, when tools, payloads and supporting services are placed on infrastructure from which they can later be used. The capabilities are usually ones the adversary either built or bought, and the hosting is usually either rented, compromised or borrowed from a legitimate web service, which is what makes this activity hard to attribute and hard to remove. Typical staging includes web content prepared for a drive by compromise

topics.title: Stage Capabilities: Drive-by Target
topics.summary: Before a drive by compromise can occur, the adversary prepares the web content that will run in a visitor's browser. This sub technique covers writing or buying the exploit and the profiling script, then placing that content on a site the intended target is likely to visit, whether the site is attacker owned or a legitimate site that has been compromised. Typical placements include injecting script tags into content management system templates, replacing JavaScript files served from a publicly w

topics.title: Stage Capabilities: Install Digital Certificate
topics.summary: Adversaries install TLS certificates on infrastructure they control so that command and control traffic is encrypted and credential harvesting pages appear trustworthy. A certificate binds a public key to a host name and carries a signature from a certificate authority, so any client that trusts that signer will complete an encrypted session without complaint. Attackers either obtain a publicly trusted certificate through ordinary, largely automated registration flows, or generate a self signed

topics.title: Stage Capabilities: Link Target
topics.summary: This sub technique covers preparing the destination that a phishing link points to. The resource is usually a web page hosted on attacker controlled or compromised infrastructure, and it commonly clones the login page of a mail provider, a virtual private network portal, or a single sign on service so harvested credentials are typed into a convincing form. The page may include client side script that decides what each visitor sees, redirecting security scanners and automated crawlers away from t

topics.title: Stage Capabilities: SEO Poisoning
topics.summary: SEO poisoning is the deliberate manipulation of search ranking signals so that attacker controlled pages appear above legitimate results for terms the target is likely to search. Search engines rank pages using crawler derived signals such as keyword relevance, inbound links, page age, and click behaviour, and each of those signals can be gamed. Adversaries stuff keywords, including hidden text a visitor never sees, into compromised sites, plant or purchase inbound links, and run cloaking logic

topics.title: Stage Capabilities: Upload Malware
topics.summary: Upload Malware is the sub-technique of Stage Capabilities in which the adversary places malicious files on infrastructure so they are reachable later, either by the victim or by their own tooling. The uploaded content is broad: first stage payloads, droppers, loaders, full backdoors, post compromise utilities and, increasingly, backdoored legitimate software. Common destinations are adversary controlled or previously compromised servers, free code hosting and paste services, decentralised file s

topics.title: Stage Capabilities: Upload Tool
topics.summary: Adversaries stage tooling on infrastructure they control or have compromised so it can be pulled down later, mid intrusion, without ever touching the target beforehand. Unlike malware, these are legitimate utilities that keep their original file names and vendor signatures, which is exactly why they survive reputation checks. The upload usually travels over ordinary web protocols to a rented virtual private server, a hijacked content management system, a public code repository, or a platform as

topics.title: Steal Application Access Token
topics.summary: Steal Application Access Token targets the bearer credentials that services use to call each other. An access token is presented instead of a password, so whoever holds the string is treated as the application or service account until the token expires. Theft therefore often needs no cracking and no interactive login, which is why it is prized in cloud, container, and software-as-a-service environments. Collection points include container file systems that mount service account tokens for Kubern

topics.title: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
topics.summary: Certificates are not only for signing and encryption; when a certificate authority issues one that maps to a user or machine identity, that certificate becomes a credential. An adversary can take it in several ways. A stolen certificate may be pulled from encrypted storage in the registry, from a certificate file left in the wrong place, or directly from the Windows certificate store through crypto interfaces. Where enrolment rights allow it, an attacker with a foothold can also request a certif

topics.title: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
topics.summary: Kerberos is the default authentication protocol in Windows domains, and it issues tickets instead of sending a password each time. A client authenticates to the Key Distribution Center (KDC) on a domain controller and receives a ticket-granting ticket (TGT), then presents that TGT to request ticket-granting service (TGS) tickets, also called service tickets, for individual services. An attacker who steals a ticket can present it without knowing the password, which is the basis of pass-the-ticket

topics.title: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: AS-REP Roasting
topics.shortTitle: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: AS-REP Roasting
topics.summary: AS-REP Roasting targets accounts that have Kerberos preauthentication disabled. Normally a client sends an Authentication Server Request (AS-REQ) holding a timestamp encrypted with the user's password hash; only a client that knows the password can produce it, and the domain controller answers with an Authentication Server Response (AS-REP) whose encrypted part is protected by the account key. topics.title: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Ccache Files
topics.shortTitle: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Ccache Files
topics.summary: Credential cache files store Kerberos tickets on disk for systems that do not keep them in a Windows style cache, and they are the Unix counterpart to the ticket material attackers dump from Windows memory. On Linux the file is usually named after the user identifier in a temporary directory, its location is chosen by the KRB5CCNAME environment variable or the Kerberos configuration file, and it is created at authentication and removed at logout. On macOS the cache is normally held in memory and

topics.title: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Golden Ticket
topics.shortTitle: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Golden Ticket
topics.summary: A golden ticket is a forged ticket-granting ticket (TGT) created with the password hash of the KRBTGT account, the domain account that the Key Distribution Center (KDC) uses to encrypt and sign Kerberos tickets. Because every domain controller trusts that key, a ticket signed with it is accepted as genuine, and the attacker can place any username, any group membership and a long lifetime inside it, including an identity that does not exist. Unlike a silver ticket, the attacker still talks to the

topics.title: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberoasting
topics.shortTitle: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Kerberoasting
topics.summary: Kerberoasting abuses the way Kerberos issues service tickets. Any authenticated domain user may ask the Key Distribution Center (KDC) for a ticket-granting service (TGS) ticket that matches a registered service principal name (SPN), and part of the returned ticket is encrypted with the long-term key of the account running that service. An attacker holding any valid account, or captured Kerberos traffic, collects those tickets and takes the encrypted part away to crack offline, without touching t

topics.title: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Silver Ticket
topics.shortTitle: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets: Silver Ticket
topics.summary: A silver ticket is a forged ticket-granting service (TGS) ticket, also called a service ticket, created with the password hash of the account that runs a specific service. The ticket is encrypted with that service account key, so the service receiving it can validate it without asking the Key Distribution Center (KDC) for confirmation. topics.title: Steal Web Session Cookie
topics.summary: Steal Web Session Cookie targets the bearer token that web services issue after a successful login. Once a browser or an application holds a valid session cookie, the server treats any request carrying it as already authenticated, so possession of the cookie is enough to act as that user without a password and often without a second factor, which is checked only at the moment of login. Cookies can be taken from several places: browser profile storage and its local database, process memory while

topics.title: Subvert Trust Controls
topics.summary: Subvert Trust Controls covers the family of behaviours that weaken or remove the signals an operating system uses to decide whether code, a driver or a website deserves trust. These signals are the ones a user actually sees: a signature that validates, a warning that a file came from the internet, a browser refusal to continue to an unknown certificate authority. An adversary can attack the check rather than the code, by altering the settings that store trust decisions, changing the permissions

topics.title: Subvert Trust Controls: Code Signing
topics.summary: Code signing binds a binary to a verified publisher identity and guarantees the file has not been altered since it was signed. This sub-technique covers the theft, purchase or creation of signing material so the payload carries a signature that validates correctly, which separates it from the invalid-signature case where the check fails and leaves a visible artefact. Threat actors have taken certificates from compromised build systems, bought them from issuers using shell companies, and abused s

topics.title: Subvert Trust Controls: Code Signing Policy Modification
topics.shortTitle: Subvert Trust Controls: Code Signing Policy Modification
topics.summary: Rather than forging a signature, this sub-technique disables the rule that demands one. On Windows that means turning on test signing so drivers only need a test certificate, or relaxing the driver signature enforcement state; on macOS it means disabling System Integrity Protection, which protects system files and the signing rules that apply to them. topics.title: Subvert Trust Controls: Gatekeeper Bypass
topics.summary: Gatekeeper is the macOS layer that decides whether a downloaded application may run, and it works with File Quarantine: the downloading application sets the com.apple.quarantine extended attribute, Launch Services starts the program suspended, and Gatekeeper then checks the quarantine flag, the system security policy, the code signature and the notarisation ticket before releasing it. topics.title: Subvert Trust Controls: Install Root Certificate
topics.shortTitle: Subvert Trust Controls: Install Root Certificate
topics.summary: Operating systems and browsers decide whether to trust a secure connection by walking a certificate chain up to a root certificate held in a local trust store. This sub-technique covers the installation of an adversary-controlled root certificate into that store, which turns the insertion into a lasting capability: every certificate signed by that root is accepted without warning, so spoofed websites load cleanly and encrypted traffic can be intercepted. Historic campaigns combined the technique

topics.title: Subvert Trust Controls: Mark-of-the-Web Bypass
topics.summary: Windows marks files that arrive from the internet with a hidden stream named Zone.Identifier, and that mark, the Mark-of-the-Web, drives several protective behaviours: Office documents open in Protected View, script hosts refuse or warn, and executables are checked against SmartScreen reputation before running. topics.title: Subvert Trust Controls: SIP and Trust Provider Hijacking
topics.shortTitle: Subvert Trust Controls: SIP and Trust Provider Hijacking
topics.summary: On Windows, Authenticode signature checking runs through the WinVerifyTrust interface, which delegates the actual work to Subject Interface Packages, known as SIPs. Each SIP understands one file format, such as portable executables, PowerShell scripts or installers, and each is registered under a globally unique identifier with a dynamic link library and an entry point function that performs the verification. topics.title: Supply Chain Compromise
topics.summary: Supply chain compromise is the parent category for attacks that modify a product or the way it is delivered before the final consumer receives it, which moves the point of failure away from the victim entirely. topics.title: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Hardware Supply Chain
topics.shortTitle: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Hardware Supply Chain
topics.summary: Hardware supply chain compromise means an adversary alters a device, or the firmware that runs on it, before the buyer ever takes delivery. The tampering is performed at a manufacturer, an integrator, a reseller, a warehouse or a courier, so the product arrives with its packaging intact and its documentation correct. Because the implant lives below the operating system, in boot firmware, a baseboard management controller, a network interface or an added component, reinstalling the operating syst

topics.title: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Dependencies and Development Tools
topics.shortTitle: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Dependencies...
topics.summary: This sub-technique narrows supply chain compromise to the building blocks developers pull in rather than the finished product they ship. The shared code that arrives from a package registry is the first target, because a single poisoned library or a typosquatted package name can be pulled into thousands of downstream applications by a routine dependency update. topics.title: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain
topics.shortTitle: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers tampering with finished application software between the moment it is completed and the moment a consumer receives it, which distinguishes it from interference with the dependencies and tools used to build it. Three behaviours sit under it. topics.title: System Binary Proxy Execution
topics.summary: System binary proxy execution covers the family of behaviours in which an adversary achieves code execution by handing work to a binary that is already present on the host and usually signed by the platform vendor. The signed image passes signature validation and often application control policies, while the actual payload is a script, library, installer package or remote object that the trusted binary loads on the attacker's behalf. topics.title: System Binary Proxy Execution: CMSTP
topics.summary: CMSTP.exe, the Microsoft Connection Manager Profile Installer, is a command-line program that installs Connection Manager service profiles used for remote access connections, and it takes an installation information file, an INF, as its input. topics.title: System Binary Proxy Execution: Compiled HTML File
topics.shortTitle: System Binary Proxy Execution: Compiled HTML File
topics.summary: Compiled HTML Help files, which carry the .chm extension, are compressed archives holding HTML pages, images and scripting content. Windows renders them through hh.exe, the HTML Help executable, using underlying Internet Explorer components, so script inside a CHM runs with the privileges of the user who opened it and outside the browser's own security context. topics.title: System Binary Proxy Execution: Control Panel
topics.shortTitle: System Binary Proxy Execution: Control Panel
topics.summary: Control Panel items are the settings applets users open through control.exe, and they exist as registered executable files or as .cpl files, which are dynamic-link libraries renamed and required to export a CPlApplet function. An adversary abuses this hosting model in two ways. topics.title: System Binary Proxy Execution: Electron Applications
topics.shortTitle: System Binary Proxy Execution: Electron Applications
topics.summary: Electron is a framework that builds desktop applications from web technology: a Chromium engine renders the interface while a Node.js runtime executes backend logic, and many everyday chat and collaboration clients such as Signal, Slack and Teams are built on it. topics.title: System Binary Proxy Execution: InstallUtil
topics.summary: InstallUtil.exe is a command-line utility shipped with the .NET Framework that installs and uninstalls server resources by executing installer components contained in managed assemblies. topics.title: System Binary Proxy Execution: Mavinject
topics.summary: Mavinject is the Microsoft Application Virtualization Injector, a signed Microsoft utility whose legitimate job is to load virtual application packages into a running process. Because it performs process injection by design, an adversary can point it at a target process identifier and a dynamic-link library path so that the library executes inside that process rather than as a new child process. topics.title: System Binary Proxy Execution: MMC
topics.summary: The Microsoft Management Console is a signed Windows host process that loads administrative user-interface modules called snap-ins, described by console files with the .msc extension. The straightforward abuse is argument-level: passing a built-in console such as the backup console with a silent or non-int

topics.title: System Binary Proxy Execution: Mshta
topics.summary: Mshta.exe is the Windows utility that runs Microsoft HTML Applications, known as HTAs, which are standalone programs built from HTML, JavaScript or VBScript and executed through Internet Explorer components but outside the browser window. topics.title: System Binary Proxy Execution: Msiexec
topics.summary: Msiexec.exe is the command-line host for the Windows Installer service, signed by Microsoft and present on every Windows installation, and it executes installation packages with the .msi extension from local or network locations. topics.title: System Binary Proxy Execution: Odbcconf

topics.title: System Binary Proxy Execution: Regsvcs/Regasm
topics.summary: Regsvcs.exe and Regasm.exe are .NET Framework command-line utilities that register managed assemblies so that they can be consumed as Component Object Model components, with Regasm targeting the assembly registration path and Regsvcs handling services installation for COM+ applications. topics.title: System Binary Proxy Execution: Regsvr32

topics.title: System Binary Proxy Execution: Rundll32
topics.summary: Rundll32.exe loads a dynamic-link library and calls a named exported function inside it, doing so without registering anything, which distinguishes it from the registration utilities in the same technique family. topics.title: System Binary Proxy Execution: Verclsid
topics.summary: Verclsid.exe is the Extension CLSID Verification Host, a signed Windows binary whose role is to verify a shell extension before Windows Explorer or the shell loads it for use. topics.title: System Information Discovery
topics.summary: System Information Discovery is the collection of host-level detail such as operating system name and version, build, patch and hotfix level, hardware architecture, hostname, and domain membership. An adversary uses that detail to decide whether a foothold is worth keeping and which later technique will work against it, so the behaviour typically appears very early and often as one burst of commands from a single process. On network devices the same result comes from the vendor command interface

topics.title: System Location Discovery
topics.summary: System location discovery is the collection of clues that indicate where a victim host physically sits. Adversaries use time zone, keyboard layout, and language or locale settings to place a machine in a country or region, and in cloud environments they may read instance metadata to learn the availability zone. topics.title: System Location Discovery: System Language Discovery
topics.shortTitle: System Location Discovery: System Language Discovery
topics.summary: This sub technique narrows location discovery to the language and locale settings of a host. Malware and operators read those values to decide whether a machine is worth infecting, often to avoid systems in countries where law enforcement attention or prosecution is more likely. topics.title: System Network Configuration Discovery
topics.summary: System network configuration discovery covers the commands and calls used to learn how a host is addressed and connected: its network addresses, subnet masks, default gateway, routing table, name resolution settings, neighbour or address cache entries and interface details. topics.shortTitle: System Network Configuration Discovery: Internet Connecti...

topics.shortTitle: System Network Configuration Discovery: Wi-Fi Discovery

topics.title: System Network Connections Discovery
topics.summary: System network connections discovery is the step in which an adversary reads the local connection tables and session state of a host to learn what it is talking to and who is using it. topics.title: System Owner/User Discovery
topics.summary: System owner and user discovery is the reconnaissance step that answers who is behind the keyboard and which accounts matter on a host. topics.title: System Script Proxy Execution
topics.summary: System script proxy execution is the abuse of a trusted, usually Microsoft signed, script that already exists on a host so that it runs an adversary's file or code on their behalf. topics.title: System Service Discovery

topics.title: System Services
topics.summary: System Services covers execution that goes through the operating system's service or daemon manager rather than a user starting a program directly. topics.title: System Services: Launchctl

topics.title: System Shutdown/Reboot
topics.summary: System Shutdown/Reboot covers deliberate attempts to power down or restart a host so that access to it is interrupted or a destructive change takes effect. topics.title: System Time Discovery
topics.summary: System time discovery is the reading of a host clock, time zone or uptime, either locally or across the network. Accurate time is rarely the objective by itself: it lets an adversary schedule a task for a quiet hour, align beacon sleep intervals, timestamp staged files, or judge whether a sandbox has been running long enough to look like a real workstation. topics.title: Taint Shared Content
topics.summary: Taint Shared Content covers any attempt to place malicious code inside a shared location so that another user runs it, including network drives, collaboration sites, and internal code repositories. The adversary rarely attacks a machine directly. Instead they append or prepend code to a legitimate binary and redirect its entry point, plant a document that carries a script, or replace a folder with a shortcut file that hides the payload and then opens the real folder so the user's expected action

topics.title: Template Injection
topics.summary: Template injection abuses the document properties that tell an office application where to fetch shared resources. Modern Office files are ZIP containers of XML parts, and one part may hold a template reference, a pointer to a formatted blueprint that the application retrieves when the document is opened. Because that pointer is just data inside the package, an adversary can repoint it at a server they control, so the payload is not stored in the document at all and only arrives at open time. St

topics.title: Traffic Signaling
topics.summary: Traffic signaling is a covert trigger mechanism: malicious code or a planted device stays inert until it sees a specific value or a specific sequence in network traffic, then enables a service, starts a task, or replies on a port. The signal can be a series of connection attempts, a packet with unusual flags, a distinctive string inside a protocol field, a particular source address, or an unusual timing pattern, which means the trigger lives in traffic rather than in a file, a registry key, or a

topics.title: Traffic Signaling: Port Knocking
topics.summary: Port knocking is the best known form of traffic signaling: the trigger is a predefined order of connection attempts to ports that are closed and therefore look unremarkable in a scan. The parent technique covers any magic value or packet characteristic; this sub-technique narrows it to the sequence of destination ports, optionally with a source, timing or protocol condition attached. topics.title: Traffic Signaling: Socket Filters
topics.summary: Socket filters let an implant stay passive until one specific packet arrives, so the host opens no listening port and sends no traffic while it waits. With elevated rights an adversary attaches a filter to a network socket, using the libpcap library or the SO_ATTACH_FILTER socket option, and the operating system evaluates every incoming frame against that rule set in kernel space. A match then triggers a host action, such as starting a reverse shell or pulling down an implant. Detection is hard

topics.title: Transfer Data to Cloud Account
topics.summary: Transfer Data to Cloud Account is exfiltration that stays inside the provider network: instead of pushing stolen data out to an external destination, the attacker copies, shares or syncs it into a second cloud account under their control on the same service. Because the traffic never crosses the organisation's internet boundary, network based monitoring for large outbound transfers or command and control channels can miss it entirely, and the transfers may even use internal provider addressing a

topics.title: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution
topics.summary: Trusted developer utilities proxy execution is the use of legitimate, usually signed, build and debugging tools to run code that the adversary supplies. Because the tool is trusted by the operating system and often already permitted by application control policy, the payload executes inside a process that defenders treat as normal. MSBuild, ClickOnce deployment and the JamPlus build utility are the documented examples, but the pattern extends to any developer tool that compiles, loads or interpr

topics.title: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution: ClickOnce
topics.shortTitle: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution: ClickOnce
topics.summary: ClickOnce is a Microsoft deployment technology for self-updating Windows applications built on the .NET platform, which install and run from a web page or a file share with minimal user interaction. This sub-technique covers its abuse as an execution proxy. An .appref-ms or .application file points at a deployment manifest, and the signed DFSVC.EXE component installs and launches the application as its child process. Because ClickOnce applications request only limited permissions, no administrat

topics.title: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution: JamPlus
topics.shortTitle: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution: JamPlus
topics.summary: JamPlus is a build utility from the Jam family that reads a .jam file describing what to build and which dependencies it needs, and it supports well known compilers and can generate workspaces for editors such as Visual Studio. This sub-technique covers its abuse as an execution proxy. A .jam file can carry commands alongside the build description, so a reputable signed developer binary performs the adversary's actions as child processes. The behaviour sits alongside the MSBuild case but is rare

topics.title: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution: MSBuild
topics.shortTitle: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution: MSBuild
topics.summary: MSBuild is the Microsoft Build Engine, a signed Microsoft executable that reads XML project files and builds the platforms and configurations they describe. This sub-technique covers its use as an execution proxy rather than as a build tool. The central abuse is the inline task, a .NET feature that allows C sharp or Visual Basic code to be written directly inside the project file; MSBuild compiles that code in memory and runs it, so no payload binary is written to disk for a scanner to find. Bec

topics.title: Trusted Relationship
topics.summary: Trusted relationship abuse means an adversary enters through a third party that already holds legitimate access to the target, rather than attacking the target's own perimeter. Managed service providers, IT contractors, cloud resellers and infrastructure vendors are typically given remote management channels, service accounts, or delegated administrative roles, and that access is often excluded from the strictest controls because it is needed for support work. Compromising the provider, or simpl

topics.title: Unsecured Credentials
topics.summary: This parent technique covers credential collection that requires no memory access and no cryptographic attack, because the secret was simply left readable. Adversaries enumerate a compromised host for the places administrators and applications habitually store secrets: plaintext notes and configuration files, script and command history, registry values, unprotected private keys, and cloud metadata endpoints. In each case the credential is available to a process that only needs read access, and o

topics.title: Unsecured Credentials: Chat Messages
topics.summary: Chat and collaboration platforms are a routine channel for sharing working credentials. Engineers paste database passwords, API keys and access tokens into direct messages, team channels, incident threads and ticket comments, where the material persists in the platform's history and search index. Rather than hunting files on disk, an adversary with access to a user endpoint, an administrator portal or an integration token can query the service directly for keywords such as password, key or token

topics.title: Unsecured Credentials: Cloud Instance Metadata API
topics.shortTitle: Unsecured Credentials: Cloud Instance Metadata API
topics.summary: This sub-technique is credential collection from the cloud instance metadata service, a link local endpoint that cloud providers expose so a virtual machine can learn about itself. The service is reachable without credentials from inside the instance and commonly returns instance identity details, network configuration, attached role names, and the temporary credentials that go with those roles. Many providers also return the user data script supplied at launch, which frequently contains secrets

topics.title: Unsecured Credentials: Container API
topics.summary: Container platforms expose management interfaces, such as the Docker remote API and the Kubernetes API server, that can return far more than workload status. An adversary who reaches an unauthenticated or loosely authorised endpoint can list containers, read their environment variables, pull application logs and inspect mounted secrets, all of which frequently contain registry passwords, cloud access keys and database connection strings. topics.title: Unsecured Credentials: Credentials In Files
topics.summary: This sub-technique narrows the parent to secrets held in files, which is the broadest case because it includes user-created notes, shared team credential stores, application configuration, source code and binaries with embedded passwords, and the copies inside backups and saved virtual machine images. topics.title: Unsecured Credentials: Credentials in Registry
topics.summary: This sub-technique is credential collection from the Windows registry, which stores configuration for the operating system and for applications, including settings that hold passwords in readable form. Typical targets are autologon values, which retain a default logon name and password so a machine signs in without interaction, and application keys that cache service or database credentials. The access pattern is a broad keyword search rather than a targeted read, because the adversary does not

topics.title: Unsecured Credentials: Group Policy Preferences
topics.summary: Group Policy Preferences allow administrators to push settings, including local account passwords, to domain computers. When such a password is configured, Windows stores it in XML files under the SYSVOL share of a domain controller, protected only by an AES key that Microsoft published in its own documentation years ago. topics.title: Unsecured Credentials: Private Keys
topics.summary: This sub-technique is credential collection aimed at private cryptographic keys, which differs from the rest of the parent because the stolen object is an authentication factor in its own right rather than a text password. A private key proves identity for remote shell access, decrypts collected files, and signs authentication assertions, so theft survives password resets for every system that trusts the matching public key. The search is extension and directory driven, since keys live in predic

topics.title: Unsecured Credentials: Shell History
topics.summary: This sub-technique is credential collection from command history, which shells write to disk so a user can review or repeat earlier input. On Linux and macOS the history file for the interactive shell, such as the bash or zsh history in the user's home directory, is flushed when the session ends and by default retains a limited number of recent commands. topics.title: Unused/Unsupported Cloud Regions
topics.summary: Unused/Unsupported Cloud Regions is defence evasion through placement: the attacker creates or moves workload into a geographic region that the victim subscribes to but never operates in, so the activity falls outside the monitoring the organisation actually watches. topics.title: Use Alternate Authentication Material
topics.summary: This is a parent technique covering lateral movement that reuses material a system generated after a successful login instead of replaying a password. The material takes three main forms: NTLM password hashes, Kerberos tickets, and OAuth or API access tokens. Each is created precisely so the user is not asked for credentials again, which means each is stored on disk or held in memory where credential access tooling can lift it. topics.title: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token
topics.shortTitle: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access...
topics.summary: This sub-technique covers lateral movement and resource access performed with a stolen application access token rather than a password. Tokens are issued by authorisation frameworks such as OAuth after a consent step, and they authorise API calls on behalf of a user or service without the caller ever handling the underlying credential. topics.title: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash
topics.shortTitle: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash
topics.summary: This sub-technique is authentication replayed with a stolen NTLM password hash instead of the plaintext password. The Windows challenge and response logon path accepts a correctly computed response to a server challenge, and the hash is all the client needs to compute it, so an attacker holding a hash authenticates without cracking it. topics.title: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Ticket
topics.shortTitle: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Ticket
topics.summary: This sub-technique is lateral movement performed by importing a stolen Kerberos ticket rather than typing a password. Tickets are the domain's normal proof of identity: a ticket granting ticket is presented to the key distribution centre to obtain service tickets, and a service ticket is presented directly to one resource. topics.title: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Web Session Cookie
topics.shortTitle: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Web Session Cookie
topics.summary: This sub-technique is session hijacking performed by replaying a stolen web session cookie instead of authenticating. After a successful login, a web application issues a session identifier and treats any request carrying it as the authenticated user, which is why the technique bypasses the second factor: the verification already happened and is not repeated. topics.title: User Execution
topics.summary: User Execution describes adversary reliance on a person to take an action that results in code running or a security decision being made in the attacker interest. It is the human step that completes many delivery chains: opening an attachment, enabling macros or add-ins, clicking through a security warning, running a downloaded installer, mounting a disk image, pasting and executing a copied command, or approving a fraudulent push notification. The technique appears wherever an adversary cannot

topics.title: User Execution: Malicious Copy and Paste
topics.shortTitle: User Execution: Malicious Copy and Paste
topics.summary: Malicious copy and paste is the sub-technique where the victim personally runs the adversary's command, having been told that it is a fix. The published pattern, often called ClickFix, is a web page or document that shows a fake error, a failed download or a verification prompt, then instructs the visitor to open a terminal or the Windows Run dialog and paste a line of text to resolve it. topics.title: User Execution: Malicious File
topics.summary: Malicious file is the sub-technique where the adversary needs the victim to open a file, rather than click a link. The parent technique covers both cases; here the payload or the trigger travels as an object. topics.title: User Execution: Malicious Image
topics.summary: Malicious image is the sub-technique in which the adversary relies on the victim deploying a prepared machine image or container image. The other sub-techniques need a click or an install; this one needs a deployment decision. A backdoored image can be published to a public registry or marketplace, given a name that closely matches a popular or official one, and then pulled by a developer or an automation pipeline that believes it is starting from a trusted base. topics.title: User Execution: Malicious Library
topics.summary: Malicious library is the sub-technique where execution happens because a user or a build pipeline installs a software package that is hostile. The parent technique covers user driven execution generally; here the payload arrives inside a dependency. topics.title: User Execution: Malicious Link
topics.summary: Malicious link is the sub-technique of user execution in which the adversary depends on the victim clicking a hyperlink rather than opening a file. The link itself is not the payload; it is a pointer, which is why filtering must judge a destination rather than an attachment. topics.title: Valid Accounts
topics.summary: Valid Accounts describes adversary use of legitimate credentials or existing accounts to gain and keep access rather than exploiting a software flaw. The accounts involved may be default or built-in accounts shipped with an operating system, application or appliance, local or domain accounts whose passwords were obtained earlier in an intrusion, or cloud, SaaS and federated identities issued to real users or service principals. The technique is attractive precisely because the resulting activity

topics.title: Valid Accounts: Cloud Accounts
topics.summary: Cloud accounts are identities created inside a cloud service provider or a software-as-a-service product, and they may be cloud-only, synchronised from an on-premises directory, or federated through a single sign-on trust. Because one identity often reaches both worlds, a stolen token or password can pivot from the cloud back into on-premises systems, for example through a software deployment tool that runs commands on hybrid-joined devices. topics.title: Valid Accounts: Default Accounts
topics.summary: Default accounts are the credentials a system, appliance, or service ships with before an administrator changes anything. They include built-in operating system logins such as Guest or Administrator, provider root users in cloud and hypervisor platforms, and vendor support or service accounts created by integration. Because these identities already exist and are frequently privileged, an adversary who finds one still carrying its factory password gains access without exploiting any software flaw

topics.title: Valid Accounts: Domain Accounts
topics.summary: Domain accounts are identities held in a central directory such as Active Directory, where access and permissions are configured once and applied across every system joined to that domain. They cover ordinary users, administrators, and service identities, so a single compromised credential can be replayed against mail, file shares, and remote desktop services on many hosts. topics.title: Valid Accounts: Local Accounts
topics.summary: A local account lives on one machine only and is defined in that host's own account database, so its permissions stop at that system. Organisations create them for users, remote support, services, and emergency administration, and because machines are frequently built from one image, the same local password can exist across an entire fleet. Adversaries abuse them in two ways: signing in locally after learning the password, or reusing that one password to move from host to host. A local administr

topics.title: Video Capture
topics.summary: Video capture is the recording of images or video through a built in camera, an attached webcam, or a video calling application. The adversary uses the same media interfaces that legitimate software uses, so the collected material may be a clip, a burst of still frames taken at intervals, or a single snapshot. topics.title: Virtual Machine Discovery
topics.summary: Virtual machine discovery is enumeration performed at the virtualisation layer rather than inside a guest. An actor who reaches a hypervisor or its management plane lists the guests the host runs, using the hypervisor command line, the management interface, or provider APIs. topics.title: Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion
topics.summary: Virtualization and sandbox evasion is the adversarial practice of first deciding whether the current host is a real user machine or an analysis environment, and only then choosing how to behave. topics.title: Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion: System Checks
topics.summary: System checks are the branch of sandbox evasion that inspects machine properties instead of human behaviour. topics.title: Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion: Time Based Checks
topics.summary: Time based checks use the clock to decide whether the host is real. Rather than reading hardware or watching the user, the sample measures how time behaves around its own execution, sampling the system clock or an uptime counter before and after a delay and comparing the observed interval with the interval it requested. topics.title: Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion: User Activity Based Checks
topics.shortTitle: Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion: User Activity Based Checks
topics.summary: User activity based checks are the branch of evasion that looks for evidence a real person is using the host, rather than evidence about the hardware. The sample inspects inputs and leftovers that accumulate on a genuine workstation: mouse movement and click frequency, browser history, cache and bookmarks, the number of files in a home directory or on the desktop, recently used documents, and whether applications are running with real session state. topics.title: Weaken Encryption
topics.summary: Weaken Encryption describes adversary activity against the encryption a network device performs on traffic that passes through it, rather than against encryption on a host. Routers, switches and firewalls commonly terminate site to site tunnels and virtual private network sessions, so their cryptographic configuration is a high value target. topics.title: Weaken Encryption: Disable Crypto Hardware
topics.summary: Disable Crypto Hardware is the sub-technique of Weaken Encryption in which the adversary turns off or bypasses the dedicated encryption processor inside a network device and forces encryption onto general purpose CPUs running software. Devices such as routers, switches, firewalls and virtual private network concentrators carry specialised chips so that bulk encryption keeps up with line rate and so that keys and intermediate values stay out of ordinary memory where they could be manipulated. topics.title: Weaken Encryption: Reduce Key Space
topics.summary: Reduce Key Space is the sub-technique of Weaken Encryption in which the adversary lowers the number of possible values a cryptographic key can take, so that recovering plaintext from captured traffic becomes cheap. Encryption strength scales with key length: each additional bit roughly doubles the search effort an attacker without the key must spend. topics.title: Web Service
topics.summary: Web service abuse is command and control that rides on legitimate public platforms rather than attacker-owned servers. The implant talks to a well-known provider, for example a cloud storage or productivity application programming interface, a social network, a paste site or a webmail draft folder, and both tasking and stolen data are stored or exchanged through that service. topics.title: Web Service: Bidirectional Communication
topics.summary: Bidirectional communication over a legitimate web service turns a public platform into a full command channel in both directions. The implant reads tasking that the adversary has placed on the service, for example a comment, a chat message, a document or a repository entry, and then writes command output back to the same service, often as another comment, an updated file or a new repository object. topics.title: Web Service: Dead Drop Resolver
topics.summary: A dead drop resolver hides the true command and control address behind content that an adversary posts on a legitimate public service, such as a social media profile, a paste site or a code repository. The implant does not carry the address of its handler. Instead it retrieves a page or record, decodes an embedded or obfuscated string, and only then contacts the real server. topics.title: Web Service: One-Way Communication
topics.summary: One way communication uses a public web service to deliver tasking without returning results over that same channel. The implant periodically fetches content from the platform and treats it as instructions, but the command output either travels over a separate channel, such as a different service or the original payload channel, or is not sent at all because the adversary only needs to push a command. topics.title: Wi-Fi Networks
topics.summary: This technique covers gaining a first foothold by joining a wireless network, either an open network that a target device also uses or a secured corporate network reached with valid credentials. The defining constraint is physics: the actor must be close enough to the access point to associate and to keep a stable link, which makes this a close access technique rather than a remote one. topics.title: Windows Management Instrumentation
topics.summary: Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) is the management data and operations layer built into Windows, exposing a uniform interface that administrators and software can use to query system state and invoke methods. topics.title: XSL Script Processing
